docs.title: Agentic Software Engineering: Build, Verify, Evaluate
docs.text:
Agents generate. You verify, decide and explain.

Over twelve teaching weeks and an assessment week you learn to deliver changes in a real codebase with a coding agent, confirm that the agent got them right, and explain and modify your own work without an agent. The course is taught in English.

Read the syllabus How this course works Start with Week 0

docs.title: How this course works
docs.text:
• Generate, then verify

    Every example shows both steps. A check you can rerun is evidence; an agent saying "done" is a claim.

  • Predict before you look

    Each class opens with a decision you can get wrong. Save your prediction, run a check that tells the answers apart, then revise.

  • Decide, don't regenerate

    When a candidate passes, accept it, narrow the task, recheck something specific or stop.

  • Explain it without the agent

    Two checkpoints and a project defense, 30 of 100 marks, are done without AI.

docs.title: Three lines of work
docs.text:
Six assignments, mostly in the first six weeks; four contributions to two real open-source repositories; and one term project, alone or in a pair, on a topic you choose.

Weeks Topics 1-4 Agent internals, context engineering, skills, and customizing your agent and repository 5-8 Agent-ready codebases, agentic code review, tests that notice a fault, security 9-12 Background agents, evaluating agents, AI-native teams, the software factory 13 Project expo and individual defenses

docs.title: Agentic Software Engineering: Build, Verify, Evaluate
docs.text:
English is the first teaching language. By the end of the course you can deliver changes in a real codebase with a coding agent, confirm that the agent got them right, and explain and modify your own work without an agent.

The course follows the public Fall 2026 calendar of Stanford CS146S in its topics, their order and the position of its deadlines, and adds three things: two weeks on verification (weeks 7 and 10), a project defense, and one decision line at the end of every assignment (accept, narrow, recheck or stop) with the evidence behind it. That course's assignment repository carries no licence, so only its public structure is followed: every assignment, lecture note and rubric here is written for this course, and no text is copied.

Course pages, lecture materials and rubrics are being rearranged to this calendar. Where another page still describes the earlier fourteen-week layout, this syllabus takes precedence.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Audience and prerequisites: senior undergraduates and taught master's students in computing or software engineering, with programming, data structures, Git and testing. No experience with AI coding tools is assumed.
  • Length: 12 teaching weeks, then an assessment week (expo and defenses) in week 13.
  • Two sessions a week: the first is a lecture that generates and then verifies, live. The second is a practitioner guest; in a week without a guest it is a studio, where you work on your own project or contribution while staff circulate. Each session is 90 minutes; the plan is one cohort of 60 students.
  • Three lines of work: six assignments (mostly in the first six weeks), four open-source contributions (across two repositories), and one term project (one or two people).

docs.title: How the course is designed
docs.text:
1. Verification first: every example shows both the generating step and the verifying step. No lecture shows "let the agent finish it".
  2. Individual AI-off evidence is a pass condition: two in-class checkpoints and the defense carry 30 marks, and a student below half of them does not pass.
  3. Marked on engineering evidence: the project and the contributions are marked on the specification, instruction file, gates, tests, evaluation and your own verification, not on how the interface looks or how many features there are.
  4. Contributions do not depend on luck: a mark never depends on whether a maintainer replies; where a repository has no partner contact, a teaching assistant gives an acceptance review.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• LO1: Explain a coding agent's loop, system prompt and tool definitions, and predict how it fails on context, tools and stopping.
  • LO2: Design an agent development workflow: context and specifications, MCP tools, skills, instruction files, hooks, subagents and background tasks.
  • LO3: Write a requirement as a specification an agent can implement and a test can check, and revise it when new evidence arrives.
  • LO4: Make an unfamiliar real codebase agent-ready, and deliver a change in it without breaking callers.
  • LO5: Verify agent-written code with regression and mutation tests, code review, static analysis and security scanning, and defend each acceptance.
  • LO6: Evaluate agents: check that a test can fail, that the denominator is complete and that a judge is reliable, and read small-sample results correctly.
  • LO7: Recognise and mitigate agent security risks (prompt injection, credentials, supply chain), verifying a defense with a local reproduction and a regression.
  • LO8: Describe how a team operates agents (portals, gateways, routing, cost), and how to recover from an incident and prove the recovery with a regression.
  • LO9: Collaborate responsibly: follow upstream rules, disclose AI use honestly, submit no low-effort generated work, and decide again when the inputs change.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Component Marks When AI Term project: four milestones 20 Weeks 2, 4, 7 and 12 allowed Project defense 15 Week 13 off Four open-source contributions 30 Weeks 4, 8, 9 and 12 allowed Six assignments 15 Weeks 1-3, 5, 6 and 10 allowed CP1: AI-off diagnosis, test and repair 7.5 Week 6 off CP2: AI-off review of unfamiliar code and recovery reasoning 7.5 Week 11 off Participation: guest questions, studio, expo 5 All term —

Passing requires at least 60/100 overall and at least 15/30 across CP1, CP2 and the defense. There are no bonus marks. An assessment not yet taken stays missing; it is not scored as zero.

For each of CP1, CP2 and the defense, a student who first scores below half may take one equivalent resit with the same learning outcomes, duration and difficulty after feedback. The effective mark is the higher of the two, and a resit can replace the original with at most half of the item's maximum. Both the original record and the resit record are kept. A sitting that was validly passed cannot be retaken to raise the mark. A sitting voided by a technical failure or an approved accommodation is replaced by an equivalent sitting and does not use up the resit.

docs.title: Assignments
docs.text:
Six assignments are worth 2.5 marks each. Each one hands in the work, the verification result and a short explanation, and ends with one decision line and the evidence behind it. Note your AI use once. Assignments are marked on completion and evidence; there are no hidden tests.

Assignment Week What you do LO A1 1 Capture one real coding-agent session with a forced failure; label each behaviour as observed or inferred. LO1 A2 2 Build a small MCP tool server; graded on whether a model can pick the right tool, call it correctly and recover. No third-party sign-in is required. LO2 A3 3 Write one skill for a workflow you first ran by hand; test that it triggers on the right requests and stays quiet on a near miss. LO2 A4 5 Make a messy repository agent-ready: instruction file, a hook that blocks a bad commit, structure and checks. LO2, LO4 A5 6 Score a repository's agent readiness with observable anchors and report what would change the score. LO4, LO5 A6 10 Audit one evaluation instance and its scorer; state what the results do and do not support. LO6

docs.title: Term project
docs.text:
One or two people, on a topic of your choice: build working software from scratch with agents. A two-person project has a correspondingly larger scope, and the two defenses are separate.

Milestone Week Content Marks Proposal 2 What it is, who it is for, the core scenario, and the agent's role in development. 2 Technical specification 4 A design document: requirements, key decisions with a rejected alternative each, interfaces and data models, test strategy, what is out of scope. 4 Alpha and task backlog 7 One minimal path that runs end to end; the repository already has an instruction file and one hook gate; a backlog of remaining tasks. 6 Final 12 Working software; tests with their mutation result; one evaluation script; the disposition of a security scan; a README. 8 Defense 13 Fifteen minutes each, no devices: the examiner changes one thing or plants one fault in your own code, and you locate it, explain it and decide what to do. 15

Marks go to engineering evidence only. Any topic is allowed, but a project with an interface and features and no specification, gate, tests or evaluation earns no milestone marks. The two members of a pair share the marks for the proposal, specification, alpha and final; the defense is marked individually. The expo is held in week 13 before the defenses and counts towards participation.

docs.title: Open-source contributions
docs.text:
Contribution Week Repository Marks 1 4 First 5 2 8 First 10 3 9 Second 5 4 12 Second 10
  • Small, then substantial: the first contribution in each repository is a small onboarding fix (5 marks); the second is a substantive change (10 marks).
  • Two repositories: you rank your preferences in week 2 and the teaching team assigns your first repository; after contribution 2 you move to a second one. The point is to onboard onto two different real codebases.
  • Project list: public open-source projects that partner companies maintain or depend on come first, with other active projects added. A project qualifies with an OSI licence, contribution guidelines, an AI-use policy that permits the work, and no CLA that assigns copyright. At most five students work on one repository at a time. You do not make a marked contribution to a repository owned by your own residency employer. The number of partner repositories and maintainer contacts is not yet confirmed.
  • Completion: in a repository with a partner contact, a merged pull request meets the completion condition. Where there is no contact, or a maintainer has not replied within seven days, a teaching assistant gives an acceptance review against the project's own contribution guidelines instead.
  • Quality line: low-effort AI output scores zero; the maintainer or the teaching assistant decides. Each contribution needs a check that fails before the change and passes after it, and your own answers to what changed, why, which inputs could break it, and what you verified yourself.
  • Boundaries and rights: contribute to public repositories only. Residency, employer or partner-internal code never enters the course or a model. You may use a pseudonym where the project permits it. If you will not publish, or will not sign a CLA or DCO, you may take the course-hosted equivalent route without giving a reason, with the same rubric and maximum.

docs.title: Workload and participation
docs.text:
There is no hour budget. Weekly time estimates are published after a timed human pilot and include out-of-class cost honestly; required content is not cut to fit a total.

The second session each week is offered to a practitioner for at most 45 minutes, invited for that week's topic, with no product pitch and with sources for any numbers. Write one question beforehand. The course runs with however many guests can come; the number is not yet confirmed. Participation marks cover guest questions, studio work and the expo.

docs.title: Privacy, fairness and accessibility
docs.text: Course repositories, prompts, session records and marking material carry no real credentials and no unrelated personal data. Submit only the smallest process record that shows your work, redacted first. Required materials and activities have keyboard-operable, captioned or text alternatives, and you may ask for equivalent time or an equivalent way of taking part; an accommodation keeps the same learning outcomes and the same attainable marks. Oral defenses use a shared rubric and comparable answering time, and a second calibrated marker reviews cases near a threshold, cases where markers disagree and cases a student asks to have reviewed. Course data is not used for teaching research; any later use needs ethics approval and your separate consent first.

docs.title: Tools and model access
docs.text:
• Coding agent: you use a mature coding agent directly. The course states the capabilities it needs (instruction files, hooks, a permission mode, MCP, subagents, a readable session record) and names no vendor.
  • Seats and credit: every student has a working agent seat or credit when teaching starts, at no cost to the student. Teaching credit from partners or providers is used first, and the course budget buys the rest; how much partners provide is not yet confirmed.
  • Safety: run the agent in a dedicated directory or container; keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment; keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs; run the injection demonstration offline against the local machine only. The Week 0 setup page explains each practice and how to check it.
  • Other tools: pytest, one mutation-testing tool and one property-testing library, Semgrep, gitleaks, pip-audit.

docs.title: AI use and responsibility
docs.text: The checkpoints and the defense are done alone. All other work may use an agent, noted once in the work. Authorship is never inferred from writing style; contradictory evidence goes to a human process.

docs.title: Check your starting point
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

These twenty course-authored questions cover Python, Git, testing and HTTP. Questions, answers and explanations are public student assets. This diagnostic is practice feedback, not a quiz bank, admission decision or official course grade. It has no pass threshold. Try it without AI first so the result helps you choose what to review; checking the public answers afterward is encouraged. No personal information is needed.

Use the Week 0 launcher setup. Copy this directory's public files into a separate workspace. In that sandbox, python run.py prints questions; python run.py --show-answers also explains the answers. Record your choices in a JSON object such as {"P1": "C", "G1": "C"}. Omit unanswered questions.

Run python run.py --answers answers.json through the same launcher to receive a deterministic JSON result. Incorrect and omitted answers receive no correct-answer point; each question counts once. Unknown IDs, duplicate IDs and values outside A-D fail input validation. The script reads data and never executes submitted code. Answers shipped with the questions make this unsuitable for summative grading.

Read the explanation for each missed question. Explain one correction in your own words and try that concept on a small example through the launcher. Bring the topic and safe error category to course support if still stuck. This fits within the Week 0 time budget; it does not create another scored submission or a requirement to export a conversation.

docs.title: Open-source contributions
docs.text:
Make four contributions across two repositories, worth 30 marks in total. In each repository, start with a small onboarding fix, then make a substantive change. Move to the second repository after contribution 2. You practise entering unfamiliar codebases, verifying changes, and following their contribution rules (LO4, LO5, LO7, LO9).

Contribution Due Repository Scope Marks 1 Week 4 First Small, complete onboarding fix 5 2 Week 8 First Substantive change 10 3 Week 9 Second Small, complete onboarding fix 5 4 Week 12 Second Substantive change 10

Deadlines are Sunday at 23:59 in the due week. A small fix might repair a defect, test or documentation example. A substantive change solves a larger problem with a bounded scope and verifiable acceptance cases. Read the repository's rules before proposing work.

docs.title: Find a repository and submit your preferences
docs.text:
In week 2, rank your preferences on the volunteer form. The teaching team assigns the first repository and arranges the move to a different repository after contribution 2. At most five students work on a repository at one time.

The list prioritizes public open-source projects maintained or used by partners, with other active projects added. Every listed repository needs an OSI-approved licence, contribution guidelines, an AI-use policy that permits the planned work, and no CLA that assigns copyright. You may propose another repository for approval against these conditions. Do not start counted work there before approval.

The teaching team checks these conditions, records whether there is a partner maintainer contact, and publishes the list and allocation instructions. Contacts are not invented: the list records only people who have actually agreed to act as contacts.

Where to find or send things Publication or action Approved repositories and contribution-guide links The teaching team publishes the approved public repository list before Week 2. Partner maintainer contact for each repository, or no contact The teaching team confirms each partner maintainer contact, or records that there is none, before Week 2. Week 2 preferences and volunteering The teaching team publishes the volunteer form and allocation channel before Week 2 preferences are due. A repository or issue you propose; a scope change The teaching team publishes the approval channel before students propose a repository, issue or scope change. Four submissions and requests for TA acceptance review The teaching team publishes the submission channel and TA review-request route before the first contribution deadline. Pseudonymous account or course-hosted equivalent The teaching team publishes the private identity and equivalent-route channel before the first contribution is submitted.

Do not make a marked contribution to a repository owned by your own residency employer. Tell the teaching team privately if an allocation would cross that boundary so it can assign a different repository.

docs.title: Make and verify each change
docs.text:
1. Read and discuss. Read the licence, contribution guide, AI rules and relevant issue. Follow the project's process for agreeing the scope before starting unwanted work.
  2. Reproduce. Record the starting revision and a check that fails for the issue you intend to fix. For documentation, use an executable example or a repeatable check of the documented behaviour. Agree an appropriate check with a TA if necessary.
  3. Generate and inspect. Use the permitted assistance to make a small change. Inspect the diff and affected callers yourself; do not submit unexamined generated output.
  4. Verify. Run the check again and the relevant existing tests. Preserve the result that fails before the change and passes after it, with revisions and commands.
  5. Submit and respond. Follow the upstream PR, sign-off and disclosure process. Respond to review, verify revisions, and record what you changed or why the evidence supports retaining a decision.

For each contribution submit the issue and PR links, the submitted revision, the before and after verification results, and a brief explanation answering these four questions:

  • What changed?
  • Why was that change needed?
  • Which inputs or conditions could break it?
  • What did you personally verify?

Add one AI-use note to the existing work record, reused by ID, or state that no AI was used. Submit the project's required artifacts and these evidence links through the course submission channel; no general conversation export or separate disclosure file is required.

docs.title: Completion and quality
docs.text:
For a repository with a partner contact, a merged PR satisfies the completion condition. If the repository has no contact, or the maintainer has not replied within seven days, a TA instead makes an acceptance review against that project's contribution guidelines. Request that review with the PR, its contribution-guide link, and the dated request or discussion showing the lack of reply. Respond to the TA's findings as you would to upstream review. Your mark does not depend on the maintainer replying.

Completion does not remove the quality requirement. Low-quality AI-generated output earns zero marks, as judged by the maintainer or TA. Each contribution needs the failing and passing verification pair and your own answers above. Neither a merge alone nor a polished explanation replaces that evidence. If the issue becomes infeasible or its rules change, tell the teaching team before continuing and agree a new scope.

docs.title: Boundaries and rights
docs.text:
• Public upstream only: external contributions go only to public repositories. Residency, employer and partner-internal code never enters the course or a model.
  • Follow the project's AI rules: disclose assistance as it requires. If it disallows your planned use, change the workflow or repository; do not conceal AI use.
  • Identity: use a pseudonym where the project permits it. The teaching team keeps the account-to-student mapping privately. Check what names and email addresses a sign-off or agreement would expose before signing.
  • Copyright: you are never required to sign a CLA that assigns copyright. A CLA granting a non-exclusive licence is your choice after reading it.
  • Equivalent route: if you do not want to publish publicly or sign a CLA or DCO, you may choose the course-hosted equivalent without giving a reason. Tell the teaching team before publishing or signing. It supplies non-public practice repositories for the same four contributions, small then substantial in each of two repositories, with a TA acceptance review, the same rubric and the same maximum marks.
  • Keep private material private: do not send participant material, credentials, teacher files or another student's unpublished work to a model or upstream. Follow the project's private reporting process for a security problem and tell the teaching team; course attack payloads and seeded defects never go upstream.

These contributions are separate from the term project. The syllabus defines their marks and rules.

docs.title: Read Trajectories Safely: Generate, Then Verify
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

The evaluation framework contains the trajectory schema, cheating-pattern detection, benchmark audits and evaluation-task templates. Results must be reproducible and report both correctness and execution evidence.

These tools read the trajectory JSONL v1 contract. They do not call models, execute commands recorded in trajectories or send trajectories over the network. Students can check their own evidence, and instructors/TAs can inspect process evidence. Generated or suggested code must still use the course safety launcher; these tools parse data only.

docs.title: Offline Use
docs.text:
Course build repository: After completing make setup at the repository root, generate a minimized copy from a fully synthetic example, then validate and inspect it:

uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.validate evals/trajectory/examples/synthetic-tools.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.redact evals/trajectory/examples/synthetic-tools.jsonl -o /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.validate /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.stats /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.viewer /tmp/course-safe.jsonl -o /tmp/course-view.html
uv run --locked pytest tests/test_trajectory_tools.py -q

Extracted student package: The package excludes the build repository's Makefile, root project and instructor-side test directory. Use the standalone route below from the student-package root in a POSIX shell, after installing the course-designated uv:

uv venv --python 3.12.13 evals/trajectory/venv
uv pip sync --python evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python --require-hashes evals/trajectory/requirements.lock
export PYTHONPATH="$PWD/src/course_llm/src"
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.selfcheck
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.validate evals/trajectory/examples/synthetic-tools.jsonl
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.redact evals/trajectory/examples/synthetic-tools.jsonl -o /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.stats /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.viewer /tmp/course-safe.jsonl -o /tmp/course-view.html

The standalone requirements.lock is exported from the course_llm dependency closure in the root uv.lock. It pins versions and hashes without resolving floating versions or installing project build tools. PYTHONPATH points to the course_llm source included in the student package. Environment preparation may download Python/locked dependencies; instructors can preinstall them or supply a matching offline wheelhouse, adding --no-index --find-links <wheelhouse> to uv pip sync. After preparation, all trajectory commands and selfcheck disable model calls and run offline without pytest or API keys. The self-check verifies synthetic trajectories and HTML round trips; it is not the build repository's full security regression tests.

Open the generated single-file HTML in a browser. Tab to step headings and expand them with Enter or Space. Tool calls use native mark highlighting; roles do not rely on color alone. The page needs no server, JavaScript, CSS, font downloads or external images. CSP blocks scripts, external resources, network connections, forms and object loading. The viewer observes records; it cannot prove model output correct. Check the task's actual test results as well.

All four CLIs accept an input path and optional -o/--output. Without an output path, the complete result goes to stdout. After successful publication, redact writes its redaction report to stderr: only call counts, removed content-field counts and removed-identifier counts, with no original text, filenames or reversible mappings. Failure returns nonzero with fixed English errors and no partial report. Existing output files remain unchanged on failure; new destinations are not created. Successful publication atomically replaces output with owner-only read/write permissions. Identical input/output paths, final-path symlinks and special files are rejected; callers must use trusted parent directories.

docs.title: Minimization Boundary
docs.text:
Reuse course_llm's TracePolicy and mandatory filtering. By default, remove every value, including original user text, assistant bodies, tool arguments, tool results and original call IDs. Unlabeled names, credentials, personal identifiers, absolute paths and long tool outputs are therefore removed in full rather than guessed with regular expressions. There is no dynamic allowlist or switch to retain bodies. Collected content receives fresh private random HMAC digests; keys are not written to disk. Existing not_collected fields retain their lengths and HMACs for correlation within one run. HTML and statistics do not display digests.

Model/tool identifiers retain only the built-in fake-v1/read/write/bash; all others become [REDACTED] and remain subject to the trajectory secret filtering. Custom tools share one redacted category, so their names cannot be distinguished. This reduces detail to support safe sharing by default. Finer categories require a separately auditable public classification contract. The viewer checks actual fields and identifiers rather than trusting an input's claimed redacted status; bodies or unknown identifiers require running redact first. Successful validation proves structure only, not authentic provenance, absence of privacy risk or billing accuracy.

docs.title: Statistics and Rejection Rules
docs.text:
• One line represents one call. steps counts returned assistant steps with usage measurements; snapshot_steps separately counts all context-snapshot steps. tools counts tool requests only in the current returned step, without adding repeated history.
  • Tokens and latency come only from the current returned step. Latency is the sum of observed call latencies, not end-to-end wall-clock time. Known costs are summed with Decimal, without inferring prices from model names. Amounts in the three examples are synthetic arithmetic inputs only.
  • Provider failures preserve missingness: cost: null, unknown_cost_calls, usage_complete: false and latency_complete: false. known_cost is a known subtotal, not the full cost.
  • Reject unknown versions, negative/non-finite numbers, duplicate JSON keys, malformed/blank JSONL, duplicate or reversed sequence numbers within a run, usage/latency repeated in historical snapshots, and inconsistent status/cost. Excerpts may have sequence gaps. v1 has no totals field; the schema rejects added summaries, and every report recomputes results.
  • Limits: 1 MiB per line including the newline; 16 MiB and 10,000 lines per file. Exceeding any limit rejects the entire input. Tokens, sequence numbers and latency cannot exceed 2**53-1; cost text is at most 64 characters, the absolute Decimal exponent at most 18, and the amount at most 1e18. These are tool resource limits, not model or industry data.

docs.title: Three Fully Synthetic Example Trajectories
docs.text:
• Single reply: Known cost and usage measurements.
  • Tool calls and follow-up reply: Count repeated context once.
  • Provider failure: Unknown cost cannot be treated as zero.

Every identifier, timestamp, amount and digest is fixed teaching data constructed by the course, with no real student or user information.

docs.title: Access, Storage, Deletion and Sharing
docs.text:
Follow the trajectory collection responsibilities without adding course policy. Creators retain only minimal excerpts needed for their work, in controlled directories inside the course workspace that are excluded from Git. Instructors/TAs read necessary evidence only through authorized course channels. Peer sharing uses self-checked minimized copies only. HTML is also process data; redaction does not make it suitable for public release.

Creators clean up original trajectories, minimized copies, reports and HTML; course administrators handle controlled copies and backups. Retention and deletion/withdrawal follow approved course arrangements. These tools set no retention period and do not automatically remove backups. If arrangements are unresolved, use only synthetic material and temporary files, delete them after verification, and record that deletion completed without retaining original content. The /tmp paths above serve synthetic demonstrations only; creators delete both temporary files afterward.

Share in order: confirm authorization and the minimum necessary data; generate a copy with redact; use validate and stats to check missingness; generate HTML with viewer; manually inspect the copy and complete the course secret scan; share through a controlled channel. Never submit environment configuration, raw interviews, credentials, complete tool output or instructor answers. If sensitive values appear, stop sharing, replace/delete affected copies and report through the course process. Automated validation does not replace manual self-checks.

docs.title: Trajectory Anomaly-Pattern Practice
docs.text: The detector and synthesizer provide seven fixed lexical clues, deterministic regression reports and an offline read-only execution entry point. Matches enter a human review queue only; they do not determine authorship, misconduct or grades.

docs.title: Clues Are Not Conclusions
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

This tool sends lexical patterns in records to a human review queue only. It does not determine author identity, integrity violations or grades. Writing style, perplexity and general AI-authorship detection are prohibited. Never convert match counts, confidence descriptions or empty reports into scores, sanctions, authorship probabilities or proof of exoneration. confidence describes observable lexical clues, not probabilities about a person. The detector connects to no gradebook, scorer or integrity system.

docs.title: Legitimate Behavior That Can Trigger Each Rule
docs.text:
Pattern Current Trigger Scope Legitimate False Positive Example Human Verification read_tests Test paths in read/read_file/list_directory; cat/head/tail/less/ls/rg/grep/find occurring with a test path. Read public tests to understand requirements. Determine whether tests are public and access is authorized; not all tests are hidden tests. history_patch A bash/shell request for git show or git log with -p/--patch; supports the global options below. Inspect an authorized historical regression and explain its cause. Check whether history is within permitted materials; show may display an ordinary file. print_pass Shell or written content contains print/echo/printf with PASS/PASSED/OK/SUCCESS. Write a console-renderer test that should print PASS. Check actual test results, output provenance and execution records. hardcode_output Literal return values in write/write_file/edit/apply_patch content, literal assignments to result/output/answer, or similar shell redirection. Implement a constant-response mock required by the specification. Check whether generalization is required, results under changed inputs and the specification's basis for the constant. modify_tests Test paths or patch content in write tools; test paths appearing with redirection, tee/rm/mv/cp/sed -i in shell. Add an authorized public regression assertion. Check modification authorization and the actual effectiveness of old/new assertions. network_answer HTTP addresses used by curl/wget or fetch/http_get/download occur with answer/solution/fix/patch/diff clues. Download an instructor-authorized patch from a course-local mock. Verify actual data provenance, authorization and attribution; a URL name does not prove its content. copy_diff git apply, patch -p, copying .diff/.patch, or writing content with unified-diff markers. Apply a disclosed teammate patch. Check provenance, collaboration scope, the student's explanation and independent verification.

These are course-authored synthetic examples, with no research-data citations or external detection performance claims. The source record says the assigned cheating-agents factsheet had not yet been delivered; the implementation infers no facts from a missing card and does not wait for uncited factsheet batches. This historical note does not assert the card's present availability.

docs.title: What Cannot Be Inferred
docs.text:
A tool request does not prove that a command executed, succeeded or affected the final artifact. Trajectories may be altered, truncated or copied and may retain only partial context; structural validation does not authenticate provenance. A trajectory alone cannot establish authorization, intent, authorship, test visibility, network-response content, artifact correctness, student learning or deserved grades.

Rules recognize only the listed tool names and command/cmd, path/file_path, content/text/patch/diff and url arguments, in ordinary objects or key/value entry lists. They do not interpret shell, expand variables, aliases, encodings, scripts, symlinks or escapes, or open paths. Strings containing multiple commands may incorrectly associate unrelated words. Python internal reads/writes, other languages, unlisted tool shapes and indirect copying may be missed. The constant-return rule is deliberately broad and cannot prove hardcoding for tests. User quotations, assistant bodies and tool results are not treated as tool requests.

The history rule only tokenizes quotes and splits on separators. It supports global git options -C, -c (separate/attached values), --git-dir, --work-tree, --namespace, --config-env (separate/equals values), and -p/--paginate, -P/--no-pager, --bare, --no-replace-objects, --no-lazy-fetch, --no-optional-locks and --no-advice. For example, git -C /workspace/repo log -p and git --no-pager show HEAD both produce clues. Global git -p is a pagination flag, not a log patch flag. Paths after log's -- and -p/--patch in other command segments do not participate. Unknown global options, unclosed quotes, wrapper commands, Git aliases, combined short options and other shell syntax may cause false negatives; the detector never executes them to determine semantics. Quoted separators may also split segments. Lexical results cannot replace verification of shell syntax or actual Git behavior.

minimal trajectories have no body; ordinary redacted policy also replaces non-allowlisted arguments and their keys entirely. Actual Client/FakeProvider/Tracer integration tests set no synthetic allowlist and verify coverage.conclusion: insufficient_evidence with empty findings for all seven request types. Argument strings containing [REDACTED…] markers are excluded from matching. The detector neither joins text across markers nor reverses digests. Partially analyzable fields or requests produce partial_evidence while retaining visible clues; see the usage guide for coverage states/counts. Current detection applies only to synthetic course exercises retaining supported arguments; do not claim coverage of real student behavior. Do not improve detection by restoring private bodies, saving or classifying real content before redaction, dynamically expanding the TracePolicy allowlist or labeling real data synthetic. Any real collection extension requires separate design, authorization and independent review. This task adds no collection metadata and does not change the frozen schema.

Every finding reports zero-based JSONL line, within-line step and within-step tool-call indexes, plus the rule version, pattern, fixed evidence labels and confidence description. It echoes no input snippets, tool IDs, model names, paths, hashes or original field values. Humans locate the evidence in an authorized original copy; reports themselves also travel through controlled channels. Repeated context across lines produces repeated clues, requiring manual deduplication by position. Counts must not be treated as independent events.

docs.title: Second Review and Appeals
docs.text:
1. Instructors/TAs check versions and indexes, trajectory completeness, redaction status and the task's permitted materials/tools.
  2. Check every legitimate counterexample above against actual execution results and artifact tests. Invite the student's explanation and accept equivalent process records created at the time. Incomplete records or absent tool coverage cannot themselves establish responsibility.
  3. Provide evidence-based written human reasons and retain the student's response; clues may be withdrawn. The detector must not trigger grade deductions, automatic rejection or integrity conclusions. Actual grading and integrity concerns follow established human course procedures.
  4. Students may seek review/appeal of facts, context or interpretation. Authorized personnel who did not make the original judgment examine the same evidence and supplements, retaining reasons for corrections and outcomes. Channels, deadlines and access follow published course arrangements; the tool creates no policy. Until arrangements are clear, use it only for synthetic exercises.

Data creators clean up temporary trajectories and reports; course administrators handle controlled copies and backups. Retention/deletion responsibilities follow the course_llm conventions. Never submit real credentials, student identities or instructor answers.

docs.title: Trajectory Anomaly Patterns: Generate, Detect, Explain, Verify
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

For LO6/LO9, first predict which tool requests will trigger clues, then run detection and explain false positives and false negatives. Begin with the detection limits and human review route. Everything here is a public, course-authored exercise, with no hidden answers, scorers or instructor-only question bank. Commands in the synthesizer are JSON strings and are never executed.

Current detection covers synthetic course trajectories that retain supported tool arguments. Ordinary minimal/redacted collection does not retain analyzable commands, paths or content; reports explicitly return insufficient_evidence. These tools provide no content-detection route for real student trajectories and do not require collection-policy changes.

docs.title: Prepare a Trusted Parsing Environment
docs.text:
After make setup in the course build repository, prepare the image. This step may download locked dependencies:

docker build -f evals/cheat_detector/Dockerfile -t course-cheat-detector:1 .

The image copies only the parser, course_llm and bundled schemas, not the workspace or instructor assets. The base image has a pinned digest; Python comes from .python-version; dependencies reuse the hashed trajectory dependency lock, adding no third-party dependencies. The local image tag must identify the image built from the reviewed source for this run. Do not use an image of unknown provenance merely because it has the same name.

docs.title: Generate Once, Then Verify Once
docs.text:
These commands only produce/parse synthetic course data; they do not execute shell commands or code inside trajectories.

uv run --locked cheat-synth --pattern read_tests --pattern history_patch --seed 17 > /tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.validate /tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl
uv run --locked cheat-detect /private/tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl
uv run --locked cheat-regression --seed 17
uv run --locked pytest evals/cheat_detector -q
uv run --locked python -m evals.cheat_detector.verify_isolation

On Linux, replace /private/tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl with /tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl. On macOS, /tmp is a system symlink and the CLI rejects symlinks in any input-path component, so use the real path. By default, cheat-detect <trace.jsonl> mounts only that explicit file read-only at /input/trace.jsonl, disables networking, uses a read-only root filesystem, drops capabilities, prevents privilege escalation and limits resources to 1 CPU, 256 MiB and 32 processes. The client deletes the container after a 45-second timeout. It reads private files as the caller (with the caller's UID/GID, or as container root under rootless Docker, which the engine maps to the caller), without changing file permissions or mounting parent directories, the Docker socket, instructor assets or credentials. It never pulls an image automatically and offers no host fallback. The Docker client requires a trusted runtime environment and local Docker permissions. Callers must control parent directories and must not replace files during execution. Paths containing commas, symlinks or special files are rejected.

worker is a passive parsing-library entry point inside the container. Calling it directly on the host does not provide isolation and is not a route for real trajectories. Inputs are limited to 1 MiB per line, 16 MiB and 10,000 lines per file. Shared strict v1 JSONL validation rejects the entire input for duplicate keys, blank lines, broken final lines or version/usage contradictions. Dependency code and bundled schemas are fixed parsing resources. Input never causes other files to be read, commands to run or models to be called. Success writes only JSON to stdout; failure returns 1 with fixed English diagnostics on stderr, without echoing input or detailed runtime errors. Matches still return 0 and do not act as disciplinary gates.

--pattern may be repeated; --seed is required. --kind positive|negative|benign|minimal selects an exercise target, absence of that clue, the same action with legitimate authorization, or missing body content. A fixed seed produces fixed JSONL bytes. Metadata, timestamps, HMAC keys and numbers are synthetic and must not be reused with real data. Callers redirect and clean up the output.

docs.title: Read Regression Reports
docs.text:
Read coverage.conclusion before findings:

Value Meaning no_tool_requests The supplied snapshot has no assistant tool requests; this says nothing about behavior outside the trajectory. insufficient_evidence Requests exist, but none has analyzable arguments for a supported tool; action clues cannot be checked. partial_evidence Only some requests or required arguments are analyzable; existing matches do not close evidence gaps. available_arguments Every request in the supplied snapshot has visible, nonempty arguments required by its supported tool shape; lexical-rule limitations still apply.

coverage.argument_availability assigns each request to exactly one of available, partial, unavailable or unsupported; their sum equals tool_requests. Shell tools require command/cmd, reads require path/file_path, write/write_file/edit require a path and content, apply_patch requires content, and network tools require url. See detection limits for aliases and coverage. Missing, non-string or empty arguments and arguments containing redaction markers are not analyzable. Unknown/redacted tool names count as unsupported. Partially available write arguments can still provide clues. The compatibility count unavailable_arguments counts only requests whose arguments were entirely uncollected or contain any redaction marker. It does not cover unknown shapes or missing keys and cannot alone establish coverage. It may overlap the four categories and is not included in their sum.

Every coverage state retains disposition: manual_review_only. Empty findings cannot substitute for the coverage conclusion; available_arguments does not establish complete detection, complete logs or a verified artifact. These are detector-report fields, without changes to the trajectory schema, collection fields or privacy contract.

cheat-regression --seed 17 reports expected/observed results per example and tp/fp/tn/fn per rule. The current fixed course regression set has 7 patterns x 4 contexts; each rule has TP=1, FP=1, TN=25 and FN=1. A positive label marks the predefined investigation target in a synthetic exercise, never an integrity violation. Authorized examples that still match count as FP; targets hidden by body minimization count as FN. These are repository-reproducible exercise counts, not industry performance, real-student false-positive rates or probability calibration. Adding samples or changing rules requires rerunning reports, updating the rule version and reviewing every item.

Read the full report manually, check overlapping rules and repeated snapshots, then explain why a match cannot prove misconduct. verify_isolation actually starts containers to verify disabled networking, read-only roots and inputs, invisible sibling files and absence of model credentials. It then detects all seven clues through the public CLI and checks that trajectories and a mock gradebook are unchanged. Missing Docker/images cause failure rather than a skip.

docs.title: Student Distribution
docs.text:
The student package contains detection/synthesis/regression source and these guides, but excludes the build repository's project entry points, Dockerfile and tests. Instructors must first supply a local course-cheat-detector:1 image built from reviewed source. Prepare the fixed dependency environment and PYTHONPATH using the student-package commands in the trajectory guide, then run modules with that environment's Python, without a root project:

evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.cheat_detector.synth --pattern read_tests --seed 17 > /tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.cheat_detector.cli /tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.cheat_detector.regression --seed 17

Use /private/tmp for input paths on macOS here as well. If the instructor image is unavailable, stop detection; do not switch to a host worker. Synthesis and regression process only inert fixed data in memory and remain available for understanding the rules.

docs.title: SWE-bench: inputs and verification boundaries for one subset
docs.text: Source-bound English reading edition. The original as_of date, source URLs, dates, locators, claim IDs and factual approvals remain in the canonical metadata. Review of this edition is separate and does not refresh those facts or authorize runtime.

docs.title: SWE-bench: inputs and verification boundaries for one subset
docs.text:
The SWE-bench Lite dataset card at revision 6ec7bb89b9342f664a54a6e0a6ea6501d3437cc2 describes the task as fixing an issue given a repository and a GitHub issue, with results verified by unit tests. Its Data Instances section separates what a system is given from what checks it:

Field Role problem_statement The issue title and body: what the system is given. base_commit The repository state before the original fix was applied. patch The answer patch from the original fix, without its test changes. test_patch The test changes from the original fix. FAIL_TO_PASS Tests tied to resolving the issue. PASS_TO_PASS Tests that should pass both before and after the fix.

Read the dataset card at that revision, especially "Dataset Summary", "Supported Tasks and Leaderboards" and "Data Instances". It names dev and test splits but declares no dataset license, so link to it rather than copying data or patches.

Use the fields to ask three questions about any reported score: what was supplied to the system, what could the tests detect, and which instances stayed in the report. A passing FAIL_TO_PASS set shows that the named tests pass; it does not show that the fix is the only correct one or that untested behavior is right.

The course's A6 evaluation exercises are course-original synthetic exercises. They are not a sample of SWE-bench, and a result on them is not a SWE-bench Lite score.

docs.title: Codex CLI: published base instructions and the update_plan tool schema at a pinned commit
docs.text:
This card records only one open-source coding agent's published base-instructions file and one tool definition at a pinned commit, for Week 2's notes section "Reading a production agent's instructions" and the optional activity "Compare two production prompts". It does not describe the complete prompt that a current Codex CLI release sends to a model: the runtime may add other templates, such as the "Sandbox and approvals" section the file mentions but does not contain, and this card infers none of them. Installation, sign-in and run records are on the Codex CLI card; sandbox and approval semantics are on the Codex card.

Open the two files at the pinned commit: the base instructions (read "Task execution", "Validating your work" and "update_plan") and the update_plan tool definition.

Use boundary: link the original at the pinned commit; do not copy the file into the course repository. The Apache-2.0 obligations are those stated in the original LICENSE. The card compares no vendors and does not judge the quality of the instructions.

Course verification: students read the pinned files side by side with the matching files of another open-source coding agent. In each of four parts (role and instructions, tools and schemas, safety and permission, stopping and plans) they pick sentences or rules and ask of each: what does it make the model do, and what enforces it: the schema, the tool's own code, a runtime permission or sandbox outside the model, or nothing visible? For example, update_plan's status values are an enum in the schema, while "at most one in_progress" appears only in the description and the instructions. This card does not establish whether other code checks that rule, so mark it "cannot tell" rather than assuming it is enforced.

docs.title: Qwen Code: the system-prompt builder and the edit and todo_write tool schemas at a pinned tag
docs.text:
This card records only one open-source coding agent's published system-prompt builder and two tool definitions at a pinned release tag, to be read beside the Codex CLI base-instructions card in Week 2's "Compare two production prompts" activity. It does not describe the complete prompt that any Qwen Code run sends to a model: prompts.ts assembles different text by interaction mode, sandbox, Git repository and environment variables, and the runtime may add context files and reminders; this card infers none of them. Permission modes are on the Qwen Code card.

Open the files at the pinned commit: the prompt builder (read the identity sentence, "Core Mandates", "Software Engineering Tasks", "Using Your Tools", "Executing actions with care" and "Final Reminder"), the edit tool, the todo_write tool and the tool names.

Use boundary: link the original at the pinned commit; do not copy these files into the course repository. Student materials quote only a few words, naming the project. The Apache-2.0 obligations are those stated in the original LICENSE. The card compares no vendors and does not judge the quality of the instructions.

Course verification: for each selected sentence or schema rule, ask what it makes the model do and what enforces it. For example, edit's required parameters are in the schema; the absolute-path rule and "a second match fails" are checked by the tool's code, which returns an error text to the model; "at least 3 lines of context" appears only in the description. todo_write's status values are an enum in the schema, while "at most one in_progress" appears only in the description. This card establishes only that todoWrite.ts itself has no such check, not whether other code checks it, so mark it "cannot tell".

docs.title: GitHub assignment submission and public feedback
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Use this guide to submit an assignment at a fixed commit, locate feedback and retry, practicing LO2, LO5 and LO9. Feedback is labeled public_only: it checks that the submission can be located and required files are present. It does not assess program correctness and is not a formal grade. The teaching team provides a GitHub submission repository containing only public student material and a reviewed checker. Do not request access to the instructor source repository. Use least privilege: the assignment repository should expose only the files and actions needed for your submission.

docs.title: Create the submission, then verify it
docs.text:
1. Fork the submission repository using the access route provided by the teaching team, then create submit/p1 in your own fork. Students have no write permission for the course submission repository; do not create branches there directly. For other assignments, use the announced submit/<assignment_id>. Submit one assignment per PR.
  2. Complete the code, verification evidence and independent reflection required by the lab. Follow Week 0 setup and your lab's launcher commands when executing agent-generated code, commands or dependency scripts. This public entry point reads data only and provides no alternative route for executing code.
  3. Maintain one artifact note in the repository-root README.md: locate the current assignment's artifact, verification results and short explanation, and assign the record an evidence ID. Add AI use once in that same record: either no AI use, or the tool/model and its purpose. You may reference an existing artifact note or compatible disclosure file by path and the same evidence ID, without copying its contents or submitting another disclosure file. README.md must be a nonempty regular file of at most 64 KiB, never a symbolic link. Redact attachments first. Do not include raw interviews, real names, credentials, instructor answers or hidden tests in the PR.
  4. Commit the verified submission files to the branch. Record the full 40-character commit SHA with git rev-parse HEAD, push to your own fork, and open a PR targeting the instructor-designated protected default branch of the submission repository. State the assignment ID, SHA and artifact-note evidence ID in the PR, without repeating the AI-use note. PR titles and bodies are for readers; the machine locates the submission using the GitHub event's head SHA.
  5. Open the PR's Course public feedback Actions run. First check that submission.commit_sha matches your submitted SHA. Then read the summary or download feedback.json from the public-feedback-* artifact. This template retains feedback for 7 days. For longer-term evidence, save a redacted file and reference it by ID.

For example, the artifact note can be these few lines. This is a course-created example; replace paths, commands and results with your actual records:

Evidence ID: p1-e1
Artifact: src/agent.py; this change stops the loop after a tool failure.
Verification: run P1's specified checks in the course launcher; record the command, expected and actual output, and reference the saved results.
Short explanation: the stop condition prevents repeated calls; the timeout boundary still needs testing.
AI-use note: no AI used.

If you used AI, replace the final line with the actual tool/model and purpose; follow the lab's red/yellow/green rules. Reflection written without AI may be included in the same note. Submit trajectories only when the lab explicitly specifies the learning objective, required excerpts and verification method. Generic conversation exports, commit trailers and additional reflection files are not required. When logs are not required, their absence does not trigger a request for more evidence or pending_human. The public entry point checks only the existence, type and size of README.md; the relevant lab's verification and human review check the artifact, evidence and note contents.

Later changes require a new commit and updates to the changed purposes and evidence in the same record. Feedback for a historical SHA describes only that submission; moving the branch does not replace the record. The formal submission is the full SHA collected by the instructor. Assignment rules determine deadlines and late submissions; the public entry point does not decide late penalties.

docs.title: Reproduce the same check locally
docs.text:
Use the trusted public_check.py supplied by the teaching team, with Python 3.12.13 and Git, and keep it outside the student submission directory. github-event.json is a redacted copy of the same PR event, supplied through the teaching team's trusted entry point. Do not use a self-edited event as formal identity evidence. Your local Git clone must already contain the commit. This command reads Git objects only; it does not execute submission files:

python3 -I /path/to/course-tools/public_check.py \
  --event /path/to/github-event.json --repository course-org/submissions \
  --assignment p1 --expected-sha FULL_40_CHARACTER_COMMIT_SHA \
  --snapshot /path/to/student-clone --ledger /path/to/local-feedback.sqlite

Replace the paths, repository and SHA with actual values. Actions invokes the same script with the same options. The instructor template pins the checker's SHA-256; versions must match. The local and Actions feedback objects should be identical. delivery describes the first receipt (recorded) or a repeat (duplicate) in this ledger and is not part of the feedback contents or any grade. You retain the local ledger for debugging only; it cannot be submitted as the instructor's ledger or authoritative grading evidence.

docs.title: Understand failures and retries
docs.text:
Exit code / state Meaning and next step 0 / accepted Commit located; the artifact-note entry README.md passes existence, type and size checks. Continue checking lab behavior and test evidence. 1 / checks_failed Inspect failed files in checks, fix them, commit and push again, then verify the new SHA. 2 / rejected The event format, repository, branch or SHA does not match, or Git cannot find the commit. Check the full SHA and event and contact a TA to collect it again. 3 / infrastructure_error A read, ledger or timeout failure. Keep the SHA; after the environment is repaired, an authorized person reruns Actions. No feedback artifact Checkout or the base environment may have failed first. Inspect the failed run step and ask a TA to rerun it; absence of an artifact does not mean acceptance.

Retrying the same event in the same ledger retains one record. Failed feedback remains failed on retry; it does not turn into success or a student score of zero. Each Actions run uses a temporary ledger. A stable idempotency_id identifies repeats across runs; the teaching team deduplicates by that ID when collecting feedback, rather than counting several artifacts as several submissions. If a checker-version change causes a ledger conflict, the TA preserves old evidence and revalidates with a ledger for the new version, without manually editing old feedback.

GitHub student identification uses a repository-scoped student pseudonym derived from the numeric repository ID and PR author's numeric ID. Login names, real names and PR bodies are not written to feedback. A pseudonym can still be linked to a person; share feedback only within the course-authorized scope. For account changes or submissions on another person's behalf, TAs verify identities and membership records. This entry point does not infer individual contribution.

docs.title: Formal grades
docs.text:
Labs provide practice and feedback. Selected evidence contributes to the portfolio or project under the current assessment rules. Formal scores require the registered grading unit and isolated runner, a trusted attestation, actual merging of the human-scored component and admission of its source. You can view and retain a valid component receipt without waiting for future assessments; future items remain missing rather than being entered as zero.

A local ledger, a green Actions check or JSON manually relabeled authoritative cannot be imported as a formal grade. If grading is not yet available or execution fails, wait for valid grading; the result is not recorded as zero.

docs.title: Check the approved model route
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Every real model call in this course goes through one approved hosted API configuration, with your own key. Week 0 setup describes, once, how to choose an item, set up your key, the budgets and the replay route. This page lists the commands that check the configuration. None of them runs code a model wrote; model text is compared as data.

The previous local inference walkthrough is retired. The commands below use the offline profile for checks that make no model call and the replay route when a recorded model response is required.

docs.title: What the configuration fixes
docs.text:
approved-models.json is the course's only model configuration. Each approved item fixes its provider, endpoint, model, request settings, context and output limits, per-run caps and review date. Other course files refer to an item only by its ID. The file's SHA-256 is the policy digest that Week 0 setup publishes. An item that is not enabled yet carries no values at all; until your item is enabled, use the replay route.

offline is the zero-model profile. Launcher runs that make no model call, or only FAKE calls, use it.

The resolver checks the whole file before anything reads a key. Unknown IDs, floating model names, extra or duplicate fields, missing or non-positive caps, a changed version or digest and model environment overrides all fail. A key can only go to the exact host the course reviewed for that item, over HTTPS on port 443.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Run these from a source checkout or the root of an unpacked student ZIP, with uv installed. The included pyproject.toml and uv.lock select a dedicated environment.

uv sync --project infra/hosted --locked
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/doctor.py
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/smoke.py
  • resolve_profile.py prints the profile ID, version and digest that the launcher checks.
  • doctor.py without options summarizes the configuration. It reads no key file and makes no network request.
  • smoke.py without options checks FAKE replies, then the course broker over a mock connection with a synthetic key. Its result always says real_model_verified: false.

Once your item is enabled, add --profile, --version and --digest from Week 0 setup to doctor.py. It then checks your key file without printing it, and --check-key adds one authentication request that sends no prompt. Doctor prints one fixed state with what to do next: key missing, key file unsafe, key invalid, budget exhausted or provider unreachable. Each message links the replay route.

docs.title: What the broker accepts
docs.text:
Your code in the sandbox can send only prompt text. The broker on your computer adds the fixed model and settings, sends exactly one request without redirects or retries, and forwards only the reply text. It refuses a reply with any field outside the course contract, a content filter stop, unexpected reasoning output or a copy of your key, and it never reads the body of an error reply. Each run has fixed request, token and cost caps; a request that would exceed them is not sent.

A failure is either "not sent", which is safe to retry, or "outcome unknown", which may still be billed. Report only the state and the policy digest when you ask for help; never paste a key, a key file or an environment dump.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text: • A slow name lookup can outlast a request's time limit. The broker's deadline cannot interrupt your computer's DNS resolver, so a request or --check-key can wait until the lookup finishes or the resolver gives up. The failure is still "not sent" and safe to retry.

docs.title: Week 1: The internals of coding agents
docs.text:
Build and verify a minimal agent loop in the first session, then inspect system instructions, tool definitions, observations and stopping. In the second session, capture one real session with your own coding agent and distinguish observed behavior from inference.

  • Notes and live-loop instructions
  • Slides
  • Session-capture studio
  • Primary sources and preparation
  • Self-check and answer guidance

Public code stays in the existing fixture directory, with request records and the viewer. The loop starter must be completed in a draft copy before its checks pass. The studio checks its own status candidate separately.

Use the safety practices in Tools and model access. A1 is due this week.

docs.title: Studio: capture and read your own session
Learning objectives
docs.text:
Explain the loop behind one real coding-agent session (LO1), separating observed behavior from inference and changing your decision when verification supplies new evidence (LO9). This studio supplies material for A1, due this week.

Work individually. A peer or the instructor may challenge a citation; the task, capture and explanation remain your own. Bring your course-provided coding agent, a terminal and a keyboard-accessible editor. All records and checks are plain text. Use the safety practices in Tools and model access.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text: This task is course-constructed. The candidate below looks plausible and handles unpadded status strings. Generate: propose a whitespace repair from the written contract. Verify: run the untouched check first to expose the missing behavior, then rerun it after the candidate changes. Keep both observations.

docs.title: Prepare a fresh draft directory
docs.text:
Run these ordinary commands from the course root. They create only public synthetic files; no installation or third-party sign-in is required by the task.

mkdir week01-studio
cat > week01-studio/status_label.py <<'PY'
def status_label(raw):
    return {"ok": "passed", "fail": "failed"}.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")
PY
cat > week01-studio/check_status.py <<'PY'
from status_label import status_label

cases = [("ok", "passed"), (" OK ", "passed"),
         ("\tfAiL\n", "failed"), ("cancelled", "unknown")]
for raw, expected in cases:
    assert status_label(raw) == expected, (raw, expected, status_label(raw))
print("PASS: four status cases")
PY
python3 week01-studio/check_status.py

Expected baseline: a nonzero exit and an assertion identifying " OK " with expected passed and actual unknown. This is the forced failure to preserve in your agent session, rather than a requirement to cause unpredictable model failure.

docs.title: Capture one real session
docs.text:
Before launching the agent in week01-studio, write your prediction: first tool, what the failed check will return, what recovery you expect, and what ends the loop. Choose a dedicated directory or container without employer or cloud credentials. Never put a key in a prompt, repository, screenshot or recording.

Start the agent with its supplied seat or credit. Use its session export or visible transcript feature; check that you can save the record before beginning. Give it:

Work only in this draft directory. For string statuses, ignore surrounding whitespace and ASCII letter case; map ok to passed, fail to failed and everything else to unknown. First run python3 check_status.py and retain its failing output. Repair status_label.py without changing check_status.py. Run the same check again, then explain what you changed and what the result covers.

Read any proposed command before approving execution. Keep the baseline failure inside the capture, including command, exit status and output. Export the session in its supported format to your private evidence directory. If export is unavailable, copy the visible messages in order into session.txt, retaining role labels and call/result identifiers when shown. Record agent name, version, date and task. Exclude credentials and private data from any excerpts you submit.

docs.title: Read and revise
docs.text:
Studio segment Action Evidence Opening Prepare files and save predictions before generation Task and unchanged prediction Capture Agent runs the failing check, repairs, checks again Original session and both results Dissection Read calls/results and inspect visible request fields Table below with citations Verification checkpoint Run the check yourself and inspect the changed file Current result and bounded diff Revision Peer or instructor challenges one citation; revise it Corrected claim and decision line

At the midpoint of the session, ask for help if recording or the first check is blocked. Continue the text participation exercise while access is restored; keep missing real-run evidence explicitly missing.

Make one row per visible request or event:

Location Instruction/context visible Tools/call arguments Returned result Continue or stop Observed claim Inference and a possible check

Identify system/developer messages and the tool list if your capture exposes them. If it exposes only chat and tool actions, say that the full request was unavailable. Do not treat a published prompt file as proof that your session sent it. Match each result to its call, inspect recovery after the forced failure, and find the check that supports the final message. Count requests separately from tool calls.

Practice with the read-only viewer and the supplied hand-authored record:

python3 lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py \
  lectures/week-02/session/sample-session.jsonl --request 4

A native export can be read directly as text. Use the viewer on your own export only if it uses its supported course-session or course-trajectory format. Do not invent a header or fabricate hidden request fields to make another format fit.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
From the course root, verify the candidate in the actual studio directory:

python3 week01-studio/check_status.py

Expected after repair: zero exit and PASS: four status cases. Confirm the check file is unchanged and the candidate only normalizes input before lookup. A passing result covers these cases; it is not proof for all strings or callers.

For the separate live-loop exercise, use the completed draft controller:

PYTHONPATH="$PWD/scripts" python3 week01-loop/verify_loop.py

The original lectures/week-02/fixture/loop.py is an unfinished starter. Checking it would not test your repaired studio candidate or your copied controller.

Keep the work, verification and brief explanation in A1. Include one AI-use note, label each behavior observed or inferred, and end with accept, narrow, re-check or stop plus supporting evidence. No unrelated session history is required.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How to notice it Correction Only saving the successful run No forced failure in the session Capture the baseline before repair Checking the wrong directory Command targets the original fixture Check the candidate you actually changed Claiming hidden instructions were seen Export omits system messages State the visibility limit Citing a final claim as a tool result No command, call ID or result at the citation Find the corresponding observation Letting the agent weaken the check Check file changed Restore it, inspect the candidate and rerun Relabelling an inference as observed Citation does not contain the claim Change the label or obtain another observation

docs.title: Text participation
docs.text: If capture is unavailable, dissect the sample with the same table. Its header says course-made-sample: it is practice evidence, not your real agent session. Predict recovery after the failed edit, reveal the next request, and revise your explanation. Complete the real capture through supported access later; preserve any missing observation rather than inventing it.

docs.title: Week 1: The internals of coding agents
Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you can:

  • LO1: explain a coding agent's loop, system prompt and tool definitions;
  • LO1: predict a failure caused by missing context, invalid tool arguments or a stop condition, then test that prediction; and
  • LO9: label a claim as observed or inferred, cite its evidence and revise your decision when a check supplies new information.

You need Python functions, dictionaries, basic tests and a terminal. The first session builds a minimal agent live and inspects a request. The second session is a studio using your own coding agent. A1 is due this week.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text: The examples in this lesson are course-constructed. The supplied session is hand-authored; your studio capture provides evidence of your own real agent run.

docs.title: One repair from contract to regression
docs.text:
The requirement says to ignore surrounding whitespace and ASCII letter case, map ok to passed, fail to failed, and other strings to unknown. A plausible candidate is:

def status_label(raw):
    return {"ok": "passed", "fail": "failed"}.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")

Generate: propose the smallest patch. Verify: before editing, derive the expected result for " OK " from the requirement. It must be passed; the candidate returns unknown. Adding .strip() before .lower() repairs that case. Retain the ordinary and unknown-status checks as well. A plausible patch needs a completed check on the changed code.

docs.title: Build the agent around a proposer
docs.text:
Open loop.py. It supplies checked, tool and last_check; run() is deliberately unfinished. A model supplies proposals, while the controller executes permitted calls and feeds observations into the next request. For the live build, a scripted proposer lets us inspect this behavior without making a model request.

Tool Accepted arguments What actually happens read path: result.txt Return the file's text write That path, plus text of at most 32 characters Replace the file; return written bash command: verify Run a fixed check for the exact bytes 4

Despite its name, bash does not accept arbitrary shell commands. For example, echo 4 > result.txt is refused. This restriction is in the tool's code; a prompt asking the model to be careful would not enforce it.

The instructor builds run() from its public five-step contract:

  1. Begin with a user message holding the task and an empty set of used call IDs.
  2. On each turn, send a copy of history to the proposer. Apply checked() and reject a reused call ID before executing any call from that reply.
  3. Append the assistant reply. With no tool calls, return the history and final.
  4. For every call in order, execute tool() and append one role: tool message with its own tool_call_id. Convert missing files and timeouts into failed observations that the next request receives.
  5. At the turn budget, return the history and step_limit.

Generate: the scripted proposer reads, writes 4 , requests verification and then sends a reply with no calls. Verify: the public checks independently assert what the controller did. A successful scripted demonstration has this sequence:

Proposed action Tool observation c1: read result.txt 5 c2: write 4 written c3: verify verified final reply with no calls Controller stops with final

A second run writes 5 instead. Its write still returns written, but the check returns check_failed. The proposer can still stop with final. Completion of the loop and correctness of the change are separate questions. A later write also makes an earlier passing check stale; last_check reports not_run until another check runs.

docs.title: Read a real agent's instructions and your visible request
docs.text:
A request can carry system or developer instructions, user context, assistant calls and tool results, with tool definitions beside the messages. A tool definition names the operation, describes its intended use and declares argument shapes. A system prompt describes the agent's role and workflow; it does not execute tests.

Source 1 and Source 2 are pinned published instruction and tool files from open-source agents. Read one stopping instruction and one schema constraint. Then inspect the corresponding information exposed by your agent during the studio. Source files describe components, while only a captured request can establish which components that run sent. A visible transcript may omit system messages or the wire request; record that limit.

Practice the request-reading method with the supplied sample:

python3 lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py \
  lectures/week-02/session/sample-session.jsonl --request 4

Identify a role/goal instruction, a tool argument rule, a stopping rule and a request for caution. Locate calls and the results matched by call ID. Request 4 proposes an edit; request 5 carries its failed result. Request 6 shows a retry and request 7 carries a failing test. Predict the next action before revealing each response. Finally locate the verification supporting the last response.

Observed: the record contains a particular call, result or instruction at a citable location. Inferred: you explain why it happened or what might happen next. An error message is observed; an explanation of the model's private reasoning is inferred.
