Use the questions in the existing request dissection and prompt dissection for this reading; this week's activity and due item are on this page.

docs.title: Finish and check the live loop
docs.text:
From the course root, make a fresh draft copy. The scripts import the existing model client for definitions, but these commands use only scripted practice.

mkdir week01-loop
cp lectures/week-02/fixture/*.py week01-loop/
PYTHONPATH="$PWD/scripts" python3 week01-loop/verify_loop.py

Before implementing run(), expect the nonzero message Write run() in loop.py first. Edit only your copy's run() using the five steps above, then rerun that same command. With the controller complete, expect Ran 15 tests and OK. Until then, the named failures tell you which behavior still needs work.

At the class help checkpoint, trace one call/result pair on paper if the controller still fails. Then complete the missing behavior and rerun the checks before the demonstration:

(cd week01-loop && PYTHONPATH="../scripts" python3 demo.py)

Expect a first line with generation: scripted-practice, stop_reason: final, check: verified and eight messages. The two COURSE_ARTIFACT lines after it, one long, are encoded copies of the two output files; you can ignore them. Inspect completion.json and result.txt in your copy. Change only CANDIDATE to "5\n" in the copied demo.py, predict, and rerun. Expect a nonzero exit and check: check_failed. Preserve the result before restoring "4\n" and rerunning. Do not use the fixture's hosted mode for this demonstration.

docs.title: Studio: capture and read your own session
docs.text:
Follow the studio to create a fresh status-label task, capture a real coding-agent session with a forced failing check, and verify the repair. Keep the original failure, the later check and a short explanation. At the revision checkpoint, check one observed claim against its citation and revise it if needed.

Use the safety practices in Tools and model access. Run the agent in a dedicated draft directory or container without employer or cloud credentials. Seats or credit are provided by the course; students do not pay.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Keep the verification tied to the candidate it tested:

  • Loop: all public checks pass in your copied controller; wrong writes fail, denied calls have no effect, and every result matches its call ID.
  • Request: point to an instruction, a tool schema, a returned result and a stop in the record. If the capture omits one, state that it was not visible.
  • Studio: retain the baseline failure, the repaired check and a bounded diff. A test on the untouched original fixture cannot verify your studio candidate.
  • Decision: end A1 with accept, narrow, re-check or stop and the specific evidence supporting it. Keep one AI-use note with the work and reuse its ID.

The loop's turn budget guarantees a bound on requests. It does not prove progress, validate the task's meaning or establish a secure process boundary around editable Python. These are properties you must distinguish when interpreting a trace.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Detection Correction Treating written or final as correctness No current passing check Run the check after the latest write Losing a refused call Next request has no result under that ID Return the refusal as an observation Reusing a call ID Two different actions have the same identifier Reject before effects and use fresh IDs Treating a prompt rule as enforcement No schema, tool check or runtime check stops a violation Name the enforcing component or say it only asks Claiming invisible system prompts were observed Capture has only visible chat messages Mark the request content unavailable Counting calls as model requests A response has several calls Count request blocks separately Calling scripted practice a real model run Proposer is demo.scripted Preserve the actual generation mode Accepting a stale passing test Another write occurred afterward Verify the current revision

docs.title: Reading and preparation
docs.text:
Before class, read the Week 1 row of the calendar and the notes. Recall Python functions, lists, dictionaries and assertions. No machine-learning course is assumed.

Read the five-step run() contract in loop.py and one success, wrong-write and refused-call check in verify_loop.py. Predict the observations before following the live build. The starter is deliberately incomplete.

docs.title: Primary-source reading
docs.text:
Two open-source coding agents publish the code that builds their instructions under the Apache-2.0 licence: Codex CLI and Qwen Code. Read the pinned files below on GitHub for the prompt comparison. Each project has a reading card that links the files at a fixed commit and records what they contain: one for Codex CLI (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) and one for Qwen Code (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7). Neither set of files is the complete prompt a release sends at run time; your session capture establishes what your run exposed. This page does not rank the two products.

  • Source 1: Codex CLI's base instructions and plan schema. Open the two files linked from the Codex CLI reading card above, pinned at commit 2351d9e1b608e6f9d9a3699b71d7eb39ee41cfa4: the base instructions (codex-rs/protocol/src/prompts/base_instructions/default.md) and the update_plan tool definition (codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/plan_spec.rs). Read Task execution, Validating your work and update_plan. Identify a stopping instruction and a required argument.
  • Source 2: Qwen Code's prompt builder and edit tool. In the QwenLM/qwen-code repository at tag v0.25.0 (commit 6788c035698a0ada471c958d1e789e96c6cddd9b), open the prompt builder and the edit tool. Read Software Engineering Tasks and Final Reminder. Separate argument-schema rules, tool validation and requests in prose.

You need not install both agents. Read the files as text, name the enforcing component where visible, and say “cannot tell” where these files do not settle it.

docs.title: Before the studio
docs.text:
Read the studio steps, then save a prediction before your own agent runs. Practice request indexing with the supplied sample record and viewer. The request questions in the dissection and schema questions in the prompt comparison help you choose citations. Use this week's studio for the task and submission.

After capture, answer the self-check. Bring one observed claim and one inference to discuss. A1 is due this week.

docs.title: Week 1 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Try each question before reading this page. These are evidence prompts, not a graded answer key: cite the fixture, the request index or your own captured record.

docs.title: The minimal loop
docs.text:
Q1. The proposer generates an assistant message containing tool calls. The controller checks the message and executes permitted calls; the tool returns the file text, written, verified or a refusal. A tool result is an observation, not the proposal that caused it.

Q2. written reports that the controller wrote bytes to the permitted path. It does not compare those bytes with the requirement. The fixed bash verification is the observation that checks the required 4\n content.

Q3. The controller answers calls in their listed order and returns one tool message per call. Each message carries the corresponding tool_call_id, including for a refused call, so the next request can match every result to its proposal.

Q4. final means a reply had no calls and the controller stopped normally. step_limit means the request budget ended. Neither stop reason proves that the candidate is correct.

Q5. “Done” after a write does not establish that the required bytes are present. Run the fixed verification on the current file and retain its result before accepting the claim.

docs.title: Reading a request
docs.text:
Q6. A valid answer names one role or goal instruction, one argument constraint from a tool definition, and one earlier message carried in request 4. Label each with its request or message location. If the capture hides system content, say that it was not visible rather than filling the gap from a published prompt.

Q7. A schema or checked() rejection prevents the malformed call from running; the tool's own code can return a refusal after the call is received. A sentence in the prompt is only a request unless a checker or runtime control enforces it. Cite one example of each from the prompt and fixture.

Q8. Count request blocks because one assistant response can contain several tool calls. The viewer's request index identifies a model request; a call ID identifies one proposed action inside that request.

Q9. course-made-sample identifies the supplied record as a hand-authored teaching example. It does not establish what a real agent sent or what a student's session did.

docs.title: Your studio record
docs.text:
Q10. An observed claim has a citation containing the event, such as a command, result or visible instruction. An inference explains why it happened or predicts a next action. A follow-up run of the same check, or a newly visible request field, can turn a bounded inference into an observation.

Q11. With no verification result, choose re-check (or narrow if a re-check is impossible). The evidence supports that a proposal or write occurred, not that the required behavior is correct.

Q12. Preserve both sentences: “I predicted ___ before the check” and “After the check on revision , I observed .” This keeps the original prediction available while recording what the new evidence changed.

docs.title: Decision line
docs.text:
Decision. Accept only the current revision and cases covered by a passing check; otherwise narrow the claim, re-check the current revision or stop. Name the command, result and next check that support the selected decision.

Retrieval 1. A generated call is an assistant proposal with a call ID; a tool effect is the returned result carrying that same ID. Record both sides before explaining what the effect means.

Retrieval 2. A final completion sentence is insufficient without a verification result tied to the latest write; preserve that result and its call or command ID.

docs.title: Agent internals and evidence
docs.text: Answer these without an agent. For every answer, cite a fixture line, a request and message index, or state that you are inferring. These formative checks are not a graded submission. Compare your work with the answer guidance.

docs.title: The minimal loop
docs.text:
1. In the fixture protocol, what does the model generate, what does the controller decide, and what does the tool return for read("result.txt")?
  2. Why is written evidence of a file effect but not evidence that the required content is present?
  3. A reply contains two calls, one refused and one allowed. In what order should their tool messages return, and what must each message carry?
  4. What is the difference between the stop reasons final and step_limit?
  5. The proposer says “done” after a write and sends no verification call. What claim is unsupported, and which command would supply the missing observation?

docs.title: Reading a request
docs.text:
1. In request 4 of the sample record, list one system instruction, one tool-schema constraint and one message carried from an earlier turn. Label each observed or inferred.
  2. How can you tell whether a rule is enforced by a schema/tool check or merely requested in prose? Give one example of each from the prompt dissection.
  3. Why must you count model requests rather than tool calls when reading a session?
  4. What does a course-made-sample provenance value establish, and what does it not establish about a real agent?

docs.title: Your studio record
docs.text:
1. Cite one observed event from your own record and one inference you made from it. What follow-up check would turn the inference into an observation?
  2. If your record has no verification result, what decision is justified: accept, narrow, re-check or stop? Explain the evidence boundary.
  3. Write one sentence that preserves the original prediction and one sentence that records what changed after the fixture check.

docs.title: Decision line
docs.text:
Finish with one of: accept, narrow, re-check or stop, followed by the specific observation that supports it and the next check that could change it.

R1. What observation distinguishes a generated call from a tool effect under its call ID?

R2. What verification result is needed before accepting a final completion message?

docs.title: The internals of coding agents
docs.text:
Week 1 · Agentic Software Engineering

Generate a proposal.Verify the effect.

LO1: explain the loop · LO9: keep evidence bounded

docs.title: A coding agent is a loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  M[Model proposes] --> C[Controller checks]
  C --> T[Tool acts]
  T --> O[Observation]
  O --> M
  C --> S[Stop or continue]

Each arrow carries a different claim.

docs.title: Start with a contract
docs.text:
ok → passed fail → failed Anything else → unknown

Ignore surrounding whitespace and ASCII letter case.

docs.title: Generate a plausible candidate
docs.text:
def status_label(raw):
    return {"ok": "passed", "fail": "failed"}.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")

What does it return for " OK "?

Predict before reading the check.

docs.title: Verify the missing case
docs.text:
The contract requires " OK " → passed.

The candidate returns unknown.

Add .strip() before .lower(), then keep the original and unknown cases.

A patch is a proposal until the regression runs.

docs.title: The fixture has three tools
docs.text:
Name Accepted action Observation read result.txt file text write at most 32 characters written bash verify only verified / check_failed

Other names, paths and arguments are refused.

docs.title: The five-step controller
docs.text:
1. Start history with the task.
  2. Send history; check the reply and call IDs.
  3. Append the reply; no calls means final.
  4. Answer every call with its own tool message.
  5. Exhausted budget means step_limit.

The public starter leaves run() for you to complete.

docs.title: Generate a successful path
docs.text:
c1 read result.txt       → 5\n
c2 write result.txt 4\n → written
c3 bash verify           → verified
final                    → no more calls

Left: generated actions.Right: observed results.

docs.title: Verify the controller
docs.text:
mkdir week01-loop
cp lectures/week-02/fixture/*.py week01-loop/
PYTHONPATH="$PWD/scripts" python3 week01-loop/verify_loop.py

Before run() is complete, the check explains what is missing. Afterwards, read the named checks and retain the output.

docs.title: A write is not a check
docs.text:
Candidate writes 5\n and receives written.

The fixed check returns check_failed.

Which claim is supported?

docs.title: Stop reasons are evidence fields
docs.text:
Field Means Does not mean final no calls in a reply code is correct step_limit turn budget ended task is complete check_failed current check failed model is useless

A later write also makes an earlier check stale.

docs.title: Practise reading the supplied request
docs.text:
python3 lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py \
  lectures/week-02/session/sample-session.jsonl --request 4

Predict first: request count, first tool, failure recovery and stop evidence.

docs.title: Mark observed and inferred
docs.text:
Observed: a request contains a call, a result or an instruction at a cited index.

Inferred: an explanation of why the agent acted or what it might do next.

The supplied record is hand-authored. Your studio capture supports claims about your agent.

docs.title: Prompt text is not always enforcement
docs.text:
A system instruction can ask for a plan.

A schema can require an argument.

A tool can reject a path.

Name the component that enforces each rule—or say it only asks.

docs.title: Count requests, not calls
docs.text:
One response can contain several calls.

Each call gets a tool result under its own ID, in response order.

The viewer's Request N blocks are the unit to count.

docs.title: Studio: force a failure, then verify
docs.text:
1. Copy a synthetic status task to a draft directory.
  2. Predict before generation.
  3. Capture the failing check and the repair.
  4. Run the check on the current candidate.
  5. Label each claim observed or inferred.

Keep the original failure and revise one explanation.

docs.title: Evidence-bounded decisions
docs.text:
Accept only the revision and cases the check covered.

Otherwise narrow the claim, re-check the current revision or stop.

A1 is due this week.

docs.title: Dashboard status demonstration
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

This public example supplies an authored candidate, its worked repair and a demonstration runner. The runner executes both functions on the same six contract cases. It makes no model calls. Its scripted candidates let you inspect one complete repair repeatedly without treating the result as a model capability measurement.

docs.title: Contract and prediction
docs.text:
The input is a Python string. Ignore surrounding whitespace and letter case in the ASCII status names. Map ok to passed, fail to failed, and every other string to unknown, including the empty string. Behavior on a non-string input is outside this exercise's contract.

Before opening the repair, predict Candidate A's output on " OK " and write the required output. Explain which operation can make them differ. Then compare the worked repair in the notes. These are worked teaching examples, not answers to a graded submission.

docs.title: Repository walkthrough
docs.text: This second example extends the same dashboard from a helper function to its caller. It is a course-authored hand trace, with a frozen source snapshot below. The proposed actions, patch and outputs are authored teaching material. No model selected these actions, and no repository test run is being reported. Read the snippets as text; the runnable six-case helper demonstration in the next section is a separate artifact with its own execution evidence.

docs.title: Request and frozen files
docs.text:
A developer needs reliable labels and a matching failed-build count. Each build has an integer ID and a string status. Preserve every record's ID and its input order. The count must equal the number of displayed rows labeled failed. Use the existing status contract for all labels. Storage, input validation and additional service statuses are outside this change.

These five named files form the entire teaching snapshot. They are printed here, not taken from a project repository or its instructor solutions.

contract.md:

Ignore surrounding whitespace and ASCII letter case in string statuses.
ok -> passed; fail -> failed; every other string -> unknown.
Keep every build ID in its input order.
failed equals the number of displayed rows labeled failed.

sample.json:

[
  {"id": 17, "status": "\tfAiL\n"},
  {"id": 18, "status": "ok"},
  {"id": 19, "status": "cancelled"}
]

labels.py (the same initial helper as Candidate A):

def status_label(raw):
    labels = {"ok": "passed", "fail": "failed"}
    return labels.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")

dashboard.py:

from labels import status_label


def dashboard(builds):
    rows = []
    for b in builds:
        label = status_label(b["status"])
        rows.append({"id": b["id"], "label": label})
    failed = sum(b["status"] == "fail" for b in builds)
    return {"rows": rows, "failed": failed}

test_dashboard.py (the existing check):

from dashboard import dashboard


def test_ordinary_failure():
    assert dashboard([{"id": 1, "status": "fail"}]) == {
        "rows": [{"id": 1, "label": "failed"}],
        "failed": 1,
    }

docs.title: Pause 1: choose context and define the change
docs.text:
Before reading the proposed sequence, identify which files establish the desired behavior, current implementation and existing observations. The printed test supplies a check, not an observed test result. Derive the required full output for the sample from the contract before examining the patch.

A bounded delegation prompt could be:

Read the contract, sample, helper, caller and checks. Explain where labels and counts can disagree. Propose the smallest repair and regression checks. Preserve all build IDs and their order. Report the files changed and the actual checks completed; identify any missing result.

An agent could perform the repeated context gathering, file edits and permitted checks, using returned observations to decide what to inspect next. That is the workflow this example makes concrete. It is not a measured speedup or an observed model success. The engineer still owns the contract and acceptance decision.

docs.title: Pause 2: follow a helper-only proposal
docs.text:
In the authored sequence, a proposed read of dashboard.py would be checked by the controller before a tool could return its bytes. Those bytes reveal two separate interpretations of the status: the helper supplies a row label, while the summary compares the raw string directly. A model could overlook the second interpretation.

Suppose the first proposed edit changes only labels.py:

-    return labels.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")
+    return labels.get(raw.strip().lower(), "unknown")

The hand-derived sample result is:

{
  "rows": [
    {"id": 17, "label": "failed"},
    {"id": 18, "label": "passed"},
    {"id": 19, "label": "unknown"}
  ],
  "failed": 0
}

The required count is 1. The helper's six cases do not call dashboard, and the existing dashboard test uses the exact raw string fail. Those checks would miss this disagreement. This conclusion follows from the printed code; it is not a recorded pass or failure. What check should be added before another proposal?

docs.title: Pause 3: use one interpretation and protect the caller
docs.text:
Keep the helper repair and propose this additional change in dashboard.py:

-    failed = sum(b["status"] == "fail" for b in builds)
+    failed = sum(row["label"] == "failed" for row in rows)

For the sample, independently expect all three rows above in the same order, with failed: 1. A full-output assertion checks the labels, count, retained IDs and order. Also retain the original ordinary-failure check and the helper's ordinary, padded, unknown and empty-string regressions. An empty build list should produce {"rows": [], "failed": 0} under the same row/count rules.

At this point the authored sequence contains a proposed repair and hand-derived expectations. Accepting an actual implementation would additionally require completed checks on the exact changed files, inspection of the diff and a review of remaining scope. A successful file write, test request or final message cannot fill that gap. Do not enter any of these hand-derived values into your model-calibration record.

docs.title: Pause 4: decide what to delegate next
docs.text: Name one useful bounded next action for an agent and one judgment you must make yourself. For example, the workflow can collect the relevant files and execute an allowed full-output regression; you must decide whether its expectations preserve the stated product behavior. If the new status completed has no supplied meaning, neither more code generation nor a green test invented by the agent settles that rule.

docs.title: Supported execution
docs.text:
The fixture is a local, scripted example. It makes no model request and needs no credentials. From the repository root, copy the public files to a temporary directory and run them with the repository's small IPC helper on PYTHONPATH:

week01_root=$PWD
week01_work=$(mktemp -d)
cp lectures/week-01/fixture/{candidate.py,repaired.py,demo.py} "$week01_work/"
(cd "$week01_work" && PYTHONPATH="$week01_root/scripts" python3 demo.py)

Inspect $week01_work/observations.json as text. The command exits zero and prints this transcript:

generation: scripted-course-candidates
candidate / ordinary: 2/2 passed
candidate / contract: 4/6 passed
repaired  / contract: 6/6 passed
regression: original cases retained

Candidate A's two failed checks are expected observations. The demonstration succeeds only when those failures and the repair's six successes match the specified matrix. An unexpected result raises an error. The exported JSON contains each input, expected and actual output, and SHA-256 hashes of the three executed source files.

The hashes bind this public record to source bytes for inspection. An editable local record is practice feedback, not an authoritative grade or proof of a model run. This demonstration makes no model request and supplies no new profile.

The public regression verifier also checks that a broken repair, an unexpectedly changed candidate or an exception cannot produce the success transcript. Run it in the same temporary directory:

cp lectures/week-01/fixture/verify_demo.py "$week01_work/"
(cd "$week01_work" && PYTHONPATH="$week01_root/scripts" python3 verify_demo.py)

Expected: five passing checks (Ran 5 tests, OK) and zero exit status. These checks support the teaching demo; they add no student submission requirement.

docs.title: Inspection and continuation
docs.text:
Read the original two checks and the two previously failing cases. Explain why each added case distinguishes Candidate A from the repair. Describe a behavior the six cases do not test. You can trace the same table without executing code; label that work as a hand trace and use the supplied transcript as a reference expectation.

Keep an absent or unexpected execution result as such; do not present the reference transcript as the output of a failed invocation. Continue the classroom discussion from the written contract and code while the local setup is repaired.

docs.title: Week 2: Advanced context engineering
docs.text:
This week treats context as an engineering input. You will preserve a constraint across research, a plan, an implementation and a check; write specifications that can fail; and design an MCP-style tool for a model reader.

The first session follows the notes, then the slides. The second session is the individual studio. Use the readings for focused source comparison and the self-check after practice.

Due: A2 and the project proposal. Use the current assignment and project pages for submission details.

docs.title: Week 2 studio: specifications and model-facing tools
docs.text:
Duration: 75 minutes, including a revision and a final check.

Purpose: turn your project proposal into failure-capable acceptance cases and make one small tool harder for a model to misuse. Work individually on a disposable copy of your project. This is formative studio work; the A2 and project proposal pages define the submissions.

Materials: your proposal, the notes, a text editor, Python 3.12, and a terminal. The retained fixture and session are optional reading.

docs.title: 1. Write cases before code (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Create a scratch directory and a proposal record:

mkdir -p week02-studio
cat > week02-studio/acceptance.md <<'EOF'
# Acceptance cases

## Case 1 — happy path
Given <precondition>
When <request>
Then <observable result>

## Case 2 — forbidden or malformed input
Given <precondition>
When <request>
Then <observable refusal and unchanged state>

## Case 3 — boundary value
Given <precondition>
When <request>
Then <observable result>
EOF

Replace every placeholder with your proposal's core scenario. Add a fourth or fifth case only when it exposes a distinct risk. For each case name the input, the observable result, and the state that must not change on failure. Predict one case that should fail before you run anything.

docs.title: 2. Make the cases executable (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Add a tiny checker beside the record. It must exit nonzero when a case is wrong:

cat > week02-studio/check_cases.py <<'PY'
def export_result(path: str) -> str:
    if not path.startswith("out/"):
        return "refused: read-only root"
    return "exported"


expected = {"happy": "exported", "forbidden": "refused: read-only root"}
actual = {
    "happy": export_result("out/summary.csv"),
    "forbidden": export_result("reports/summary.csv"),
}
missing = [name for name, value in actual.items() if value != expected[name]]
if missing:
    print("failed:", ", ".join(missing))
    raise SystemExit(1)
print("passed:", ", ".join(actual))
PY
python week02-studio/check_cases.py

Replace export_result with the smallest behavior from your project or a synthetic function. Keep the first failing output by changing the forbidden path temporarily, then restore it and make the smallest change that makes the checker pass. If your project cannot run locally, use a pure Python function in the scratch directory and state that boundary in the record.

docs.title: 3. Tighten one model-facing schema (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Choose one small tool your project uses. Copy its current name, description, schema and error text into week02-studio/tool-before.json. Add a closed schema, a required field, or an allowed path/enum. Make the error name the bad field and a repair. Save the revised form as tool-after.json.

If you do not have a tool ready, start with this deliberately loose example:

cat > week02-studio/tool-before.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "export_report",
  "description": "Write a CSV report.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "path": {"type": "string"},
      "rows": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "object"}}
    }
  }
}
EOF
cat > week02-studio/tool-after.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "export_report",
  "description": "Write a CSV below out/; never writes reports/.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "required": ["path", "rows"],
    "properties": {
      "path": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^out/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+\\.csv$"},
      "rows": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "object"}}
    }
  }
}
EOF

Run this direct schema smoke test (it uses only the standard library):

python - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path
before = json.loads(Path("week02-studio/tool-before.json").read_text())
after = json.loads(Path("week02-studio/tool-after.json").read_text())
assert after != before, "revise at least one model-facing field"
schema = after.get("inputSchema", after)
assert schema.get("type") == "object"
assert schema.get("additionalProperties") is False
assert schema.get("required"), "name a required input"
print("schema smoke test passed")
PY

Run three calls through a tiny stub so the schema and handler boundary are both exercised:

cat > week02-studio/check_tool.py <<'PY'
import json
import re
from pathlib import Path

schema = json.loads(Path("week02-studio/tool-after.json").read_text())["inputSchema"]
assert schema["type"] == "object" and schema["additionalProperties"] is False
assert set(schema["required"]) == {"path", "rows"}

def call_tool(args):
    unknown = set(args) - set(schema["properties"])
    if unknown:
        return "refused: unknown field " + sorted(unknown)[0], False
    if any(field not in args for field in schema["required"]):
        return "refused: missing required field", False
    if not re.fullmatch(r"out/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+\.csv", args["path"]):
        return "refused: path; use out/<name>.csv", False
    return "exported", True

for args, expected, reached in [
    ({"path": "out/summary.csv", "rows": [{"id": "1"}]}, "exported", True),
    ({"path": "reports/summary.csv", "rows": []}, "refused: path; use out/<name>.csv", False),
    ({"path": "out/summary.csv", "rows": [], "extra": 1}, "refused: unknown field extra", False),
]:
    result, handler_called = call_tool(args)
    assert result == expected and handler_called is reached
    print(result)
assert not Path("out/summary.csv").exists(), "stub must not write files"
PY
python week02-studio/check_tool.py

The valid call reaches the stub handler; the two invalid calls are rejected first, with a field-specific repair and no file effect. Replace the example with your tool and keep the same three observations. The invalid calls must be rejected before the handler changes state, and their messages must tell the model what to fix.

docs.title: 4. Handoff and verify (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Write a six-line handoff containing the goal, constraint source, current files, last failed check, remaining unknown and next action. Compare each line with the evidence you collected. Then rerun the happy and failure cases after the schema edit. Finish with one decision line: Decision: accept | shrink | recheck | stop — evidence: <commands or paths>.

A partner is not required. At minute 45, pause for a staff check-in if your case cannot fail or your tool has no observable refusal. More time or an approved access accommodation should preserve the same cases and evidence.

docs.title: Studio record
docs.text: Keep acceptance.md, the before/after schema, the smoke-test output, the first failing run, the corrected run and the decision line in the scratch directory until feedback. Do not put credentials in the proposal, prompt, screenshots or logs. Use the Week 0 safety practices for any coding agent you choose; the studio commands themselves use no model or network.

docs.title: Dissect a recorded agent session
docs.text:
The loop you finish in the Week 1 notes shows the idea in miniature. A mature coding agent runs the same loop, but every request carries far more: long instructions, a set of tool definitions and the whole conversation so far. In this activity you read one recorded session request by request. You predict first, check each prediction against the record, and then compare what you saw with your own Week 1 loop.

The session shipped with this page, sample-session.jsonl, is course-made: the course team wrote it by hand in the same format a recording of a real agent uses. It shows what to look for. It does not describe how any product behaves, and it contains no measured numbers.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Optional practice. It earns no marks and has no submission. Week 1 uses the questions of step 3 when you read your own session for A1, and Week 2 uses the record to look at how a request grows.

Estimated time: about two and a half hours for all five steps: predictions, the request-by-request reading, the comparison with your loop and the short write-up. This is an estimate, not a limit; steps 1-4 stand on their own if you have less time.

Order:

  1. Do steps 1-4 on the published record.
  2. Swap tables with a partner as described under Review, and revise.
  3. Step 5 needs the completion.json your own Week 1 loop wrote, so do it once your run() passes its checks. Then write up the records.

Materials:

  • the record: session/sample-session.jsonl, or a teaching-team recording of a real agent if one has been published beside it (see below);
  • the viewer: session/show_session.py;
  • for step 5, your copy of the Week 1 loop and the completion.json it wrote;
  • the notes section on reading a production agent's instructions.

Grouping: work alone or in pairs. You may discuss the record with a partner, but each person writes their own predictions, dissection and comparison.

Cost: everyone dissects the same published record. The activity makes no model call and needs no API key or agent seat.

AI use: red. Write your predictions, dissection and comparison without AI; the point is your own reading.

docs.title: Which record to use
docs.text: The header line of each record names its source. "provenance": "course-made-sample" is the hand-written sample. "provenance": "teacher-recording" is a real session that the teaching team captured; its header gives the agent's name and version, the recording date and a list of what was redacted. When a teacher recording sits beside the sample in session/, dissect the teacher recording and use the sample only to practise the steps. Otherwise, dissect the sample.

docs.title: Step 1: predict before you open the record
docs.text:
Read only the task in the header line: the agent must change a status label in a small repository and keep its tests passing, which touches a source file and a test file. Then, before running the viewer, write down your answers:

  1. How many requests will the agent send to the model to finish this two-file change?
  2. Which tool will it call first?
  3. Will the instructions and tool definitions be sent once, or with every request?
  4. Will any tool call fail? If one does, what will the agent do next?
  5. How will the size of the request change from the first request to the last? Will anything sent earlier be removed or rewritten?
  6. Why will the loop stop, and what evidence will the agent have for its final message?

Keep these answers unchanged. You compare them with the record in step 4.

docs.title: Step 2: read the record request by request
docs.text:
Run the viewer from the course root. It uses only Python's standard library, reads the file and prints text. It never runs anything found in the record and never uses the network.

python3 lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py lectures/week-02/session/sample-session.jsonl

The summary prints one block per request: whether the instructions and tools were sent again, which messages are new since the previous request, which earlier messages changed, and what came back. To see everything one request sent and received, including the full instructions, every tool schema and every message, name the request:

python3 lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py lectures/week-02/session/sample-session.jsonl --request 4

Expected: the summary starts with a Session: line naming the source and ends with an End of record block. A file the viewer cannot read as a session record gives one error: line naming the problem and its line number.

docs.title: Step 3: dissect
docs.text:
Fill one row per request. Keep each cell short and cite what you saw.

Request New or changed instructions Tools offered (count; any change) What came back: text, tool calls or both How the results return What was re-sent, cleared or rewritten Continue or stop, and why

Then answer these questions. Label every answer [observed] when you can point to it in the record (give the request number and message index, for example request 5, [11]), or [inferred] when you are reasoning from what you read without having seen it happen. Both kinds are acceptable. A wrong label is the mistake to avoid.

A. The instructions. Open the instructions in request 1. Sort each sentence into the four groups from the notes: role or goal, tool contract, stopping or escalation rule, request for caution. Pick one sentence from each group and say which failure it guards against. Then say what, if anything, enforces it: a tool schema, the tool's own checks, a sandbox, an approval step, or nothing. Where does the description of the environment (working directory, date) sit in the request? Find a message that was added in the middle of the conversation rather than at the start. Who wrote it, which role does it use, and why might an agent add it there instead of repeating it in the instructions?

B. The tools. How many tools were offered, and did the set change during the session? Choose two tools that do different kinds of work, for example a file-editing tool and the planning tool, or the command tool. For each one: copy the relevant part of its schema; say which parameters are required, which are optional and what the tool deliberately does not let the model choose; find one sentence in its description that looks as if it was added because a model kept making the same mistake, and name that mistake. Which constraints does the schema enforce, and which does the description only ask for?

C. What the model returned. For each response, was it text, tool calls or both? Find a response with more than one tool call. Were those calls independent of each other?

D. How results return. How does each tool result find its call? What did the agent see when a tool call failed, and what did it do in the next request? Count the requests between the failure and the recovery, and quote the error text exactly.

E. Where and why the loop stopped. Which response ended the loop, and how can you tell from the record alone? Find the observation that supports the final message. Is the final claim verified by an observation in the record, or only stated? Would the record let you detect a final message that claimed more than the agent had checked?

F. What was re-sent, cleared or rewritten. How did the request size change across the session, and what accounts for most of it? Which earlier messages changed between two requests, what replaced them, and what information did that remove? Did the agent need that information again, and how would it get it back?

G. Plans and task state. Where does the agent keep track of which steps are done? If it records a plan or task list, list every place the plan appears: tool calls, tool results and any message added in the middle of the conversation. What does the result of a plan update tell the agent, and what does it not check? Find a request where the plan, as last recorded, is behind what the tool results already show, or say there is none. For each item marked completed at the end, cite the observation that shows the step was done. If the agent keeps no plan, say where its task state lives instead.

docs.title: Step 4: check your predictions
docs.text: Put each prediction from step 1 next to what you observed. For the prediction that was furthest off, write two or three sentences: what in the record surprised you, and what you would now expect from your own loop in the same situation.

docs.title: Step 5: compare with your Week 1 loop
docs.text:
Open the completion.json that demo.py wrote in your copy of the Week 1 loop (the notes use the directory week01-loop). It is one JSON object: the whole message history of one scripted run, the stop reason and the status of the last check. Open your loop.py beside it.

Answer from the two records side by side:

  • What does your loop send as its first message, and what does the recorded agent send? Where do your tool names and argument rules live: in a schema the model sees, in your validation code (checked), or both?
  • Does your loop pass the whole history on every turn? Compare that with what the recorded agent re-sent or cleared.
  • How does each loop decide to stop, and what evidence does each have at that point?
  • Where does each loop keep track of which steps are done, and what would happen to that record if old messages were dropped or cleared?

Then choose:

  • one behaviour you would copy into your loop, and
  • one behaviour you would change if you built the recorded agent,

each with its evidence (request number and what you saw) and the check that would show it working: a test, a trace you would inspect, or a failing case that should now stop correctly. A behaviour you copy without a check is a claim, not an improvement.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
Nothing is handed in. Keep, in your own notes:

  • your six predictions as you wrote them before reading the record;
  • the request table and your answers to A–G, each labelled and cited;
  • the prediction check and your copy/change choices with their checks.

Name the record you dissected by its file name and provenance. Cite request numbers and quote only the lines your answer depends on. The labels and the citation style are the ones A1 asks for on your own session; if you reuse an answer there, check every quoted line for keys, personal data and private code first. Never include an API key, a header or an environment value.

docs.title: Review
docs.text: Swap your table with a partner. The partner checks one [observed] answer against the record using its request number, and marks any place where a final message or success claim has no supporting observation. Revise that answer. The partner's check is feedback; your explanation remains your own.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake How to notice it Small correction Counting tool calls instead of requests Your request count differs from the number of Request N blocks One response can hold several calls; count model requests Treating the final message as evidence Your answer to E quotes only the last message Find the tool result that supports it, or say there is none Treating a plan item marked completed as evidence Your answer to G cites only a plan update Find the tool result that shows the step was done Assuming an instruction is enforced You cannot name what would stop the model from ignoring it Look for a schema rule, a tool check or a sandbox; otherwise it only asks Missing what the agent wrote into the conversation You attribute every user message to the person Read the message itself; an agent can add messages in any role Labelling an inference as observed Your citation points to a message that does not show the claim Change the label or find the request that shows it

All materials are plain text. The viewer output, tables and record can be read with a screen reader or keyboard-only editor; no diagram or colour is needed for any step.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you can:

  • LO2: choose, order and check context for a coding-agent task, and design a small MCP-style tool whose name, schema and errors guide a model toward a safe call.
  • LO3: turn a project proposal into executable acceptance cases, including a case that must fail, and use the cases to connect research, a plan, implementation and verification.

Every example below has a generate step and a verify step. The examples are course-authored and synthetic; they are not claims about a product or a benchmark.

docs.title: One constraint, four places to lose it
docs.text:
Suppose a proposal says: “A report may read reports/, but it must never write there.” A direct request to an agent—“add CSV export”—does not say where the rule came from or how to check it. The constraint can disappear in four transitions:

  1. Research: the agent reads an old README but not the current permission test.
  2. Plan: the plan says “add export” and drops the read-only boundary.
  3. Implement: the tool schema exposes path with no allowed-root description.
  4. Verify: the test checks that a CSV exists but never attempts a write to reports/.

Generate: write a one-paragraph plan for the export request. Verify: underline the constraint, its source, the implementation boundary and the negative test. If one is missing, the plan is incomplete even when the generated code looks plausible.

docs.title: Research, plan, implement
docs.text:
Use three short artifacts rather than one unbounded prompt:

Phase Question Artifact that can be checked Research What is true at this revision? Evidence table with paths, symbols and unknowns Plan What small change would satisfy the request? Ordered steps, boundaries and acceptance cases Implement What code expresses that plan? Patch plus the commands that exercise each case

Generate: for the synthetic export request, make an evidence table with two rows naming the export handler and its rejection test. Mark an unknown explicitly rather than guessing. Verify: open both files at your checkout revision; change “confirmed” to “cannot tell” when the source does not show the claim. A plan is more useful when a reader can disagree with one row and run one check.

docs.title: A specification that can fail
docs.text:
Write acceptance cases as observable input and output. The following cases are deliberately small:

Given an export root called out/
When the request names out/summary.csv and rows are valid
Then the file is created and the command reports exported

Given the same root
When the request names reports/summary.csv
Then no file is written and the command reports refused: read-only root

Given the same root
When a row is missing its id
Then no file is written and the command reports invalid row: id

Generate: implement the smallest function that could satisfy the three cases. Verify: run the positive case and each negative case against a fresh temporary directory. A specification that only says “export works” cannot reveal a missing refusal or a partial write.

The project proposal due this week is the first version of this artifact. Keep its core scenario, boundary and three to five failure-capable acceptance cases together. Revise it when research shows that a case is not observable.

docs.title: Context packets and compaction
docs.text:
A context window is a working budget. Tool output, repeated reads and failed attempts consume it; a later request can then miss the one constraint that mattered. The retained session recording and dissection let you inspect this effect without making a model call. The course-written compaction script shows it on one hand-written session. It reads the session file beside it, so run it from its own folder:

(cd lectures/week-03/fixture && python compaction.py full)
(cd lectures/week-03/fixture && python compaction.py auto)

full keeps all 19 messages, reports "check": "passed" and exits 0. auto clears the older tool results, loses the line that says not to edit view.py, reports "check": "failed" and exits 1. No model is called in either run.

Generate: before shortening a history, write a handoff with the task, source of each constraint, current file state, last failed check and next action. Verify: compare each line with the recorded messages, then rerun the check on the current revision. A summary that says “tests passed” without the tested revision is not evidence.

When most entries are stale or contradictory, restart with a written handoff and reread the next files. Compacting is a choice about information, not a guarantee that the model will remember the right information.

docs.title: Tool design for a model reader
docs.text:
A model sees a tool's name, description, input schema and returned message. Treat these as a contract, not decoration. A small example:

{
  "name": "export_report",
  "description": "Write a CSV below out/; never writes reports/.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "required": ["path", "rows"],
    "properties": {
      "path": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^out/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+\\.csv$"},
      "rows": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "object"}}
    }
  }
}

Generate: propose a call for out/summary.csv and one for reports/summary.csv. Verify: validate both against the schema and run the handler. The first should reach the handler; the second should produce a short, actionable error and no file effect.

Use five design checks:

  1. Name: a verb and object make the intended action selectable.
  2. Description: state the allowed root and the important exclusion.
  3. Schema: make required fields, types, closed properties and simple patterns machine-checkable.
  4. Errors: identify the bad field and the next repair; never return a traceback.
  5. Result: return the observation the next decision needs, including refusal and partial-failure states.

MCP names the protocol family used to connect a model application with tools and resources. The protocol does not make a vague tool safe: the handler still enforces its boundary, and the controller still has to pass the result back to the model. Read the interface as a model reader would, then test the behavior with calls.

docs.title: Reading a production agent's instructions
docs.text: The factsheet readings compare two pinned open-source files. Select one rule about plans, one about a tool schema and one about stopping. For each, write four labels: what the text asks the model to do, what code checks, what the runtime checks and what remains unknown. A description can ask for three lines of context while tool code enforces only a single-match rule; keep those claims separate. Do not infer current releases from a pinned source.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text: The studio is an individual 75-minute pass over your own project proposal. You will write three to five acceptance cases that can fail, then tighten one small tool schema and error message. Keep the before/after schema and every command result. The retained Week 1 fixture and session remain available for inspection.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Use this order:

  1. Check each research claim against the file and revision named in the evidence table.
  2. Validate every acceptance case once on a fresh temporary directory, including its expected failure.
  3. Validate the revised schema with a valid call, an invalid call and an unknown field.
  4. Record the command, exit status, observed output and the decision to accept, shrink, recheck or stop.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Prompt first, evidence later: search the relevant files and record unknowns before asking for an implementation.
  • A plan with no rejection: add a malformed or forbidden input whose expected result is an observable refusal.
  • A schema that accepts everything: close the object and constrain paths, enums or bounds that the handler relies on.
  • An error that only says “invalid”: name the field and a repair, then test that the model receives the message.
  • Confusing a generated answer with verification: rerun the acceptance case after the last write; preserve the failed result and tested revision.
  • Treating a protocol name as enforcement: identify the handler and runtime checks; mark anything else as unknown.
  • Compacting away the rule: keep the task, constraint source, current state, open failure, paths and next action in the handoff.

docs.title: Compare two production prompts
docs.text:
The Week 1 loop keeps a short tool contract for a model, the CONTRACT text in demo.py. A production coding agent sends much more: a role, working rules, a permission policy, a stopping rule and a schema for every tool. Two open-source coding agents publish the code that builds that text under the Apache-2.0 licence: Codex CLI and Qwen Code. In this activity you read the same four parts in both, at fixed commits, and ask the same two questions of every sentence you pick: what does it make the model do, and what, if anything, enforces it?

You read the original files on GitHub. This page links them and quotes only a few words, always naming the project; it does not copy the files. Facts about the files come from two reading pages, one for Codex CLI (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) and one for Qwen Code (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7). Neither agent's files are the complete prompt a release sends at run time, and this page does not rank the two products.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Optional, about 45 minutes. It earns no marks. It extends the notes' section on reading a production agent's instructions and replaces the shorter single-file reading. Parts 1-4 need only a browser. Part 5 is a written plan.

Before you start: your Week 1 run() passes its checks, or you have read its five steps in the Week 1 notes. You can name its three tools and its two stop reasons.

AI use: red. Write your answers yourself; the point is your own reading.

Output: one table for Parts 1-4 and a short Part 5 plan, for your own notes. Nothing is handed in.

docs.title: The files
docs.text:
Part Codex CLI, commit 2351d9e Qwen Code, tag v0.25.0 (commit 6788c03) 1. Role and instructions default.md: the opening paragraph and capabilities list, "Task execution", "Validating your work" prompts.ts: getDefaultCoreIdentitySentence, "Core Mandates", "Software Engineering Tasks" 2. Tools and schemas the apply_patch example in "Task execution"; plan_spec.rs for update_plan "Using Your Tools" in prompts.ts; edit.ts for edit; todoWrite.ts for todo_write 3. Safety and permission the approval sentence in the capabilities list; "Validating your work"; the rules that begin NEVER or Do not "Denied Tool Calls", "Respect Tool Decisions", "Executing actions with care", the sandbox sections 4. Stopping and plans the first paragraph of "Task execution"; "update_plan" under "Tool Guidelines" "Final Reminder"; the todo_write description in todoWrite.ts

Open both Codex CLI files, the base instructions default.md and the tool definition plan_spec.rs, from the links on its reading page; the Qwen Code files are linked in the table and on its reading page.

default.md is Markdown: read it as it stands. prompts.ts is TypeScript that builds the prompt. Text between backticks is what the model receives, and ${...} inserts a value, often a tool name such as ${ToolNames.EDIT}; the names are listed in tool-names.ts. Which sections appear depends on the interaction mode, the sandbox configuration and whether the directory is a Git repository, and an environment variable can replace the whole default base prompt with a file. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) Read the interactive default.

docs.title: Record
docs.text:
Use one row per sentence or rule. Pick at least two per part, one from each agent.

Part Agent Section and a few words What it makes the model do What enforces it Where you saw that

For what enforces it, choose one: the schema (a malformed call is rejected before the tool runs); the tool's own code (it checks and returns an error text to the model); a runtime permission or sandbox outside the model; or nothing visible. Write "cannot tell" when you did not open the code that would decide, and say which file you would need.

docs.title: Part 1: role and instructions
docs.text:
1. Find the sentence in each file that says what the agent is and what its goal is. Which words could change a choice the agent makes on a dashboard repair, and which only name it?
  2. Find each agent's rule for checking work after a change. The Codex CLI file ties when to run tests and lint to the approval mode; the Qwen Code file asks for the project's own checks before reporting a change complete, and for an honest report when a check failed or was not run. (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) For each, describe a run in which the agent reports a change without having run a test. Which field in your Week 1 completion.json would show that case, and with what value?

docs.title: Part 2: tools and schemas
docs.text:
1. Compare update_plan with todo_write: required and optional fields, the allowed status values, and where "one step in progress" is written. In todoWrite.ts, read validateTodos: list what it checks, and say whether it checks that limit. For Codex CLI, can you tell from the files you opened? Mark "cannot tell" where you cannot.
  2. In edit.ts, read the edit tool's description, its parameter schema, validateToolParamValues and calculateEdit. Sort each rule into required by the schema, checked by code with an error returned to the model, or only asked in the description. Start from two: "at least 3 lines of context" is only asked, while a second match without replace_all fails with an error that gives the count. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) What does the model see on its next turn when it breaks each kind?
  3. The Codex CLI file names apply_patch and shows one call. Did you open its schema? If not, name what you would need to read before you could sort its rules the same way.
  4. Sort your own loop the same way: what does checked reject, what does tool refuse, and what appears only in the CONTRACT text of demo.py?

docs.title: Part 3: safety and permission rules
docs.text:
1. In the Qwen Code file, "Respect Tool Decisions" says the runtime enforces tool permissions, while "Denied Tool Calls" asks the model not to reach a denied action another way, through a shell, a generated script or an alias. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) Why might a product need that request as well as the runtime check? For your loop, name one route that tool closes and one that only the environment the agent runs in closes (the dedicated directory or container of the safety practices).
  2. The Codex CLI capabilities list refers to a "Sandbox and approvals" section that the file itself does not contain. (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) What does that tell you about where the rest of the prompt comes from, and what would you need to read next?
  3. Pick one sentence from "Executing actions with care" or a sandbox section in the Qwen Code file. Describing a sandbox to the model does not create one: which control outside the prompt would have to exist for the sentence to be true? Compare with the permission comparison in the notes.

docs.title: Part 4: stopping and plans
docs.text:
1. Both files ask the agent to keep going until the request is resolved; the Qwen Code file also names an exit, reporting the specific blocker. (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) Neither sentence can stop a loop. Which code stops your run(), and what would a production agent need in place of your step_limit?
  2. A plan step marked completed is the model's own claim. Which observation would you need before you accept it? Compare your answer with question G of the session dissection.

docs.title: Part 5: change one part for your own project
docs.text:
Choose one sentence or schema rule from either file that you would change or add if the agent were working in your own project repository. Examples: name the acceptance command instead of "the project's own test commands", or require a passing check after the last write before any final reply. Write three things:

  • The change and where it belongs: the product's base prompt, a repository instruction file (Week 3), a tool schema, or controller code. If a rule can be checked in code, say why you would or would not still put it in the prompt.
  • The predicted effect, as something a session record would show: which call appears, the stop reason and the check status.
  • The verification: which line of a record, or which check, would show the effect.

Keep this part a written prediction. The scripted proposer in the Week 1 demo.py never reads CONTRACT, so adding your sentence there changes nothing you can observe in scripted practice. Write the record you would expect with and without the change: did a verify call follow the last write, and what were the stop reason and the check? If you later try the sentence in a real agent session, one run of each version is one observation, not a rate; report it that way. Either way, also say which part of your loop already reports the truth regardless of the prompt: last_check stays not_run or check_failed whatever the model writes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake How to notice it Small correction Treating a sentence as a guarantee Your "what enforces it" column says the prompt Name a schema, a code check or a runtime control, or write "nothing visible" Guessing about code you did not open You wrote "enforced" for a rule whose checker you never read Write "cannot tell" and name the file to read Reading prompts.ts as one fixed text You quote two sandbox sections as if both were sent Pick one branch and say which condition selects it Copying long passages into your record Your table holds whole paragraphs Give the section and a few words; link the pinned file Judging one product better Your answer ranks the agents Compare what each rule does and what enforces it

All files are plain text on GitHub and can be read with a screen reader or keyboard; no diagram or colour is needed for any step.

docs.title: Week 2 readings: context and tool contracts
docs.text:
Read the notes first. Before opening an explanation, predict which constraint each phase will preserve and which acceptance case should fail. After the studio, use the self-check to name the evidence you would rerun.

The only external readings below are pinned primary sources recorded in the course factsheets. Read the named sections at the cited revision; the factsheets are source records, not a substitute for the primary files.

docs.title: Source 1 — Codex CLI instructions and plan schema (optional, 20 minutes)
docs.text: Read the pinned base-instructions factsheet, especially its named primary-source sections “Task execution”, “Validating your work” and update_plan; follow its pinned source links. Then read the pinned plan-schema source named there. Scope: identify one instruction, one schema-enforced field and one rule whose enforcement the files do not establish. Record the pinned revision in your notes.

docs.title: Source 2 — Qwen Code prompt builder and edit schema (optional, 20 minutes)
docs.text: Read the pinned prompt-builder and tool-schema factsheet, then follow its named primary-source links for the prompt builder, edit and todo_write. Scope: compare a description-level request with a behavior checked by code, then write a call that should return a useful error. Do not infer behavior outside these files.

docs.title: Source 3 — course contract (required, 10 minutes)
docs.text: Read the Week 2 schedule, which is generated from SYLLABUS.md §4. Confirm the Week 2 topic, LO2/LO3 and the A2 and proposal due items. Scope: connect the studio record to the current course outputs.

docs.title: Optional local inspection
docs.text: The retained session recording and dissection are deterministic course material. From the repository root, use python lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py lectures/week-02/session/sample-session.jsonl to inspect request growth. This command reads the record and does not call a model.

docs.title: Week 2 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Use these explanations after a first attempt. They describe the evidence a student should be able to reproduce from the proposal, schema and checks.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: The research artifact names the permission test and its revision; the plan repeats the read-only boundary; the schema constrains the path; and the negative case attempts a write under reports/ and expects an unchanged state.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: The plan phase lost the boundary. Read the current permission test and the export handler, record the paths and unknowns, then write a case that distinguishes an allowed path from a forbidden one before editing.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: For example: “Given a row without id, when export is requested, then no file is written and the result is invalid row: id.” Run it against a fresh temporary directory and check both the result and the directory contents.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: The model can attempt any string. The handler must reject a path outside out/ before writing. The error should name path and say to use an out/<name>.csv path.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: The unknown-field rule is schema-level. The description-level request is not evidence of runtime enforcement unless a visible handler or runtime check supports it; mark that enforcement as unknown.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: Keep the task and acceptance check, the source of each constraint, current file state, the last failed check and tested revision, remaining unknowns, and the next action. After a write, rerun the acceptance case on the new revision.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: Return the refusal under the call's ID as the next tool observation. It should identify the rejected field and the repair, then let the model choose a corrected call. A refusal is an observation about one attempted input; it does not show that the requested outcome was achieved, so the controller must still verify the resulting state.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Separate the requested behavior from enforcement. Identify the schema rule, the handler check and any runtime boundary you can see. If the source does not show a check, write “cannot tell” and propose the smallest call that would reveal it.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text:
Retrieval 1. Add a research row naming the read-only test and a negative case that attempts the forbidden write; verify both against the current revision.

Retrieval 2. Make the error identify path and the allowed out/ form, then run a valid and invalid call and keep both observations.

docs.title: Week 2 self-check: context and tool contracts
docs.text:
Answer these questions after the studio, then check each answer against the notes and the source you cite. They are formative and add no separate submission. Keep one correction in your work record. The public answer guidance is available after your first attempt; use the notes to explain each answer.

  1. A proposal says “never write under reports/.” Name one research artifact, one plan line, one schema field and one negative acceptance case that preserve this constraint.
  2. A plan says only “implement CSV export.” Which phase lost information, and what evidence would you collect before editing?
  3. Write a Given/When/Then case for a malformed row. What must remain unchanged when it fails, and what command would observe that?
  4. A tool description says “use a path under out/,” but its schema accepts any string. What can the model attempt, what should the handler enforce, and what error should it return?
  5. A tool schema rejects an unknown field, while the description asks for three lines of context that the code never checks. Label each rule as schema, handler or description.
  6. A context summary says “tests passed” but omits the tested revision. What six items belong in a handoff, and which check must be rerun after the next write?
  7. A valid call returns a refusal. What should the controller send to the model next, and why is a refusal an observation rather than proof that the task is complete?
  8. Compare one rule from Source 1 or Source 2: what does the text request, what code checks, what runtime checks, and what remains unknown?

R1. A later plan omits the read-only boundary. What one research artifact and one negative case would you add before implementation?

R2. A tool returns “invalid” without naming a field. What schema or error change would make the next model call easier to verify?

Finish with: Decision: accept | shrink | recheck | stop — evidence: ....

docs.title: Advanced context engineering
docs.text:
Week 2 · LO2, LO3 and LO9

How does a constraint survive a model's next step?

docs.title: Today’s thread
docs.text:
Prompt → research → plan → implement → verify

MCP-style tools are contracts for a model reader.

docs.title: One constraint
docs.text:
“Read reports/; never write there.”

Where can it disappear?

docs.title: Four losses
docs.text:
1. Research misses the permission test.
  2. Plan says only “add export.”
  3. Schema accepts any path.
  4. Test checks only that a CSV exists.

docs.title: Generate, then verify
docs.text:
Write a one-paragraph plan.

Then underline the source, boundary and negative test.

docs.title: Research artifact
docs.text:
Question Evidence What is true? path + symbol + revision What is unknown? explicit cannot tell

Research records claims; it does not edit code.

docs.title: Plan artifact
docs.text:
An ordered list of small steps:

  • boundary
  • acceptance case
  • implementation point
  • check and expected failure

docs.title: Implement artifact
docs.text:
Patch only what the plan names.

Keep the command that exercises each case.

docs.title: A specification that can fail
docs.text:
Given out/
When path is reports/summary.csv
Then no file is written
And the result says refused: read-only root

What would a passing test observe?

docs.title: Three cases
docs.text:
• happy path
  • forbidden or malformed input
  • boundary value

A “works” sentence is not an acceptance case.

docs.title: Context is a budget
docs.text:
Reads, logs, failed attempts and instructions accumulate.

A later turn can miss the one constraint that mattered.

docs.title: Handoff before compaction
docs.text:
Keep:

  • task and acceptance check
  • constraint source
  • current file state
  • last failed check and revision
  • unknown and next action

docs.title: Restart or compact?
docs.text:
Compact when the next raw result still matters.

Restart with a written handoff when history is stale or contradictory.

Verify the handoff against the transcript.

docs.title: A model-facing tool
docs.text:
{"name":"export_report",
 "description":"Write below out/; never writes reports/.",
 "inputSchema":{"type":"object",
  "additionalProperties":false,
  "required":["path","rows"]}}

docs.title: Five contract checks
docs.text:
1. Name: verb + object.
  2. Description: boundary and exclusion.
  3. Schema: types, required fields, closed object.
  4. Error: bad field + repair.
  5. Result: the next observation.

docs.title: Which call is allowed?
docs.text:
{"path":"out/summary.csv","rows":[]}
{"path":"reports/summary.csv","rows":[]}

The first reaches the handler. The second is refused before an effect.

docs.title: Errors are context
docs.text:
refused: path must start with out/

Short, actionable, and returned under the call's ID.

docs.title: MCP is an interface family
docs.text:
A protocol name does not enforce a boundary.

The schema, handler and runtime each have a job.

docs.title: Read a pinned source
docs.text:
Choose one rule from Source 1 or Source 2.

Ask: text, schema, code, runtime—or unknown?

docs.title: Studio: cases first
docs.text:
Write three to five cases for your project proposal.

Predict one failure before running it.

docs.title: Studio: tighten one schema
docs.text:
Save before and after.

Test one valid call, one invalid call and one unknown field.

docs.title: Verify the revision
docs.text:
Run every case after the last write.

Record command, exit status, output and decision.

docs.title: Common traps
docs.text:
Prompt first. No rejection case. Open schema. Vague error.

A fluent answer is not a check result.

docs.title: Week 2 handoff
docs.text:
Due: A2 and project proposal.

Keep the acceptance cases, schema diff and evidence together.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Which constraint did your tool make visible?

docs.title: Public files
docs.text:
• demo.py
  • loop.py
  • verify_loop.py

docs.title: Public files
docs.text:
• sample-session.jsonl
  • show_session.py

docs.title: Week 3: Agent skills and the CLI
docs.text:
This folder teaches one repeatable loop: run a workflow by hand, encode it as a SKILL.md, test three expected triggers and one near miss, then preserve the evidence from a command-line run. The studio prepares A3 and its accept/narrow/recheck/stop decision line.

Start with notes, use the direct checker command in activities, and finish with the self-check. The readings name the course-authored skill examples and the checker. The checker is fixture/skill_check.py.

docs.title: Week 3: Agent skills and the CLI studio
Learning objectives
docs.text: This studio turns one repeated workflow into a tested skill. You will run it by hand, write a SKILL.md, predict three matches and one near miss, run the supplied checker, and preserve the evidence from one command-line agent session. The work supports LO2 and is the main preparation for A3.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text: Use the release-check example in the lecture notes. The hand run is the baseline. The skill is a proposal. The trigger table records a prediction and an observation; the checker reports structure, not whether an agent really selected it.

docs.title: Build and test one skill
docs.text: Time: 70 minutes. Format: individual work with a ten-minute peer check. Materials: your project repository, the course checkout, and the read-only checker in lectures/week-03/fixture/skill_check.py. No special runner or paid account is required for the file check.

docs.title: 1. Choose and run a workflow (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Choose a non-destructive workflow you have already done twice. Write its shell commands and run them once by hand. Run steps 1 to 3 from the root of your own project repository: git rev-parse needs a Git repository, and every studio file goes in an A3-work/ directory there. The commands below are one such workflow:

mkdir -p A3-work/hand-run
printf '%s\n' "revision: $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" | tee A3-work/hand-run/run.txt
git status --short | tee -a A3-work/hand-run/run.txt
git diff --check 2>&1 | tee -a A3-work/hand-run/run.txt

Add the project's focused test command and its output. If a command fails, preserve the failure and explain whether the skill should stop or continue. Do not run model-generated unknown commands in a directory containing employer, cloud, or other real credentials.

docs.title: 2. Write the skill (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Still in your project root, create the directory and file, then edit the file in your normal editor:

mkdir -p A3-work/skills/my-workflow
# Write A3-work/skills/my-workflow/SKILL.md from the notes' three-section example.

The front matter name must match my-workflow (or your chosen hyphenated directory). The description must say what the workflow does and include when. In Steps, name the commands. In Judgement, state at least one stop or branch. In Verification, name the exact check command and the evidence it leaves.

docs.title: 3. Predict four requests (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Copy this starter into A3-work/trigger-test.yaml and replace the prompts with your own:

skill: my-workflow
observer: agent
observer_detail: CLI run on the fixed revision of the student's project; each boolean is tied to the saved selection evidence.
prompts:
  - id: matching-request
    prompt: Run my repeated workflow and report the check output.
    should_trigger: true
    predicted: true
    observed: false
  - id: matching-words
    prompt: Inspect the same workflow before we review the change.
    should_trigger: true
    predicted: true
    observed: false
  - id: matching-paraphrase
    prompt: Perform the repository check I have used twice and preserve evidence.
    should_trigger: true
    predicted: true
    observed: false
  - id: near-miss
    prompt: Implement a new feature and add its tests.
    should_trigger: false
    predicted: false
    observed: false

The observed values are placeholders only. Fill them after the agent run. If any observation differs from should_trigger, add a revision section naming the description change and recheck exactly those IDs. Do not rewrite the original prediction.

docs.title: 4. Run the CLI and preserve evidence (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Run the coding-agent command supplied for your seat once on the fixed revision of your project. Keep the exact request and output in A3-work/agent-run.txt; do not include secrets. If the CLI does not print skill selection, record selection: not shown there. Keep each YAML observed value boolean and explain its evidence in observer_detail. Then change to the course checkout, where the checker lives, and run it with paths that point into your project:

PROJECT_ROOT=/path/to/your/project
uv run --locked python lectures/week-03/fixture/skill_check.py \
  "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/skills/my-workflow/SKILL.md" \
  "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/trigger-test.yaml"
