The command reads YAML and Markdown only. It does not execute your skill or claim that the agent selected it.

docs.title: 5. Compare and decide (10 minutes)
docs.text: Make a four-row prediction-versus-observation table. Cite the hand-run file, the CLI run, the checker output, and the revision. Write one sentence at the end: accept, narrow, recheck, or stop, plus the evidence ID. A peer checks that the near miss is actually near and that no observation was invented.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Your studio record is complete when the following commands run from the course checkout (the git -C commands read your project wherever you run them):

PROJECT_ROOT=/path/to/your/project
uv run --locked python lectures/week-03/fixture/skill_check.py \
  "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/skills/my-workflow/SKILL.md" \
  "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/trigger-test.yaml"
git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" rev-parse HEAD
git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" diff --check

Expected evidence is Structure checked., the fixed revision, a clean diff check (or the failure you recorded), and the four-row table. A structure failure is a repair-and-rerun case; it is not a reason to change observed to make the table look better.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing the skill before doing the workflow by hand.
  • Using four prompts that all contain the skill name; at least three positive prompts must test the description in natural language.
  • Calling a near miss an error rather than evidence about the description boundary.
  • Filling observed from expectation when the CLI did not show selection.
  • Running an agent outside the course safety practices or leaving a key in the transcript.

docs.title: A3 handoff
docs.text: Submit the skill, trigger test, hand-run evidence, CLI evidence summary, checker output, prediction table, and one final decision line. A3 is due this week.

docs.title: Week 3: Agent skills and the CLI
Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you can:

  • run a repeated command-line workflow by hand and describe the inputs, decisions, and checks it actually needs;
  • package that workflow in a small SKILL.md, keeping the description specific enough to select and the body short enough to load;
  • write three requests that should trigger the skill and one near miss that should stay quiet, then compare your predictions with an observed run; and
  • preserve command output, the exact request, the repository revision, and the final verification result as evidence.

The skill is a workflow description, not a permission grant. A skill can suggest a command; the normal shell, repository policy, and your review still decide whether it runs. The examples on this page are course-authored records, not model observations.

docs.title: Do the workflow once by hand
docs.text:
Suppose a project has a repeated release-check routine. Before writing a skill, do one run without an agent:

git status --short
git diff --check
uv run --locked pytest -q

The first command tells you whether unrelated edits are present, the second catches whitespace errors, and the last command is the project's check. Record the revision with git rev-parse --short HEAD and keep the output. If the check fails, write the failure and stop; do not hide it behind a skill.

docs.title: Encode the procedure
docs.text:
A skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md. Its YAML front matter names the skill and describes when it applies. The body explains steps, judgement, and verification. This small example is deliberately narrower than “help with this repository”:

---
name: release-check
description: Run the repository's release checks and report evidence when a change is ready for review.
---
## Steps
1. Read the requested boundary and run `git status --short`.
2. Run `git diff --check`, then the repository's test command.
## Judgement
- If unrelated files are modified, stop and report them before testing.
- If a check fails, keep its output and do not call the change ready.
## Verification
Run `git diff --check` and `uv run --locked pytest -q`; include the revision and output.

The description is the selection surface. The format uses progressive disclosure: metadata is available before activation, while the body is loaded after selection and bundled resources only when needed (tools/agent-skills; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1). A long explanation in the description makes unrelated requests look like matches; a vague description makes the skill invisible. Compare the hand run with the skill line by line: which step is new, which evidence is preserved, and which decision would be impossible from the output alone?

docs.title: Test selection, including a near miss
docs.text:
The course kit contains three complete examples: research-codebase, plan-change and review-diff. Read only each SKILL.md description first. For research-codebase, predict this table before looking at its trigger record:

Request Prediction Reason “Trace this request and cite the files and lines you observed.” trigger It asks for a read-only path record. “Tell me what the handlers and tests do before we discuss edits.” trigger It asks for current facts before a change. “Build a read-only call-path record for this unfamiliar module.” trigger It names the same bounded research job in new words. “Implement the change and add a regression test.” stay quiet It asks for implementation, the near miss.

Now open trigger-test.yaml and compare predicted with observed. The checker verifies the record's shape and that it contains at least three positive prompts and one negative prompt; it cannot observe a model's hidden selection. Keep a mismatch instead of rewriting history, describe the description change under revision, and recheck only the mismatched prompts.

Run the same check for the other two kit examples. Their trigger records are synthetic course examples, so label them as such in your notes. A passing structure check is not evidence that a particular agent selected the skill.

docs.title: Evidence from a CLI run
docs.text:
A command-line session is evidence only when another reader can identify what happened. Save these fields for the run that uses your skill:

Field Example evidence Request the exact prompt, copied before the run Revision git rev-parse HEAD Selection the CLI's skill-selection line, or “not shown” Calls and output the command, exit status, and relevant stdout/stderr Verification the exact check command and its result Boundary files changed, or git diff --name-only if none

Keep the transcript in a scratch directory outside the repository's product files, then copy only the short evidence summary needed for A3. Never put a key in a prompt, screenshot, transcript, or repository. Follow the course safety practices when you run an agent.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Use your own project or the smallest repository you are currently working on. Choose a workflow you have already performed at least twice: for example, a focused test-and-review check, a release-note check, or a read-only status report. Do not choose a destructive workflow. Work in your own project repository's A3-work/ directory and keep the repository revision fixed while you compare predictions.

  1. Hand run (15 minutes). Write the workflow as shell commands. Run it once by hand, save the output, and mark each line as input, decision, action, or check.
  2. Write (20 minutes). Create A3-work/skills/<your-name>/SKILL.md with the same three sections as the example. The description must say what the skill does and when it applies. Keep the body below 500 lines.
  3. Predict (10 minutes). Add three requests that should trigger and one near miss to A3-work/trigger-test.yaml. Fill predicted before you run the agent. Use a neutral observer_detail such as the CLI name and date; do not invent a classmate or teacher.
  4. Run and observe (15 minutes). Use your provided coding-agent CLI once on the fixed revision. Preserve the exact request and the CLI output. Keep observed as true or false, based only on the selection evidence the CLI actually reports. If selection is not shown, write selection: not shown in A3-work/agent-run.txt and explain the basis for each boolean in observer_detail; do not put that phrase in the YAML boolean field.
  5. Check (10 minutes). Run the structure checker, compare prediction with observation, and record one correction or a justified “no change.” The decision line at the end of A3 must say accept, narrow, recheck, or stop, followed by the evidence ID that supports it.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Run the checker from the course checkout, with paths that point to the files in your project. Run the Git commands from your project root. These commands are offline and use only the repository tools:

PROJECT_ROOT=/path/to/your/project
mkdir -p "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/skills/release-check"
# Write A3-work/skills/release-check/SKILL.md and A3-work/trigger-test.yaml now.
uv run --locked python lectures/week-03/fixture/skill_check.py \
  "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/skills/release-check/SKILL.md" \
  "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/trigger-test.yaml"

git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" rev-parse HEAD
git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" diff --check
git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" diff --name-only

The checker must print Structure checked. and no structural problems. Then inspect the trigger table yourself: there are at least three should_trigger: true prompts and one near miss, and observed records what the CLI showed. A successful checker run does not prove that the agent selected the skill. A failed checker run is useful evidence: fix the smallest structural problem, rerun the same command, and keep both outcomes in your A3 record.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Starting with a description instead of a hand run. Re-run the workflow manually and record the command and output before editing SKILL.md.
  • Making the description a slogan. Replace “helps with code” with a task and a when clause; test the near miss again.
  • Calling the near miss a failure. A skill staying quiet for an implementation request is the expected result. Keep the prediction and observation side by side.
  • Treating skill_check.py as an agent. It reads files only. It checks structure and consistency, not selection; do not report its output as a model run.
  • Saving only a final summary. Keep the request, revision, command, exit status, and verification result so another person can reproduce the claim.
  • Putting credentials in evidence. Stop, remove the secret, revoke it with the provider, and tell the teaching team. Follow the safety practices in the course tools and model access guidance before continuing.

docs.title: Week 3 readings: skills and command-line evidence
Learning objectives
docs.text: Use a skill description as a testable selection boundary and read a command-line record as evidence with a revision, command, result, and verification step. The format's progressive-disclosure claim is scoped by (tools/agent-skills; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1).

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
Read the three course-authored skill examples in this order:

  1. Source 1 — research-codebase/SKILL.md and trigger-test.yaml: a read-only repository map, with three requests that should trigger and an implementation request that should stay quiet. Scope: description wording, source locations, and the distinction between predicted and observed selection.
  2. Source 2 — plan-change/SKILL.md and trigger-test.yaml: a bounded plan before implementation. Scope: acceptance criteria, allowed files, and a near miss that asks only for current facts.
  3. Source 3 — review-diff/SKILL.md and trigger-test.yaml: review evidence for an existing diff. Scope: reproducing findings, classifying them, and preserving the verification command.
  4. Source 4 — fixture/skill_check.py: the course checker. Scope: front matter, required sections, links inside the skill directory, four to twelve prompts, and the rule that a mismatch must be recorded and rechecked. It reads data; it does not run a model or select a skill.
  5. Source 5 — Agent Skills specification: the primary source named by (tools/agent-skills; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1). Scope: progressive disclosure from metadata to the activated body and then to bundled resources.

Open each source at the paths above. The trigger records are synthetic course examples; do not describe them as observations from a classmate, teacher, or model.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text: Before the studio, annotate one source with two questions: which words in its description set the trigger boundary, and what output would prove a run happened? Bring the questions to the studio. No additional external reading is required for A3.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Use the direct command from the studio to check your own files. Keep the checker output separate from the agent transcript: they answer different questions.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a source file as an automatic host rule; the host's discovery and precedence must be observed for the agent you use.
  • Calling a synthetic trigger record a real model run.
  • Citing a skill card without naming which file and scope you read.

docs.title: Week 3 self-check answer guidance
docs.text:
Write your own record first. These are bounded checks, not a report of a real agent run.

Retrieval 1. should_trigger is the intended boundary, predicted is the student's expectation before the run, and boolean observed records the selection evidence the CLI showed. If the CLI omits selection, the transcript says selection: not shown; the YAML field remains boolean and observer_detail explains the basis.

Retrieval 2. Run uv run --locked python lectures/week-03/fixture/skill_check.py with the two student paths. It checks file structure and consistency; it cannot observe hidden skill selection or prove that a model ran.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: The answer names the hand-run commands, their inputs and decisions, and the exact focused check command. The saved output and revision make the baseline reproducible.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: The three positive prompts describe the same workflow in different words. Each has a prediction made before the run; the student cites the description words that set the boundary rather than copying the description into every prompt.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: The near miss asks for implementation or a new feature rather than the selected workflow. “Stays quiet” means the CLI reported no selection; when selection is not shown, the transcript records selection: not shown and the YAML keeps a boolean supported by the record. It never means inventing a positive observation.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: The five fields are the exact request, repository revision, selection line (or a selection: not shown entry in the transcript), command with exit status and output, and verification command with its result.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: skill_check.py proves front matter, sections, links, prompt counts, and any required mismatch revision. It reads data only; it does not run a model, execute a skill, or certify that a host selected one.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: The revision mapping states what description changed and lists exactly the mismatched prompt IDs with their rechecked observations. The original prediction remains in the file.

docs.title: Week 3 self-check: Agent skills and the CLI
Learning objectives
docs.text: Use these questions to check whether you can explain a skill boundary, test a near miss, and preserve command-line evidence before submitting A3. Answer guidance is available after you write your own record.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text: For a research-codebase skill, classify this request: “Implement the requested change and add a regression test.” It is a near miss because it asks for implementation, while the skill description is for a fact-only map before proposing a change.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
R1. Retrieval 1. Name the three fields that distinguish an intended trigger, your prediction, and what a CLI run actually showed.

R2. Retrieval 2. Name the command that checks your SKILL.md and trigger record, and state one claim that command cannot make.

  1. What did your repeated workflow do by hand, and which command was its verification?
  2. Which three requests should trigger your skill? Why is each one different in wording?
  3. Which request is the near miss? What would “stays quiet” look like in your CLI record?
  4. Which five fields let another reader identify a command result? Give your own values.
  5. What does skill_check.py prove, and what can it not prove?
  6. If observed differs from should_trigger, what must the revision section contain?

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Run your own checker again and compare every predicted and observed value with the saved CLI evidence. A correct answer includes the command and revision, not only a final sentence.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Confusing the intended trigger (should_trigger) with your prediction (predicted) or the observed record (observed).
  • Treating a checker pass as evidence that an agent used the skill.
  • Omitting the near miss or changing it until it triggers.

docs.title: Agent skills and the CLI
docs.text: Week 3 · LO2

docs.title: Today
docs.text: Run a workflow by hand → encode it → test its trigger boundary → keep CLI evidence.

docs.title: A skill is a procedure
docs.text:
• SKILL.md front matter: name and description
  • Body: Steps, Judgement, Verification
  • Selection is a claim to test

docs.title: Start by hand
docs.text:
git status --short
git diff --check
uv run --locked pytest -q

Save the revision and output before writing the skill.

docs.title: The description is the boundary
docs.text:
Specific: “run release checks and report evidence when a change is ready for review.”

Vague: “help with code.”

Which one stays quiet for “implement a new feature”?

docs.title: The body is the procedure
docs.text:
## Steps
1. Read the boundary.
2. Run the check.
## Judgement
- Stop on unrelated edits.
## Verification
Run `git diff --check` and the focused test.

A procedure does not grant permission.

docs.title: Three positives, one near miss
docs.text:
Request Expected Trace a request and cite files trigger Report handlers before edits trigger Map an unfamiliar module read-only trigger Implement the change and add tests quiet

Predict before opening the trigger record.

docs.title: Read the kit examples
docs.text:
research-codebase · facts before edits

plan-change · bounded plan before implementation

review-diff · reproduce findings in an existing diff

Read descriptions first; bodies are loaded after selection.

docs.title: What the checker checks
docs.text:
skill_check.py checks:

  • front matter and directory name
  • required sections and links
  • 4–12 prompt records
  • mismatch revision details

It does not run a model or observe hidden selection.

docs.title: Run it directly
docs.text:
# From the course checkout; PROJECT_ROOT is your project.
uv run --locked python lectures/week-03/fixture/skill_check.py \
  "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/skills/my-workflow/SKILL.md" \
  "$PROJECT_ROOT/A3-work/trigger-test.yaml"

Expected: Structure checked.

docs.title: Prediction versus observation
docs.text:
• should_trigger: your intended boundary
  • predicted: what you expected before the run
  • observed: what the CLI actually showed

A mismatch is evidence. Keep it and revise the description deliberately.

docs.title: CLI evidence
docs.text:
Keep the exact request, revision, selection line (or “not shown”), command, exit status, stdout/stderr, and verification result.

A final summary without its command is a claim, not evidence.

docs.title: Safe command line
docs.text: Use a dedicated directory. Keep employer and cloud credentials out. Do not paste keys into prompts, screenshots, logs, or commits. For generated commands, inspect before running.

docs.title: Studio handoff
docs.text:
A3 contains:

  1. hand-run commands and output
  2. SKILL.md
  3. four trigger records
  4. CLI evidence summary
  5. checker output and one decision line

docs.title: Verify before accepting
docs.text:
git rev-parse HEAD
git diff --check
git diff --name-only

Then compare every observed value with the saved transcript.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• writing before the hand run
  • a description broad enough to match everything
  • treating quiet as failure
  • inventing an observation the CLI did not show
  • reporting checker output as model behavior

docs.title: Exit question
docs.text:
What is the nearest request that should stay quiet for your skill?

Write it down before you submit A3.

docs.title: Week 4: Customizing your agent and repository
docs.text: This directory is the Week 4 lecture and studio. You will write repository instructions, turn one safety rule into a Git hook gate, and delegate a bounded task to a subagent role. Every example pairs a generated proposal with a check. The studio produces one instruction file, one blocked commit record and one passing commit record for your project repository.

docs.title: Week 4 studio
docs.text: This 90-minute studio is individual work with a written alternative. Use a disposable copy of your project repository. Do not place credentials, employer data or private material in it. The commands below use only ordinary git and python.

docs.title: Studio sequence
docs.text:
Minutes Activity Evidence to keep 0–15 Name one failure an agent could cause in your repository failure and the rule that prevents it 15–30 Write and review AGENTS.md instruction file and one peer question 30–55 Install the hook and make it block a bad commit blocked.txt and the nonzero exit 55–70 Fix the change and commit it passed.txt and git show --stat 70–85 Specify one subagent role and inspect its hand-back role contract and checked hand-back 85–90 Decide what to accept or narrow one decision line with evidence

Keyboard-only editing and a text record provide the same outputs. A partner may read your rule, but each student makes the decision and keeps their own records.

docs.title: 1. Write the instruction file
docs.text:
From the root of a disposable checkout, create AGENTS.md:

cat > AGENTS.md <<'__INSTRUCTIONS__'
# Repository instructions

- Scope: Python files under `src/`; keep public names stable.
- Before editing: read the target function and its tests; name both in your note.
- After editing: run `python -m pytest tests -q` when the repository has tests.
- Stop: do not change lockfiles or files outside this checkout for this task.
__INSTRUCTIONS__

Replace the paths and command with ones that exist in your repository. Under the file, write a four-row table in instruction-review.md: each rule, the failure it prevents, and the evidence a reviewer could inspect. Mark any rule that is only a request; an instruction file alone cannot enforce it.

docs.title: 2. Install a small hook gate
docs.text:
First, from this course checkout, copy the course-written hook to a temporary path. Keep the same shell open while you work in your disposable project checkout:

HOOK_SOURCE="$(mktemp)"
cp lectures/week-04/example/pre_commit.py "$HOOK_SOURCE"

From the root of a disposable project checkout, make a directory if the project has no src/:

mkdir -p week04-studio-hook/src
cp "$HOOK_SOURCE" week04-studio-hook/pre_commit.py
cd week04-studio-hook
git init -q
git config user.name "Week 4 practice"
git config user.email "week4@example.edu"
cat > .git/hooks/pre-commit <<'__HOOK__'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]))

from pre_commit import run

paths = subprocess.check_output(
    ["git", "diff", "--cached", "--name-only"], text=True
).splitlines()
event = {"event": "before_commit", "paths": paths}
raise SystemExit(run([json.dumps(event)]))
__HOOK__
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

The copied hook is course-written teaching code. Read it before using it. It checks staged paths and returns 2 for a protected path or an unused import; it does not execute the staged file.

Create the intentionally bad change and capture the failed attempt:

printf 'import json\n\nvalue = 1\n' > src/report.py
git add src/report.py
status=0
git commit -m "practice: blocked import" > blocked.txt 2>&1 || status=$?
cat blocked.txt
echo "exit status: $status"
[ "$status" -ne 0 ]

The command must leave the commit uncreated and blocked.txt must contain the hook's finding. If it commits, stop and inspect the wrapper before proceeding; do not rewrite the record to make it look blocked.

Now fix the violation and capture the passing run:

printf 'value = 1\n' > src/report.py
git add src/report.py
git commit -m "practice: pass the gate" > passed.txt 2>&1
cat passed.txt
grep -F "PASS: no protected file" passed.txt
git show --stat --oneline HEAD

Keep blocked.txt, passed.txt, and the commit hash in hook-record.md. Explain that the hook proves this staged-path check ran; it does not prove the Python behavior is correct. Run the repository's focused test separately when one exists.

docs.title: 3. Give a subagent a role
docs.text:
Write role-contract.md with exactly one role. This is a prompt and review exercise; you may use your coding agent directly, but do not give it credentials or an unrestricted command tool.

Role: researcher
Task: locate the function that parses one report and its callers.
Allowed tools: read files, search text, run one named read-only test.
Forbidden: edits, network, dependency installation, commits.
Hand-back: research.md with file/function references, the test command and two open questions.
Stop condition: stop if the parser is generated or the named test is absent.

Ask for the hand-back using that role contract. Open every cited file and run the named read-only check yourself. In role-review.md, mark each claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, with the location or output that supports the mark. If you continue to an implementer role, pass only role-contract.md, research.md and the named files; record its diff and test output separately. A role name without an allowlist and hand-back is not a boundary.

docs.title: 4. Decision line
docs.text:
End studio-record.md with one line:

Decision: accept | narrow | recheck | stop — evidence: blocked.txt, passed.txt, and role-review.md

Choose the word that matches your evidence. A clean hook run can support accepting the staged-path invariant; it cannot support accepting untested application behavior.

docs.title: Week 4: Customizing your agent and repository
Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of the lesson, you can:

  • LO2: write an instruction file whose rules name the failure each rule prevents;
  • LO2, LO9: distinguish a request an agent may skip from a hook gate that blocks the commit event, and verify both a blocked and an accepted commit;
  • LO2, LO3: give a subagent a role with a separate instruction, a small tool allowlist, and a hand-back contract, then check the hand-back against the contract;
  • LO3: carry the same boundaries into the technical specification due this week.

The examples are course-written and synthetic. They are prompts and checks for practice, not records of a real model run or a repository's production policy.

docs.title: Start with a failure, then write the rule
docs.text:
A repository has a Python command that reads a configuration file. A rushed agent makes three tempting mistakes:

Failure to prevent Instruction rule Evidence that can check it The command is changed without its regression test “For every behavior change, name the test that distinguishes old and new behavior.” The change note names a test and the test runs A generated command writes outside the checkout “Use paths below the repository root; stop and ask when a path is outside it.” A negative path case is refused A commit changes the lockfile while fixing a parser “Do not change dependency files in a parser change.” The staged path list contains no lockfile

The rule is useful because it predicts a failure. “Be careful” is a request with no observable check. Write the rule as a sentence that an agent can act on and a person can inspect.

docs.title: Instruction files are scoped context
docs.text:
Create AGENTS.md at the repository root and, when a subdirectory needs a stricter rule, place a more local instruction file there. Keep the file short enough to read. A good entry names the scope, the allowed command, the expected evidence and the stop condition:

# Repository instructions

- Scope: Python files under `src/`; keep public function names stable.
- Before editing: read the named function and its tests; report file and function names.
- After editing: run `python -m pytest tests/test_parser.py -q` and report the result.
- Stop: do not change `pyproject.toml`, lockfiles or files outside this repository.

The request “please run the parser tests” can be skipped by a hurried agent. The stop rule can be checked by a reviewer, but it is still an instruction until a gate enforces it. An instruction file gives context and a decision procedure; it does not make the filesystem or Git refuse an action by itself.

docs.title: A request and a gate have different jobs
docs.text:
A request is a message to the agent: “run the focused test and report the output.” A gate is attached to an event the repository controls: “before a commit, refuse staged Python files with an unused import.” The agent may omit the request. Git invokes the hook even when the agent forgets the request. A hook is therefore a narrow invariant, not a replacement for tests or review.

The studio uses the course-written hook in example/pre_commit.py. It accepts a JSON event, checks protected paths and reports an unused Python import without importing or running the file. The studio wraps it as .git/hooks/pre-commit; the wrapper supplies the staged path list. It returns exit code 2 for a finding and exit code 0 for a clean list.

Generated proposal: add import json to report.py, stage it, and commit. The hook should stop the commit because json is unused. Verification: read the hook output, fix the import, stage again and commit; the second run should print PASS and exit 0. Keep both records. A blocked run is evidence that the gate fired; it is not evidence that the final change is correct.

docs.title: Subagent roles are separate contracts
docs.text:
A role is more than a label such as “reviewer.” Give the subagent its own instruction, tools and output contract. For a bounded parser change, use three roles:

Role Instruction it receives Allowed tools Required hand-back Researcher Locate the parser and its callers; change nothing read files, search, run one existing test research.md with file/function references and open questions Implementer Change only the named function and preserve the contract read, edit that file, run the named test diff plus test output and a remaining risk Reviewer Judge the issue, diff and evidence without editing read diff, read evidence, run the named test each finding marked confirmed, refuted or cannot tell

The parent agent or person chooses whether to continue after each hand-back. The subagent cannot enlarge its allowlist, declare its own work correct or silently replace a missing artifact. A generated hand-back is still a proposal: open every cited location, run the stated check and record what the check does not establish.

Generated proposal: ask a researcher to “find the parser.” Verification: reject a hand-back that names no file and function. Ask for the bounded report again or stop. Then pass only research.md and the named files to the implementer. A reviewer who sees the issue, diff and test evidence in a fresh context can check the contract rather than trust the implementer's summary.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Follow the studio. You will write an instruction file for your own repository, install a hook that blocks one intentionally bad staged change, and retain one blocked and one passing commit record. Use ordinary git and python; do not put keys or employer data in the practice repository.

For the second session, use a guest's workflow or complete the studio continuation. Bring the same instruction file and gate to your project's technical specification. Contribution 1 and the technical specification are due this week; link the evidence you actually have.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The studio has two independent checks:

  1. python pre_commit.py (through the Git wrapper) returns a nonzero exit for the bad staged change and prints the finding; the saved blocked.txt records the command and output.
  2. The corrected staged change commits with exit 0 and the saved passed.txt contains the PASS line. git show --stat --oneline HEAD confirms which files entered the commit.

For the role exercise, compare each hand-back with its contract. A complete report names locations, allowed tools, the exact command and its result. It does not claim that a model run happened when you used a course-written example.

docs.title: Verification boundaries
docs.text:
• A blocked hook run proves that Git presented the recorded staged paths to this hook and that the hook returned a nonzero status. It does not prove the application behaves correctly.
  • A passing hook run proves only that this input satisfied this hook's narrow checks. Run the focused test and inspect the diff separately.
  • A role hand-back is evidence only for the fields it names. Open every cited location and rerun the named check; mark an unsupported claim cannot tell.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating an instruction as a permission boundary. Add a testable hook or a human review step for the invariant; keep the request for useful context.
  • Writing a hook that edits files or runs arbitrary commands. Read and parse the staged paths, refuse malformed input, and return a clear nonzero status.
  • Giving every subagent the whole repository and every tool. Narrow its files and tools, then inspect the hand-back in a fresh context.
  • Recording only the passing commit. Preserve the blocked output too, and label what each record proves and what it leaves open.
  • Copying a generated snippet without reading it. Compare the diff, run the check and make the decision yourself.

docs.title: Week 4 reading path
docs.text:
Read the notes and run the studio before the optional sources. The course examples are sufficient; no account, installation or external service is required.

  • Source 1 — instruction files: read the Custom instructions with AGENTS.md section of the Codex CLI documentation recorded in (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5). Scope your reading to how instructions are discovered and combined. Compare that context mechanism with the studio's rule table; do not infer that instructions enforce filesystem permissions.
  • Source 2 — hooks: inspect the copied pre_commit.py and the Git event and exit-status contract described in the studio. This is a course-written synthetic example; record its input, blocked output and passing output rather than treating it as a vendor claim.
  • Source 3 — role context: read the subagents claim and its cited locator in (studies/humanlayer-context-engineering; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1). Scope the claim to limiting context and returning a compact hand-back. Treat the article's workflow as a proposal to test, not as evidence that a role is safe or effective.
  • Source 4 — skills as instructions: read the scope and progressive-disclosure claim in (tools/agent-skills; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1). Scope your comparison to a description, instructions and on-demand resources. A skill description does not grant a tool permission.

For each source, write one sentence naming the source section, the claim you used and the check in your studio that could support or challenge it. Factsheet cards are citations for this page; they are not published reading material.

docs.title: Week 4 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Answers should name an observable failure, a boundary and evidence. Equivalent wording is fine when the evidence remains checkable.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: For example: “For a parser change, keep the public function name stable and run the named parser test.” The failure is an accidental API break or an untested behavior change. Evidence is the diff, the test command and its output.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: The request is agent context and can be omitted; the hook is invoked by Git at the commit event and its nonzero exit prevents the commit. The agent can claim it ran the test without running it, so inspect the command output and the commit result.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: No. A gate needs a nonzero exit for the bad staged input and a commit that is not created. The shell status and git log/git show observation settle it.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: pyproject.toml is the finding because it is a protected dependency file for this task. The Python file may still receive the unused-import finding if it contains one; each finding must be fixed before the passing run.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: It leaves application behavior, test coverage and the correctness of unstaged files unverified. Run the focused test and inspect the committed diff.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: Example: allowed tools are read-only search and one named test; forbidden action is editing or committing; hand-back field is research.md with file/function references. The parent opens the location because a generated summary is a claim, not proof.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: The test-output field is missing. Pause or return the work until the implementer supplies that evidence; a diff alone cannot establish the behavior.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Cannot tell. The hand-back has no location, input, command or output, so there is no evidence to confirm or refute safety.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: Stop when the target is outside the role's files, the required test is absent, a tool would need a forbidden capability or the hand-back cannot satisfy its contract. Record the exact boundary and ask for a narrower task.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text: Any decision is defensible only when its evidence matches it. For example: “Decision: accept — evidence: blocked.txt has the nonzero finding, passed.txt has PASS, and git show identifies the commit.”

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text:
An instruction might say “before editing src/parser.py, read its tests and report the focused test.” A gate might refuse a commit that stages pyproject.toml with that parser change. The first check establishes context was requested; the second establishes the staged-path invariant at the commit event. Neither proves parser semantics.

Retrieval 1. The hook's green result does not show that the focused test ran. Read the test command and its output, then inspect the commit result.

Retrieval 2. Open the cited file and run the named check yourself. A summary without a location and observable result remains cannot tell.

docs.title: Week 4 self-check
docs.text:
Answer without an agent, then compare with the public answer guidance. These questions are formative. Use the studio records as evidence rather than guessing what an agent “must have” done.

  1. Write one instruction-file rule for a parser change. Name the failure it prevents and the evidence a reviewer can inspect.
  2. What is the difference between the request “run the focused test” and a pre-commit hook that exits 2 for an unused import? Give one way the request can be skipped.
  3. A hook prints a finding but exits 0. Did it gate the commit? What observation settles it?
  4. Your staged paths are src/report.py and pyproject.toml; the rule forbids dependency changes in a parser task. Which path should the hook report, and why?
  5. A passing hook run is recorded. What application behavior does that record leave unverified?
  6. Give a researcher subagent two allowed tools, one forbidden action and a hand-back field. Why does the parent still inspect the cited file?
  7. The implementer returns a diff but no test output. Which contract item is missing, and should the parent continue?
  8. A reviewer says “looks safe” without a file, input or command. Mark the hand-back confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and state the missing evidence.
  9. When should a role stop and ask for a narrower task? Give one concrete boundary.
  10. End with a decision line for your studio: accept, narrow, recheck or stop. Name the record that supports it.

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text:
A project specification says “the agent should follow repository rules.” Rewrite it as one observable instruction and one event-time gate. State what each check proves and what it cannot prove.

R1. A request says “run the focused test,” but the agent reports only a green hook. What observation is still missing?

R2. A subagent returns a file name and a confident summary. What evidence lets you decide whether its hand-back is confirmed?

docs.title: Customizing your agent and repository
docs.text: Week 4 · Instruction files, hook gates and subagent roles

docs.title: The failure comes first
docs.text:
An agent changes a parser and also edits the lockfile.

What rule would have predicted and prevented that failure?

docs.title: One rule, one failure, one check
docs.text: Failure Rule Check Lockfile changes with parser Keep dependency files out of parser fixes staged path list Test is omitted Name and run the focused test command output Path escapes checkout Stop on an outside path negative path case

docs.title: An instruction file is scoped context
docs.text:
AGENTS.md can state:

Before editing: read the target and its tests.
After editing: run the focused test.
Stop: do not change lockfiles for this task.

The rule is readable. It is not yet a Git permission boundary.

docs.title: Request versus gate
docs.text:
Request: “Run the focused test and report it.”

Gate: “At before_commit, exit 2 when a staged Python file has an unused import.”

A request can be skipped. Git still invokes the gate.

docs.title: Generate, then verify
docs.text:
Generated proposal: add import json to report.py.

Verification: stage it, commit, read the nonzero hook result; remove the import and commit again; read the PASS result.

The first record proves the gate stopped that input. The second proves the clean path passed.

docs.title: A hook is a narrow invariant
docs.text:
A hook should:

  • read the staged paths;
  • reject malformed input and protected paths;
  • return a nonzero status for a finding;
  • avoid importing or executing the staged file.

It does not replace tests, review or a specification.

docs.title: Live gate: bad commit
docs.text:
$ git commit -m "practice: blocked import"
src/report.py:1: unused import 'json'
STOP: fix the findings above, then run the hook again

The commit is not created. Save this output as evidence.

docs.title: Live gate: good commit
docs.text:
$ git commit -m "practice: pass the gate"
PASS: no protected file and no unused import in 1 file(s)

Now inspect git show --stat. A green hook leaves application behavior unverified.

docs.title: Role is a contract
docs.text:
A subagent role supplies:

  1. one instruction;
  2. a small tool allowlist;
  3. a named hand-back;
  4. a stop condition.

A label such as “reviewer” supplies none of these by itself.

docs.title: Researcher role
docs.text:
Instruction: locate the parser and its callers; change nothing.

Tools: read, search, one named read-only test.

Hand-back: research.md with file/function references, command and open questions.

Stop: parser is generated or the named test is absent.

docs.title: Implementer role
docs.text:
Instruction: change only the named function and preserve its contract.

Tools: read, edit that file, run the named test.

Hand-back: diff, test output and one remaining risk.

The parent opens the diff and decides whether to continue.

docs.title: Reviewer role
docs.text:
Instruction: judge issue, diff and evidence without editing.

Tools: read the named files and run the named check.

Hand-back: each finding is confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with evidence.

A summary without a location or input is not a finding.

docs.title: Fresh context, smaller boundary
docs.text:
Pass the implementer only the role contract, the research record and named files.

Pass the reviewer the issue, diff and evidence. Do not pass the implementer's private plan.

A fresh context makes the contract visible; it does not make the reviewer infallible.

docs.title: Studio output
docs.text:
You will keep:

  • AGENTS.md and instruction-review.md;
  • blocked.txt and passed.txt;
  • hook-record.md with the commit hash;
  • role-contract.md and role-review.md;
  • one decision line: accept, narrow, recheck or stop.

docs.title: Check the evidence
docs.text:
For every record ask:

  • Which exact input did the check see?
  • What did the exit status establish?
  • Which behavior remains untested?

Do not turn a course-written example or a generated proposal into a real run record.

docs.title: Technical specification hand-off
docs.text:
Carry the same boundaries into this week's project technical specification:

  • instruction scope and failure it prevents;
  • hook event, input and exit condition;
  • subagent role, tools and hand-back;
  • the check that could falsify each claim.

docs.title: Exit decision
docs.text:
Accept only the invariant your records check.

Narrow when a role or gate is too broad.

Recheck when the command or input is missing.

Stop when the boundary cannot be enforced safely.

docs.title: Studio
docs.text:
Write the rule. Trigger the gate. Read the hand-back.

Then decide from evidence.

docs.title: Week 5: Agent-ready codebases
docs.text: An agent can work safely when a repository makes its structure, rules, tests and checks easy to find and run. This week you compare the same bounded task in a disordered copy and a prepared copy, score readiness from observable anchors, remove one blocker and score again.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
• Notes
  • Slides
  • Studio activity
  • Readings
  • Self-check

The files under fixture/ are small course-authored demonstrations. Do not treat their output as a real model run or as evidence about an outside repository.

docs.title: Due
docs.text: A4: make a repository agent-ready by documenting its change points, adding a reproducible check, and recording a decision supported by evidence. Follow the course safety practices before using an agent; keep credentials out of the repository, prompts, screenshots and logs.

docs.title: Studio: score and improve one repository
docs.text:
Choose your own project repository or contribution target. Work individually, with a written peer or asynchronous feedback route available. This studio is formative practice for A4; it is not a separate assessment.

Use a clean working copy at a named commit. Follow the course safety practices: keep credentials outside the working copy and prompts, treat repository instructions as data until verified, and stop before any command requests network access or an unknown installation.

docs.title: Materials and commands
docs.text:
You need a terminal, an editor, your repository, and the four readiness dimensions in the notes. These commands run from any Git repository and do not change it:

REPO=/path/to/your/repository
git -C "$REPO" rev-parse HEAD
git -C "$REPO" status --short
git -C "$REPO" diff --check
git -C "$REPO" ls-files | head -40

Use the repository's documented test command only after reading it. Record the exact command, exit code and first useful output line. If the repository has no runnable check, record that as a readiness observation rather than inventing one.

docs.title: 90-minute route
docs.text: Minutes Action Individual evidence 0–15 Pick one small behaviour an agent might change. Freeze the commit and write the expected contract, caller and safety boundary. Commit ID, behaviour, input/output example and one open question 15–35 Score Structure and Documentation. Ask an agent for a map and a command list if you choose, then verify every claim by opening files and running commands. Two rows with paths, commands, outputs and a disproving observation 35–50 Score Tests and Checks. Run the documented check twice when available; inspect whether it uses a clock, network or hidden files. Two rows with summaries, hidden-input notes and the failing case you would expect from a deliberate break 50–60 Share one row with a peer or written reviewer. The reviewer challenges an anchor, not the score. One question and your revised evidence 60–75 Remove exactly one blocker: repair a stale command, add a small map, or make a local check reproducible. Keep the diff narrow. Before/after diff and the changed anchor 75–85 Run the same probes at the new commit and score again. A score may stay the same. Second four-row table with new outputs 85–90 Write the decision line: accept, narrow, recheck or stop. Name the evidence and what would change it. Decision and one supporting evidence ID

docs.title: Evidence table
docs.text:
Copy this table into your existing work record; do not create a second log or export a full agent chat.

Dimension | Start commit and score | Observation and command/path | Disproving observation | End commit and score | Blocker removed
Structure | | | | |
Documentation | | | | |
Tests | | | | |
Checks | | | | |
Decision | accept / narrow / recheck / stop | Evidence IDs: | What would change it: | |

If an agent supplied the initial map or score, add one AI-use note using your existing disclosure ID. The note records the proposal; your paths and command results are the evidence. Do not copy credentials, private records or a raw session transcript into the repository.

docs.title: Help and failure handling
docs.text:
At the first command that fails, stop and show the command and exit code to the instructor or peer. If the repository's documentation disagrees, keep both lines visible, choose the safest bounded command, and record the conflict. If you cannot run a local check, leave the Tests or Checks score at the evidence-supported level and write the missing prerequisite.

A successful-looking refactor is not accepted until the original caller cases, the requested structure and the local check have all been inspected. End with the decision line required by A4.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you can:

  • locate a change point from a repository map and name the callers, rules and checks that constrain it (LO4);
  • ask an agent for a bounded proposal, then verify the proposal with independent tests, a diff and a local check (LO4, LO5);
  • score Structure, Documentation, Tests and Checks from observable anchors, name a disproving observation, and explain what evidence would change the score (LO4, LO5);
  • keep repository text and generated commands inside the approved safety boundary (LO7).

A repository is agent-ready when a fresh session can find the relevant code, learn the local contract, run a short check and report what it did not check. Readiness is a property of evidence at a named revision, not a feeling about how tidy the tree looks.

docs.title: One task, two repositories
docs.text:
The task is deliberately small: replace a chain of status conditionals with a lookup while preserving whitespace, case and the unknown fallback. The public fixture contains the same function in three states:

  • before.py is the disordered starting point: the caller and contract are not written beside the function;
  • rejected.py is a tempting proposal that removes strip();
  • refactored.py is a structure change that keeps the contract.

The request is generated as text and inspected before it is copied into a candidate. The request is never executed as code. Verify the candidates from the root of your course checkout; the verifier reads the variant files that sit beside it, so it gives the same result from any directory:

python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py rejected
python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py refactored

Each command prints one line of JSON. The first exits with status 1 and reports the three padded inputs that fail:

{"cases": 10, "failures": [{"actual": "unknown", "expected": "passed", "input": " ok "}, {"actual": "unknown", "expected": "failed", "input": "\tfail\n"}, {"actual": "unknown", "expected": "passed", "input": " PASS "}], "if_statement_count": 0, "passed": 7, "scope": "course synthetic fixture; public feedback, not a grade", "variant": "rejected"}

The second exits with status 0:

{"cases": 10, "failures": [], "if_statement_count": 0, "passed": 10, "scope": "course synthetic fixture; public feedback, not a grade", "variant": "refactored"}

The result establishes those ten cases only. It does not prove behavior for every string or prove that a caller accepts the change.

Now run the same fixed cases against the starting point:

python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py before

{"cases": 10, "failures": [], "if_statement_count": 3, "passed": 10, "scope": "course synthetic fixture; public feedback, not a grade", "variant": "before"}

before and refactored both pass all ten cases; only if_statement_count differs (3 and 0). The cases cannot tell the two states apart, which is the point: behaviour is preserved, and what changed is how much a fresh session has to guess. In before.py a session must infer the contract from a chain of conditionals. In refactored.py the lookup table and the fallback are visible beside the change point. In a real project, a prepared repository would also name its entry point, contract and offline check in its context files; the agent still needs permission to read and edit, but the repository has removed avoidable guesses.

docs.title: What the comparison can and cannot show
docs.text:
The fixture is one function, so it cannot show every kind of blocker. The rows below are illustrative: they are the kinds of observation you will record in the studio on a whole repository, not results of the commands above.

Observation Supported claim Missing evidence The session found status_label in two file opens The map points to this change point for this revision Other behaviours may have different maps The documented check exits zero on the refactored copy These cases pass at this revision Callers, permissions and unlisted inputs The disordered copy has three test commands, two of which fail Documentation is a blocker for a fresh session Whether the implementation itself is correct A hook rejects an unused import with exit 2 The hook can stop that class of change Other checks and bypass paths

An agent may propose the score, but you choose it. For each dimension record the path or command, revision, observed result, the highest level whose anchors are all present, and one observation that would disprove the score.

docs.title: Four observable readiness dimensions
docs.text: Use levels 1–4. A level includes every lower-level anchor.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• 1: no map from a behaviour to its change point;
  • 2: a map exists, but a checked entry is wrong or mixes unrelated responsibilities;
  • 3: checked entries are accurate, the change point has one responsibility, and the probe reaches it in three file opens or fewer;
  • 4: a deliberate boundary violation fails a test or check.

Evidence is a behaviour, the files opened in order, a path:line change point and, at level 4, the failing result.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• 1: no context file or no runnable command;
  • 2: commands exist but one fails as written, or no invariant names the check that protects it;
  • 3: every listed command runs at the scored revision and at least three invariants name their checks;
  • 4: an automated check runs the documented commands and fails when one goes stale.

Evidence is the context-file path, each command and exit code, and the invariant-to-check list.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• 1: no runnable test exercises the change point;
  • 2: one run passes but a hidden input, nondeterminism or a deliberate break goes undetected;
  • 3: two repeatable runs agree, stay within the chosen budget, use no hidden input, and a deliberate break fails;
  • 4: failure messages identify the broken behaviour and mutation evidence accounts for surviving gaps.

Evidence is the two summaries, the hidden-input search, and the deliberate-break result.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• 1: no automatic gate;
  • 2: a gate can be run by hand but is not required, or it ignores an unused import;
  • 3: one offline command runs the required gates and exits non-zero for an unused import;
  • 4: the gate runs before a commit is offered and a secret canary is stopped by the project scanner.

Evidence is the gate command, failing and passing output, and the point where the gate is required.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Use the studio activity on your own project or contribution target repository. First freeze a baseline at a named commit. Give the agent only the files needed to answer one bounded question; inspect its proposal as untrusted text. Then run the repository's documented check and inspect the diff. If a command needs a credential, network access or an unknown install, stop and revise the boundary rather than running it.

Your first score is a four-row table with one evidence link and one disproving observation per row. Remove one blocker that is within your scope—for example, reconcile two test commands, add a map from a behaviour to its module, or make a check command deterministic. Run the same probe at the new commit and score again. A tidy directory without a changed observation does not raise a score.

Time-box the work: 15 minutes to choose the task and baseline, 25 minutes to score, 25 minutes to remove one blocker, 15 minutes to rerun the probes, and 10 minutes to write the decision. Ask for help at the first failed command; reserve the final ten minutes for revision.

docs.title: Supported execution
docs.text: Run the fixture commands on this page directly. Before running a project's own check, follow Tools and model access.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Run the public fixture before and after reading the candidate:

python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py rejected  # expected: exit 1, 7 of 10 passed
python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py refactored  # expected: exit 0, 10 of 10 passed

For your repository, run the exact command it documents, record its exit code and inspect the changed-file list:

git status --short
git diff --check
git diff --name-only

A passing check is evidence for the inputs it covered. A score changes only when the observed anchor changes at a named revision. If the same command passes because its tests were deleted, its scope was weakened, or the agent supplied a result without a command, keep the old score and record the finding.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake How to detect it Correction Scoring from a polished README A listed command fails or names a missing file Run each command at the scored revision and lower the row until it passes Treating an agent's score as evidence No path, revision or output is attached Ask for one observable anchor and one disproof before recording a number Refactoring only for shorter code The candidate passes happy paths but loses normalization or a caller contract Add the distinguishing case, restore the invariant, and rerun the unchanged check Calling contradictory docs a test failure The same command is written three ways Choose one bounded source of truth and verify the chosen command, leaving the conflict recorded Running a generated command blindly It asks for a key, network or an unpinned install Stop, inspect the trust boundary, and run it only in a dedicated directory or container that holds no credentials; otherwise record the missing prerequisite Raising a score after deleting tests The test count or covered paths shrink Compare the old and new test lists and keep the score unchanged

End the work record with one decision: accept, narrow, recheck or stop. Name the evidence that supports it and the observation that would change it.

docs.title: Week 5 reading paths
docs.text:
No external reading is required. The lesson uses the public, course-authored fixture and your own repository evidence. Read in this order:

  1. Notes, especially the four readiness dimensions and the comparison of disordered and prepared copies.
  2. The public starting function, then predict the cases in the verifier before opening the candidate files.
  3. Studio instructions, and the exact command your repository documents for its local check.
  4. Self-check, answering from paths and outputs rather than from an agent's confidence.

The fixture's command output is a reproducible teaching observation, not an industry statistic or a real model run. Do not cite a card or a README as a published source; name the file, revision, command and output that you actually checked.

docs.title: Week 5 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Tie each conclusion to an anchor, a scored revision and an observation that another reader could repeat. These are sample reasoning paths, not a substitute for recording your own evidence.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: The missing Structure anchor is the map from a behaviour to its change point: four file opens without naming the caller also exceeds the three-open limit of level 3. A level-2 score claims that a map exists, so it is disproved if no file at the scored revision maps this behaviour to its caller and change point; the score is then 1.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: Level 2 is supported: commands exist, but two of the three fail as written. Record the one command that succeeds at the scored revision and its output. Running the listed alternatives at the same revision, then updating the README to match the successful path, would raise the evidence.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: The distinguishing input is " PASS " (or another padded value): the rejected variant does not strip whitespace, while the refactored variant preserves input normalization. The fixed case list, including aliases and the unknown fallback, is the evidence.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: The Tests anchor is unsupported because the date is uncontrolled. Supply a fixed date or inject a clock and run both test cases again at the scored revision.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: Exit 2 establishes that the check rejected the unused import. It does not establish that other checks, a clean input or a complete check sequence succeeds; run those separately and record their commands and outputs.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: Request the scored revision, exact command and path, observed output, and the reason the anchor level follows. A bare number cannot be reproduced or challenged.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: A caller test with " PASS " catches the regression because the shorter function returns unknown. Run the old and refactored implementations against the same fixed cases and keep the failing rejected result alongside the passing result.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Do not run that instruction with a real key or an unpinned installer. Use an isolated safe environment, replace the key with a placeholder, pin the dependency, and record the README path plus the command and output that can be reproduced without credentials.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: Revisit the score downward or leave it unchanged until the six missing cases are explained. A smaller passing set does not prove improved readiness: compare the old and new test inventories and restore or justify every removed case.

docs.title: Retrieval prompts
docs.text:
Retrieval 1. Record the case, the context paths and the scored revision, then rerun the same command.

Retrieval 2. A clean tree says nothing about a measurable limit or check; name both before increasing the score.

docs.title: Week 5 self-check
docs.text:
Answer in your existing work record, then compare with a peer or the public answer guidance and the notes. These prompts are preparation and carry no separate marks.

  1. You have opened four files and still cannot name the caller of a function. Which Structure anchor is missing, and what observation would disprove a level-2 score?
  2. A repository lists pytest, make test and python -m unittest, but only one works at the scored commit. Which Documentation level is supported, and what evidence would raise it?
  3. Why does python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py rejected fail while the refactored variant passes? Name the input that distinguishes them.
  4. Two identical test runs pass, but the tests read the current date. Which Tests claim is unsupported, and what fixed input would remove the uncertainty?
  5. A hook exits 2 for an unused import. What does that establish about Checks, and what does it leave untested?
  6. An agent says “readiness 4” without a revision, command or path. What must you request before recording a score?
  7. The refactored code is shorter but a caller sends padded input. Which verification step catches the regression?
  8. A README asks you to paste a key into an environment variable and run an unpinned installer. What boundary applies, and what safe evidence can you collect instead?
  9. After removing one blocker, the test count falls from 24 to 18 and the remaining tests still pass. What should happen to the score and why?

docs.title: Retrieval prompts
docs.text:
R1. Retrieval 1. What recorded case, context paths and scored revision turn a generated proposal into a verified observation?

R2. Retrieval 2. Which measurable check and limit are missing when a readiness claim relies on a clean directory tree alone?

docs.title: Agent-ready codebases
docs.text:
Week 5 · Structure, documentation, tests and checks

A tidy tree is a hypothesis. Evidence decides.

docs.title: Today
docs.text:
• Give the same bounded task to a disordered and a prepared repository.
  • Find the blockers that make an agent guess.
  • Score four dimensions from observable anchors.
  • Remove one blocker and test whether the score changes.

docs.title: The task
docs.text:
Replace status conditionals with a lookup.

Preserve whitespace, case, aliases and the unknown fallback.

The proposal is text until a person inspects and verifies it.

docs.title: Two copies, one task
docs.text:
An illustrative contrast, not fixture output.

Disordered copy Prepared copy Three possible test commands One command at the scored revision Contradictory rules One named contract Check needs an unknown install Check runs locally Change point is hidden Map names the caller and module

docs.title: What the comparison proves
docs.text:
It shows which guesses the repository forces a fresh session to make.

It does not prove the implementation is correct, all callers are covered or every command is safe.

docs.title: Generate, then verify
docs.text:
Ask for a bounded expression as text.

Inspect the diff and expected behavior.

python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py rejected
python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py refactored

docs.title: A rejected shortcut
docs.text:
LABELS.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")

What disappeared?

strip() was part of the contract.

docs.title: The verified refactor
docs.text:
LABELS.get(raw.strip().lower(), "unknown")

The structure changed.

The behavior cases remain.

docs.title: Evidence is bounded
docs.text:
A passing fixture supports its listed inputs at one revision.

A caller map supports the paths you opened.

A hook failure supports the rule it actually enforced.

docs.title: Four dimensions
docs.text:
1. Structure
  2. Documentation
  3. Tests
  4. Checks

Each score is the highest level whose anchors you can show.

docs.title: Structure: find the change point
docs.text:
1 No map.

2 A map exists, but an entry is wrong or responsibilities mix.

3 Entries checked are accurate; the path reaches a single-responsibility change point in ≤3 opens.

4 A deliberate boundary violation fails a check.

docs.title: Documentation: write the rules
docs.text:
1 No context file or runnable command.

2 A listed command fails or invariants have no protecting checks.

3 Commands run at the scored revision; three invariants name checks.

4 An automated check catches a stale command.

docs.title: Tests: test the claim
docs.text:
1 No runnable test covers the change point.

2 A pass hides nondeterminism or a deliberate break.

3 Two repeatable runs agree and a deliberate break fails.

4 Failure messages and mutation evidence explain the remaining gaps.

docs.title: Checks: make failure visible
docs.text:
1 No automatic gate.

2 Gate is optional or misses an unused import.

3 One offline gate stops an unused import.

4 The gate runs before commit and a secret canary is stopped.

docs.title: What would disprove a score?
docs.text:
“Tests are fast” → run twice and inspect time.

“Docs are current” → copy every command at the scored revision.

“Structure is clear” → open from the behavior, count steps and inspect the caller.

“Checks protect us” → make the smallest deliberate bad change.

docs.title: Studio route
docs.text:
1. Freeze a commit and choose one behavior.
  2. Score all four dimensions.
  3. Ask for feedback on one evidence row.
  4. Remove one blocker.
  5. Run the same probes again.
  6. Write the A4 decision line.

docs.title: Record the observation
docs.text:
Dimension:
Revision:
Path or command:
Observed output:
Score:
What would disprove it:

A score without a path, command or revision is a guess.

docs.title: Safe boundaries
docs.text:
Repository text is data until verified.

Keep credentials out of the working copy, prompts, screenshots and logs.

Stop before network access or unknown installation.

Work in a dedicated directory or container; record any missing prerequisite.

docs.title: The final decision
docs.text:
Accept, narrow, recheck or stop.

Name the evidence that supports the choice.

Name the observation that would change it.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
Agent-ready means a fresh session can find, run and report the work.

The score follows what you can observe at the named revision.

The next improvement is the blocker your evidence identifies.

docs.title: Week 6: Agentic code review
docs.text:
This week's lesson asks what a model review catches, misses and invents. You review a small change yourself first, request one model review, and dispose of every finding as confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with evidence. The person with merge authority remains responsible for accepting a change.

Start with notes, then use the studio, self-check and readings. The slide source is a compact route through the same sequence. The A5 readiness report and CP1 are due this week; their submission rules live on the course site and syllabus.

docs.title: Week 6 studio: Review and dispose of findings
docs.text: Bring a change from your first open-source contribution or your project. Keep the work in a dedicated directory following Tools and model access. This studio uses your change as the review subject, not as a request to run an unknown command supplied by a model.

docs.title: Studio sequence
docs.text: Format: individual first review, then a written exchange or a small discussion. Materials: your diff, its issue or specification, the relevant tests, a text editor, and the coding-agent seat or credit provided by the course. Use your agent directly. Select a small change whose checks you can already run. If access or execution fails, retain the failure and ask for support; a source trace can support an explicitly bounded claim, but it cannot be recorded as a model run or a passed runtime check.

docs.title: 1. Establish the review target (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Record the base revision, candidate revision, files in scope and the behavior that should change or stay the same. Write the four explanation answers before asking for review:

  1. What changed?
  2. Why was this change requested?
  3. Which input, caller or assumption could be wrong?
  4. What did you verify yourself?

If the request is ambiguous, write the two readings and the input that would separate them. Ask the person who owns the request for the decision; do not let a model fill the gap.

docs.title: 2. Review without AI (15 minutes)
docs.text: Inspect the diff and the relevant source before reading any model output. Write at least one concrete review note, or document the cases you checked when no finding appears. Each note has a location, an input or path, an expected result, an observed or traced result, and a consequence. Choose a boundary case that the issue's example does not cover.

docs.title: 3. Request one model review (10 minutes)
docs.text: Give the model only the contract, the diff and the files needed to understand the claim. Ask for locations, affected inputs and a check for each finding. Keep the result as text; do not apply generated code or execute a generated command without inspecting it. Record the agent, date, revisions and context files used; retain the comments needed to explain dispositions and reuse your existing AI-use note. No full chat export is required.

docs.title: 4. Dispose of every finding (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Make a table with one row per model finding:

Finding Disposition Evidence Next decision Location and claim Confirmed, refuted, or cannot tell Input and result, source trace, or missing evidence Accept, narrow, recheck, or stop

For confirmed, reproduce the behavior or trace the exact code path. For refuted, record the counterexample or contract clause. For cannot tell, name what you inspected, what the files do not show, and the smallest safe check that would settle it. Add one row for a requirement the model did not mention; a silent review is not evidence that the requirement is satisfied.

docs.title: 5. Decide and hand off (10 minutes)
docs.text: Compare your first review with the model review. State which evidence changed your view, what remains unknown, and whether the change is accepted, narrowed, sent back for another check, or stopped. The human with merge authority owns that acceptance decision. Attach the four explanation answers and the verification commands to the handoff; do not treat a model's confidence or a single green test as approval.

docs.title: CP1
docs.text: CP1 takes the first 30 minutes of the second session, on paper, without AI.

docs.title: Participation and accessibility
docs.text: All required material is plain text and can be completed with a keyboard. An approved written or asynchronous exchange can replace live discussion while preserving the same individual first review, finding dispositions and evidence. Keep one work record; do not copy private chat, personal data or credentials into it.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you can:

  • review a small change against its stated behavior before reading a model review (LO5);
  • reproduce, refute, or leave unresolved each model finding with a bounded check (LO5); and
  • explain what a silent review does not establish and who owns an acceptance decision (LO9).

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text:
An archived build is analogous to an inactive account: ownership must not bypass the edit restriction. This course-created guard is a small demonstration, separate from any student project or graded instance. Review the change yourself before asking a model to review it:

 def can_edit(active: bool, owner: bool, staff: bool) -> bool:
-    return active and (owner or staff)
+    return owner or staff and active

The contract is small and explicit: boolean inputs may edit exactly when the account is active and is an owner or staff member. An active outsider and every inactive account must be denied. The code above is the intentionally regressed candidate in fixture/access.py; it is included so you can inspect and verify a concrete defect.

First write one review note without a tool. Include a location, an input, the expected result, the observed or traced result, and the consequence. The input active=False, owner=True, staff=False separates the two readings of the expression: the candidate allows it because and binds more tightly than or, while the contract requires denial. A passing active-staff example cannot establish the inactive owner case.

Save that first note before reading further. Run the unchanged public checks from the course root using the supplied code, after inspecting it:

python lectures/week-06/fixture/check_access.py -v

The bundled candidate fails test_inactive_owner and the inactive assertion in test_overlapping_roles, with exit 1. Record your actual output, not this prediction. The public checks cover the eight boolean combinations. After an agent proposes return active and (owner or staff), inspect the diff, apply only that expression in a separate copy, and rerun the unchanged checks there. All seven tests should pass. A deny-all patch would fail the active owner and staff cases. Inspect the tests too: changing their expectations to fit the candidate would not verify the contract.

docs.title: The model reviews; you verify each point
docs.text:
Now request a review of the same diff with the contract and the exact files in context. Treat each comment as a hypothesis. A useful comment names a location and a check; a confident tone is not evidence. The model might catch the precedence bug, miss it after seeing only a happy path, or invent a requirement to parse strings even though the contract accepts booleans only.

After saving your own note, classify this course-authored comparison as you would model output. It is synthetic text, not a real model run:

Claim Disposition and check “An inactive owner can edit.” Confirmed: the input above reproduces the contract violation. “Parse the string false before deciding access.” Refuted: boolean inputs are the explicit contract; the claim invents scope. “A caller in another file relies on inactive owners being allowed.” Cannot tell: the provided function and checks contain no caller. Record the files inspected and request the caller and its agreed behavior.

If the model only reports the string claim, it misses the actual inactive-owner defect. Compare your first finding with every model comment; keep any finding the model omitted.

The same precedence pattern appears in this older notation:

allowed = is_owner or is_staff and not archived
allowed = (is_owner or is_staff) and not archived

The current fixture uses active, owner and staff; the older names are only a notation bridge. In either form, an inactive or archived owner is the separating case.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Follow the studio guide. Bring one change from your first open-source contribution or from your project. Before using a model, inspect the diff and write a small review record. Then run one model review with the same contract, diff and relevant tests in context. For every finding, choose exactly one disposition:

Disposition Evidence to record Confirmed A reproducible input and observed result, or a source trace that proves the claim. Refuted A check or code reading that contradicts the claim, with the relevant input or line. Cannot tell What you inspected, what is missing, and the smallest next check that would decide it.

Finish with one sentence about the review's coverage: a reviewer reporting no finding only says that no finding was reported for the supplied context. It does not prove that the change is correct or that an unmentioned requirement is satisfied.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
