Add what the first two do not show: other repositories and directories the agent's working directory or container can see, the tools and MCP servers it has enabled, and whether its permission mode asks before a command runs.

Write two columns, need and reach, and mark every entry of reach that the task does not need. For each marked entry decide: narrow it now, or keep it with an owner and a reason. This is the portal check from the lecture, applied to a team of one.

docs.title: 2. What one accepted change cost (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Choose the most recent change in your project that you accepted from your agent. Find it:

git log --oneline -10
git show --stat HEAD

Replace HEAD with the commit you chose if it is not the latest. From your agent's session records, count every run that led to this change, including the ones that failed, timed out or were abandoned, and any run spent on an approach you rejected along the way. Use the unit your agent reports (requests, tokens or credit) and do not convert it into a price. Add the minutes you spent reviewing and checking the change yourself.

Write one line: runs, total in your agent's unit, and review minutes for this one accepted change. If your records cannot show an earlier run, write cannot tell for that part and the record you would keep next time. One change is one observation about your own process; it is not a finding about any model.

docs.title: 3. One regression for one fix (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Choose a defect you have already fixed in your project, with the fix committed. Find the commit before the fix:

git log --oneline -- FILE

Here FILE is the source file the fix changed. Write a test that states the required behaviour for the input that showed the defect, and commit it. Then show that the test can fail: put the file back as it was before the fix, run the test, restore the file and run the test again. BEFORE is the commit before the fix and TEST is your test file:

git checkout BEFORE -- FILE
python -m pytest TEST -q
git checkout HEAD -- FILE
python -m pytest TEST -q
git status --short

Expected evidence: the first test run fails on the assertion about the defect, the second passes, and git status --short prints nothing for FILE, which shows the file is back at your current version (untracked files such as a test cache may still be listed). Keep both outputs beside their revisions. Three results need a second look:

  • The test passes on the earlier file. It does not reach the defect. Change the input, not the claim.
  • The test fails on the earlier file for another reason, such as an import error. That is not evidence about the defect. If the fix changed several files, name them all in both git checkout commands.
  • The defect depends on timing or order. A test that sometimes passes on the earlier file proves nothing; force the order, as row 2 of the lecture's replay does.

If you have no fixed defect yet, take one open item from your backlog instead: write the test first, keep its failing output, and record the regression as half done.

docs.title: 4. Decide and exchange (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Finish the operating note with one decision line: accept, narrow, recheck or stop, and the evidence behind it. Then exchange notes with a partner in writing. Each of you asks one changed-condition question, for example "what would your regression show if two requests arrived together?", and the other answers with the input, the expected result and the check that would decide it.

Your operating note holds:

Task and what it needs
Reach: what the agent can reach; entries beyond the need, each narrowed or kept with owner and reason
One accepted change: runs, total in the agent's unit, review minutes; what the records cannot show
Regression: defect, BEFORE and current revisions, failing output, passing output
Not covered: one condition the regression does not test
Decision: accept | narrow | recheck | stop, with the evidence

docs.title: After class: fixture practice
docs.text:
If you did not finish the lecture's predictions, do them now from the course checkout. Each takes a prediction first and a run second; the commands and their expected output are in the notes.

Part Predict by hand Then run Portal The grant that allows each of the five calls, and what each grant can reach org_check.py portal, then the narrowed copy Gateway For each of the six runs, the request where the policy stops it; the line that holds the key org_check.py gateway Budget How many requests are sent with cap 10, reserve 4 and actual 1; then with request 2's reply lost budget_ledger.py, then --lost-reply 2, then one variation of your own Cost Units and review minutes per accepted change org_check.py cost Route Supported or not for each of the three choices, with the deciding line org_check.py route Replay Replies and stored jobs for each of the four rows under each handler retry_replay.py in all three modes

docs.title: Observe before you repair
docs.text:
The draft, the log and the three outcomes are in the notes.

Minutes Action Retained work 0-7 Read agent_rca.json and one log line. For each claim, predict confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and the field or line that would decide it Three predictions 7-17 Run check_rca.py once without options, then once with --path for each page a claim names The summaries you used 17-27 Open every cited line. Give each claim one outcome with the line, or the missing field, that decides it Three outcomes with evidence 27-35 For a claim you cannot decide, write the next check and the result that would confirm or refute it. Rewrite the proposed repair so that it acts only on confirmed claims, with a rollback condition and a user-path check Next check and bounded mitigation

From the course checkout:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/check_rca.py
python lectures/week-11/fixture/check_rca.py --path /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/
python lectures/week-11/fixture/check_rca.py --path /domains/ci_dashboard/import

With the first prefix the summary reads 12 records, with a p95 of 61.4 ms before 10:05 and 912.6 ms after. With the second it reads 8 records, with 2 server errors in 4 requests before 10:05 and 0 in 4 after. The script never gives an outcome; that part is yours.

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text:
Leave the job table behind. While a service runs revision R7, an on-call agent asks the deployment tool to "roll back one revision". The call times out, so the agent sends the same request again. The first call had in fact completed, and the service already runs R6.

State what the second call must return and which effect it must not cause. Write the recovery assertion you would check afterwards. Then describe a later rollback that the tool must still carry out, and say what tells it apart from a repeat.

docs.title: Participation and accessibility
docs.text: All required material is plain text and can be completed with a keyboard. An approved written or asynchronous exchange can replace the live exchange while preserving the same individual note. Planned times organise support; they do not penalise extra time or an approved arrangement. Keep one operating note; do not copy private chat, personal data or credentials into it, and record a variable's name, never its value.

docs.title: Week 11: Building an AI-native team
docs.text: Every incident, log, record, unit and agent summary on this page was written by the course for teaching. None is a measurement of a real system, model, gateway or price.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you can:

  • describe the four shared pieces a team uses to operate agents (a tool portal, a model gateway, cost per accepted change and a routing policy), the problem each one solves and the check that would reveal each one failing (LO8);
  • check an agent's own report on its work against the records, and say which line refutes it (LO8);
  • check a draft root-cause analysis against a request log before any repair, marking each claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell (LO8);
  • prove a recovery with a regression that fails on the incident build, fails on a repair that only looks right and passes on the real repair (LO8); and
  • state what your evidence does not cover and decide to accept, narrow, recheck or stop (LO9).

docs.title: From one agent to a team's agents
docs.text:
So far the controls around your agent have been your own: a dedicated directory, no credentials in the environment and keys kept out of everything you share, as Tools and model access asks. When a whole team works this way, those jobs move into shared services. Four pieces recur:

Piece The problem it solves What it concentrates Tool portal Nobody can say which agent may call which tool on which repository Every grant Model gateway Keys, budgets and logs are scattered across laptops and CI Every key and every cap Cost per accepted change Spending is reported per token or per run, which says nothing about results The definition of what a change cost Routing policy Every task goes to the most expensive route by default The choice of route for many tasks at once

Each piece concentrates authority, so one review reaches every agent and so does one mistake. For each piece this lesson does the same two steps. Generate: a record stands in for what a team's agents and services produced, and its agent_summary is the claim, as if an agent had reported on its own work. Verify: you check the records by hand, write the result you expect, then run a check and compare.

Run every command on this page from the course checkout. The scripts use only the Python standard library, call no model, open no network connection and write no file; if your system has no python command, type python3. Read org_check.py before you run it: each of its four commands applies one stated rule to one JSON file and ends with a result: line.

docs.title: Tool portal: compare the grant with the task
docs.text:
A portal is one service that lists which tools exist, who may call each one and on what, and records every grant. A hook in your own repository checks one call before its effect; a portal applies that idea to everyone at once.

org-portal.json holds one task, three grants and one agent session of five calls. The task is to read the log of failed build #121 in the ci-dashboard example repository and open a draft pull request there. The session's third call reads a private repository because the build log told the agent to compare a settings file. The agent's summary reads:

Every call I made stayed within my grants, and the portal refused the one call it did not cover.

Before running anything, match each call to the grant that allows it, and list what each grant can reach. Then run the check:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/org_check.py portal lectures/week-11/fixture/org-portal.json

It exits 1 and prints:

task repositories: ci-dashboard
call 1 ci.read_log ci-dashboard: allowed by G1
call 2 code.read ci-dashboard: allowed by G2
call 3 code.read release-config (private): allowed by G2; outside the task
call 4 deploy.run ci-dashboard: denied, no grant covers this tool; the tool did not run
call 5 code.open_draft_pr ci-dashboard: allowed by G3
G1 ci.read_log reaches: ci-dashboard
G2 code.read reaches: ci-dashboard, docs-site, hr-notes (private), release-config (private); beyond the task: docs-site, hr-notes, release-config
G3 code.open_draft_pr reaches: ci-dashboard
result: OVER-BROAD - grants reaching beyond the task: 1; calls outside the task that a grant allowed: 1

The summary is true, and that is the lesson. Every call was checked against a grant and the one uncovered call was refused. The portal worked exactly as configured, and the agent still read a private repository the task never needed, because grant G2 names every repository. Checking each call against its grant is not enough: when the grant itself reaches further than the task, every call passes. In one public demonstration, an agent's single GitHub MCP connection could reach both public and private repositories; injected text in a public issue led the agent to write private information into a public pull request, and the disclosers recommend limiting repository access (incidents/github-mcp; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1).

Treat a grant like code: it has an owner, a reason and a test showing that a call outside it is denied and leaves no effect. Narrow G2 in a copy and watch the same session again:

mkdir week11-org
cp lectures/week-11/fixture/org_check.py lectures/week-11/fixture/org-*.json week11-org/

In week11-org/org-portal.json, change the repositories of grant G2 from ["*"] to ["ci-dashboard"]. Write the line you expect to change, then run:

python week11-org/org_check.py portal week11-org/org-portal.json

It now exits 0 and prints:

task repositories: ci-dashboard
call 1 ci.read_log ci-dashboard: allowed by G1
call 2 code.read ci-dashboard: allowed by G2
call 3 code.read release-config (private): denied, no grant covers this repository; the tool did not run; outside the task
call 4 deploy.run ci-dashboard: denied, no grant covers this tool; the tool did not run
call 5 code.open_draft_pr ci-dashboard: allowed by G3
G1 ci.read_log reaches: ci-dashboard
G2 code.read reaches: ci-dashboard
G3 code.open_draft_pr reaches: ci-dashboard
result: WITHIN THE TASK - every grant reaches only the task's repositories; 2 calls denied

Call 3 is now the denied call that tests the grant. Delete week11-org when you have finished the week's practice.

docs.title: Model gateway: what it refuses
docs.text:
A gateway is one controlled place between code that wants a model and the service that answers. Describe a gateway by what it refuses:

Job What the gateway does The check that reveals it failing Keep the key outside the work The agent's side sends a prompt; only the gateway holds the provider key Search everything on the agent's side for the key Fix the destination It sends only to routes on its list A request on an unlisted route appears as sent Cap each run It refuses, before sending, a request past the run's request or token cap A request past the cap appears as sent Survive an outage When the provider is unavailable, a stated fallback answers The record shows a different fallback, or none Keep logs minimal It records counts and status, not prompt or reply text Read one log record

Products exist for this. In LiteLLM, for example, virtual keys control model access and track spending, key settings can bound budgets, budget periods and request and token rates, and one logging setting keeps message content away from logging providers while request metadata is still tracked (tools/litellm; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2). A setting is a claim until a record shows it enforced.

org-gateway.json holds a policy (at most 4 requests and 3000 tokens per run, two listed routes, a fallback named replay that answers from a recorded reply, and the placeholder key sk-EXAMPLE) and six runs, each with the gateway's decisions and the lines the agent's side logged. The agent's summary reads: "All six runs followed the gateway policy." Replay the policy over each run by hand, adding each request's reservation before it is sent, and search the logged lines for the key. Then run:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/org_check.py gateway lectures/week-11/fixture/org-gateway.json

It exits 1 and prints:

policy: at most 4 requests and 3000 tokens per run, each request reserving its worst case before it is sent; routes: route-large, route-small; fallback: replay
R1 route-small: 3 requests sent, 900 tokens used; matches the policy
R2 route-small: request 5 was sent; the policy refuses it before sending (request cap 4); DIFFERS
R3 route-large: request 3 refused before sending (2000 used + 1200 reserved > 3000); matches the policy
R4 route-preview: request 1 was sent; the policy refuses every request on a route it does not list; DIFFERS
R5 route-large: provider unavailable at request 1; fallback replay used; matches the policy
R6 route-small: 1 request sent, 250 tokens used; matches the policy
sandbox-side log: the key appears in R6 line 2
result: POLICY NOT ENFORCED - 2 runs differ from the policy (R2, R4); the key reached the sandbox side in R6

Three separate failures refute the summary: a fifth request that was sent, a request on a route nobody listed, and a key in a log on the agent's side (the check calls that side the sandbox side). R3 is the gateway working: 1000 tokens remained, and the third request was still refused because it could have used 1200. R6 matches the policy on every request and still leaks the key, so a policy replay and a key search are two different checks.

docs.title: A budget reserves before it spends
docs.text:
R3 shows the rule that makes a cap protect anything: the gateway reserves a request's worst case before sending it and settles to the actual amount after the reply. A gateway that only reported spending afterwards would protect nobody's money. The whole rule is the Budget class at the top of budget_ledger.py, about twenty lines; read reserve and settle now.

The units are course-made numbers, not prices. A run's cap is 10 units. Each request reserves 4, the worst case for its prompt and output limits, and each reply actually costs 1. Predict how many requests are sent, then run:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/budget_ledger.py

request 1: sent, reply cost 1; spent 1 of 10
request 2: sent, reply cost 1; spent 2 of 10
request 3: sent, reply cost 1; spent 3 of 10
request 4: sent, reply cost 1; spent 4 of 10
request 5: sent, reply cost 1; spent 5 of 10
request 6: sent, reply cost 1; spent 6 of 10
request 7: sent, reply cost 1; spent 7 of 10
request 8: refused before sending (Request exceeds the remaining budget.) spent 7 of 10

Three units remain, and the eighth request is refused because it could cost four. Now let request 2 lose its reply. The gateway cannot tell whether the provider charged for it:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/budget_ledger.py --lost-reply 2

request 1: sent, reply cost 1; spent 1 of 10
request 2: sent, reply lost, reservation of 4 kept; spent 5 of 10
request 3: sent, reply cost 1; spent 6 of 10
request 4: sent, reply cost 1; spent 7 of 10
request 5: refused before sending (Request exceeds the remaining budget.) spent 7 of 10

One lost reply cost the run three requests. A timeout marks where observation stopped; it does not show that nothing happened. The incident later in this lesson turns on the same sentence.

A cap is a hard stop, not a warning. Design an agent task so that its required work finishes inside the cap, or so that it stops and reports. Splitting the work across runs to get around a cap defeats the protection.

docs.title: Cost per accepted change
docs.text:
A run's total measures one run. What a team needs to know is what an accepted change cost: every run that led to it, including failed and retried attempts, plus the time people spent reviewing it. Runs spent on changes that were rejected count too, because the team paid for them. Cost per token rewards cheap output that nobody can merge.

org-changes.json records the runs and reviews behind four changes:

Change Runs (units) Decision Review minutes fix-118 a1 6 (checks failed), a2 6 accepted 20 fix-119 a3 3 accepted 10 fix-120 a4 3, a5 2 rejected 15 fix-121 a6 2 (timed out, retried), a7 2 accepted 15

The agent's summary reads: "A change costs about 3 units: that is the trace total of run a3." Compute the cost per accepted change by hand, then run:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/org_check.py cost lectures/week-11/fixture/org-changes.json

It exits 0 and prints:

change fix-118 accepted: runs a1 6 (checks failed), a2 6; 12 units; review 20 minutes
change fix-119 accepted: runs a3 3; 3 units; review 10 minutes
change fix-120 rejected: runs a4 3, a5 2; 5 units; review 15 minutes
change fix-121 accepted: runs a6 2 (timed out, retried), a7 2; 4 units; review 15 minutes
all runs: 7 runs, 24 units; review: 60 minutes; accepted changes: 3
trace total of one run, for comparison: a3 3 units
result: cost per accepted change is 8 units of model use and 20 review minutes

Eight units, not three: 24 units over 3 accepted changes. Run a3 belongs to the one change that was accepted on its first run, which is why quoting it flatters the total. Report review minutes beside the units in the same way and do not convert them into a price. Exit 0 here means only that the figure is defined; the check exits 1 when no change was accepted.

docs.title: Route to a cheaper option only when your evaluator says it is good enough
docs.text:
A routing policy sends each task to the cheapest route that passes the evaluator and escalates when a check fails. A cheaper route may be a smaller model, fewer requests, a smaller output limit or no model call at all. Whether it is good enough is a measurement: run the same frozen cases on both routes and compare them case by case.

org-routes.json holds a policy, "Send each task to the cheapest route that passes at least 90% of its frozen evaluator cases", three route choices and the evaluator results behind them. The route names are placeholders. The agent's summary reads: "Routing moved all three tasks to a cheaper route without losing quality." Decide for each task whether the chosen route passes every case the current route passes, on the revision in use. Then run:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/org_check.py route lectures/week-11/fixture/org-routes.json

It exits 1 and prints:

policy: Send each task to the cheapest route that passes at least 90% of its frozen evaluator cases.
status-is-failed: 12 frozen cases; current route route-large; chosen route no-model
  route-large r2: 12 of 12
  no-model r1: 11 of 12; fails case 7
  route-small r2: 10 of 12; fails cases 7, 11
  no-model: NOT SUPPORTED - fails case 7, which route-large passes
summarize-log: 8 frozen cases; current route route-large; chosen route route-small
  route-large r2: 8 of 8
  route-small r2: 8 of 8
  route-small: supported - passes every case route-large passes, at 1 unit per request instead of 4
label-flaky-test: 10 frozen cases; current route route-large; chosen route route-small
  route-large r2: 9 of 10; fails case 4
  route-small r1: 9 of 10; fails case 4
  route-small: NOT SUPPORTED - the results for route-small are for r1 and the route is now r2; rerun the frozen cases
result: 1 of 3 route choices supported by the evaluator

All three choices satisfy the 90% rule, and only one is supported. In the first task the cheaper route passes 11 of 12 and loses the one case the current route gets right: a rate hides which case was lost. In the third the two routes fail the same case, but the cheaper route's results are for an older revision; a route's name does not guarantee unchanged behaviour, so the frozen cases are rerun whenever a route or a model changes. Even a fresh, complete pass says nothing about inputs that are not among the frozen cases.

docs.title: Rolling it out: what each piece can hide
docs.text:
Rolling model access out to a whole team brings the shared pieces' failure modes with it. For each risk, name the check that would detect it:

Risk Check that would reveal it Keys copied into repositories and CI instead of held by the gateway Secret scanning and key rotation; the gateway is the only holder Groups bypass the gateway with personal tools, so caps and logs miss that work Compare the model use you can see with the work being delivered Logs quietly become a store of prompts holding code or customer data Minimal records by default; read one record One cap for everyone either blocks real tasks or protects nothing Set caps per task from measured runs; every refusal says what to do next A gateway or provider outage stops everyone at once A tested fallback, such as a recorded reply or a path that needs no model Adoption is judged by usage rather than results Evaluator results and incident records, not token counts

Apply the boundary test from the security week to each piece: a denied call stays denied through every route, and permitted work still succeeds.

docs.title: An incident: observe before you repair
docs.text:
Operating agents includes the day something breaks. On the ci-dashboard example, revision R2 went live at 10:05:00, and a user then reported that the project page was slow. Before anyone changes code, an agent drafts a root-cause analysis. The draft in agent_rca.json was written for this lesson; no model produced it. It cites lines of request_log.jsonl, ten minutes of request records. Each line is one request with its time, request ID, method, path, status and duration, and nothing from the query string, form or body:

{"timestamp":"2026-11-24T10:05:41+0000","event":"request","request_id":"w11-23","method":"GET","path":"/domains/ci_dashboard/projects/2","status":200,"duration_ms":884.1}
ID The draft claims Cites lines H1 R2 broke imports: the import endpoint has returned server errors since the deploy. 6, 14, 31 H2 From 10:05 the project page's p95 rose from about 60 ms to about 900 ms; other pages held. 23, 28, 34 H3 The cause is R2's project page running one database query per build. 23, 28, 34

It proposes: "Roll back R2, and add automatic retries to imports."

Predict before running. For each claim, write confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and the field or line you expect to decide it. Then run check_rca.py. The second command summarises only the paths that begin with the prefix you give:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/check_rca.py
python lectures/week-11/fixture/check_rca.py --path /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/

The first command exits 0 and prints:

request log: 40 request records from 10:00:02 to 10:09:58 UTC
window       requests  5xx  error rate  p95 ms
10:00-10:05  20        2    10.0%       58.9
10:05-10:10  20        0    0.0%        884.1
p95: nearest rank, the ceil(0.95 x n)-th smallest duration in the window

H1: R2 broke imports: the import endpoint has returned server errors since the deploy.
  line 6   10:01:12  POST  /domains/ci_dashboard/import      500    14.2 ms  w11-06
  line 14  10:03:40  POST  /domains/ci_dashboard/import      500    13.8 ms  w11-14
  line 31  10:07:51  POST  /domains/ci_dashboard/import      400     9.6 ms  w11-31

H2: From 10:05 the project page's p95 rose from about 60 ms to about 900 ms; other pages held.
  line 23  10:05:41  GET   /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/2  200   884.1 ms  w11-23
  line 28  10:07:05  GET   /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/5  200   912.6 ms  w11-28
  line 34  10:08:40  GET   /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/5  200   856.7 ms  w11-34

H3: The cause is R2's project page running one database query per build.
  line 23  10:05:41  GET   /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/2  200   884.1 ms  w11-23
  line 28  10:07:05  GET   /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/5  200   912.6 ms  w11-28
  line 34  10:08:40  GET   /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/5  200   856.7 ms  w11-34

The script counts and prints; it does not judge. Give each claim one outcome, as you did for review findings in Week 6:

  • Confirmed: the log shows the claim as stated, for the path, window and effect it names.
  • Refuted: the log shows something the claim rules out, such as a cited line from before the time the claim names, or a window without the effect it asserts.
  • Cannot tell: no field in this log could show the claim either way. Name the missing observation and the check that would supply it.

Work the three claims yourself before the studio. Three cautions apply to any request log:

  • A cited line supports a claim only if its time, path and status say what the claim says. Open every one; a draft that cites lines has not yet been checked.
  • Over a few requests, a percentile is the slowest one or two. Each window here holds six project-page requests, so their p95 is the slowest of the six. Read the lines behind a summary.
  • A change that starts when a revision goes live confirms the timing, not the cause. Timing can justify a reversible mitigation; it does not tell you which code to repair.

Act only on what you confirmed. A mitigation that rests on timing alone, such as rolling back a revision, must be reversible, state its rollback condition and end with a check of the user path. A code repair waits until a check that can see its cause has run. Drop any part of a proposal that rests on a refuted claim, but keep the claim's lines if they show something else worth following up.

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text:
A second incident on the same example. The dashboard acknowledges a retry request for build 42, then the reply is lost. The operator retries and a second job is created. retry-B42-7 identifies one user operation; req-a and req-b identify two delivery attempts for that same operation.

Time Request Operation key Observation Stored effect 00:00 req-a retry-B42-7 Server receives retry for build 42 None yet 00:01 req-a retry-B42-7 Transaction commits Job J81 queued; build 42 retrying 00:02 req-a retry-B42-7 Reply is lost; client times out J81 still queued 00:03 req-b retry-B42-7 Client repeats the same operation Unprotected handler creates J82 00:04 query-c retry-B42-7 Operator reads stored state Two jobs: J81 and J82

Decision: which evidence separates a failed request from a successful effect whose reply was lost? The client's timeout cannot: a timeout describes an observation boundary; it does not prove nothing happened. The persisted job and its operation key can.

Write the requirement before any repair. A repeated request with the same key and the same build returns the existing job and creates none. The same key with a different build is a conflict and creates nothing. A new intended retry uses a new key and gets a new job. Two deliveries of the same request that arrive together still create one job. These are the four rows below, and the last column is what a repair must show:

Row Replay input Required replies Required jobs 1 req-a commits, its reply is lost, then req-b repeats J81 J81 1 2 req-a and req-b arrive together with the same key and build J81 J81 1 3 The same key is reused for build 43 J81 conflict 1 4 A later intended retry uses retry-B42-8 J81 J82 2

Generate. Ask for a bounded repair tied to the event chain. Suppose the agent replies with the obvious one: look the key up, and insert a job only if none is found. Its summary says the duplicate is fixed, and on the incident as it happened (row 1) that is true.

Verify with a regression. retry_replay.py plays the four rows against an in-memory database with one of three handlers: unprotected (the incident build), check-then-insert (the agent's proposal) and repaired. It exits 0 only when every row meets the requirement. Run it on the incident build first:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/retry_replay.py unprotected

It exits 1 and prints:

mode: unprotected
row  replies       jobs (build/attempt)  build 42 shows
1    J81 J82       J81 42/7, J82 42/7    J82
2    J81 J82       J81 42/7, J82 42/7    J82
3    J81 J82       J81 42/7, J82 43/7    J81
4    J81 J82       J81 42/7, J82 42/8    J82
rows meeting the repaired requirement: 1 of 4

The check can fail, and it fails on the build that had the incident. Now the proposal:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/retry_replay.py check-then-insert

It exits 1 and prints:

mode: check-then-insert
row  replies       jobs (build/attempt)  build 42 shows
1    J81 J81       J81 42/7              J81
2    J81 J82       J81 42/7, J82 42/7    J82
3    J81 conflict  J81 42/7              J81
4    J81 J82       J81 42/7, J82 42/8    J82
rows meeting the repaired requirement: 3 of 4

Row 1, the incident as reported, now passes. Row 2 still stores two jobs: both requests looked the key up before either one inserted, so both found nothing. A regression that replayed only the reported sequence would have accepted this repair.

The real repair puts identity where the database can enforce it: a unique (pipeline, operation_key) stored with the job in one statement, so that a repeated matching request returns the existing job, the same key with another build is refused, and a batch with one conflicting row saves nothing. A check followed by a separate insert can still race, so uniqueness and atomicity belong to the persistence boundary.

python lectures/week-11/fixture/retry_replay.py repaired

It exits 0 and prints:

mode: repaired
row  replies       jobs (build/attempt)  build 42 shows
1    J81 J81       J81 42/7              J81
2    J81 J81       J81 42/7              J81
3    J81 conflict  J81 42/7              J81
4    J81 J82       J81 42/7, J82 42/8    J82
rows meeting the repaired requirement: 4 of 4

In rows 1, 3 and 4 the first reply answers req-a, and in row 1 that is the reply the client never saw. Row 2 lists its two replies in sorted order, because either request may write first. The last column is the user's view: the dashboard shows the job of a build's greatest attempt, so in row 4 it shows J82. Check the stored jobs as well as the replies, then the user's view.

What makes this a regression that proves the recovery. Three runs, kept together:

  1. It fails on the incident build (exit 1, one row of four).
  2. It fails on the repair that only looks right (exit 1, three rows of four).
  3. It passes on the repair (exit 0, four rows of four), and stays in the test suite.

A test that has only ever passed cannot show that it would catch the defect.

A regression for a race must force the order. Row 2 runs its two requests in two threads, and each handler pauses just before its first write, so both finish any lookup before either one writes. Remove that pause and the race appears only sometimes. In a copy of the file with the self.between() line of the check-then-insert branch deleted, 20 runs on the author's machine printed 3 of 4 three times and 4 of 4 seventeen times. Your counts will differ; the point is that seventeen green runs would have accepted a broken repair. The fixture guide gives the steps.

Acceptance decision. Declare recovery only after the user can observe the required state and duplicate effects are excluded for the tested path. Roll back if the change rejects a new authorised operation or corrupts the existing job mapping. The replay runs this lesson's reasoning on an in-memory table; it is not evidence about any service you run. Evidence that your own project recovered comes from a regression in your own repository.

docs.title: Agents that keep running after deployment
docs.text: An agent that acts in a deployed system, for example by triaging alerts or proposing a rollback, is one more service to operate. Give it credentials scoped to its task, a spending and action budget, and a switch that stops it without a deploy. Log what it read, what it proposed and what it changed, so that a postmortem can separate the agent's action from the incident it responded to. Keep irreversible operations behind a person's approval. In Replit's public account of one incident, its agent deleted data from a user's application database while development changes could still reach production, and the user restored the database through a rollback feature the agent did not know about (incidents/replit-db; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1). Put the agent in the runbook: who is paged when it misbehaves, how to disable it, and how to recover what it changed. Retried agent actions need the same idempotency you just examined for retried requests, and an agent's grants and caps are the portal and gateway from the first half of this lesson.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
The second session opens with CP2; the studio guide covers the rest. In the studio you work in your own project repository: you compare what your agent can reach with what one task needs, count what one accepted change cost you in runs and review minutes, and write one regression that fails before a fix of yours and passes after it.

Before the studio, finish the predictions this page asked for: the five portal calls, the six gateway runs, the two ledgers, the cost per accepted change, the three route choices, the three claims of the draft analysis and the four replay rows for each handler. Where an observation differs from your prediction, keep both and find the line you misread.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
For the shared pieces, the evidence is your prediction beside the check's output:

Check Expected evidence What a failure looks like portal on the supplied file Exit 1, result: OVER-BROAD, with G2 reaching three repositories beyond the task Exit 0 on your narrowed copy means the grant now fits; exit 2 means the JSON you edited no longer parses or lacks a field gateway Exit 1, R2 and R4 differ from the policy and the key appears in R6 line 2 Calling R3 a failure: a refusal before sending is the policy working budget_ledger.py Seven requests sent and the eighth refused; with request 2's reply lost, four sent and the fifth refused A prediction of ten sent requests ignores the reservation cost Exit 0, 8 units and 20 review minutes per accepted change Quoting 3 units repeats the summary's single run route Exit 1, one of three choices supported Counting two supported means a stale revision was accepted

For the log check, every claim carries exactly one outcome and the line, or the missing field, that decides it. A claim the log cannot decide stays cannot tell, with its next check written beside it; your rewritten repair acts only on confirmed claims and names its rollback condition and the user-path check that ends it.

For the recovery, run the regression in all three modes and keep the three results together:

python lectures/week-11/fixture/retry_replay.py unprotected
python lectures/week-11/fixture/retry_replay.py check-then-insert
python lectures/week-11/fixture/retry_replay.py repaired

Expected evidence: exit 1 with 1 of 4, exit 1 with 3 of 4, then exit 0 with 4 of 4. The failure case to recognise is the middle one: a repair that passes the reported sequence and fails the forced race.

These checks apply stated rules to course-made records. A result is evidence about the rule you applied; it says nothing about how a real portal, gateway, route or model behaves.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake Better next action Accepting an agent's summary because every call it made was allowed List what each grant can reach and compare it with what the task needs Treating a refusal before sending as a gateway fault Replay the policy: reserved worst case plus what is already used, against the cap Reading spend from the program's own output Read the gateway's record, and search the agent's side for the key separately Treating a timed-out request as free Count its whole reservation until the outcome is known Quoting one run's total as what a change costs Divide all runs and all review minutes, rejected work included, by the accepted changes Calling a cheaper route good enough because its pass rate is close Compare case by case on the same frozen cases and the revision in use Accepting a draft's claim because it cites log lines Open each cited line and compare its time, path and status with the claim Treating a slowdown that starts with a deploy as its cause Record the timing as confirmed and the cause as cannot tell until a check that can see the cause has run Deduplicating retries with a lookup followed by a separate insert Put a unique operation key and the job insert in one statement or transaction, then force the concurrent order and count stored jobs Calling a recovery proved because the new test passes Show the same test failing on the incident build, and on the repair you rejected Declaring recovery because the health endpoint is green Check the state transition and the displayed result for the affected operation

A source citation, a fluent explanation or a successful demonstration does not supply a missing observation. State the next check and why it would change your decision.

docs.title: Running agents as a team
docs.text:
The required reading is the notes and the studio guide; the week's row in the syllabus calendar lists what is due. Before the first session, read the learning objectives and the event table in the continuing dashboard case, and write which observation separates a failed request from a lost reply.

The four sources below are optional. Each entry names the part to read and what to use it for.

  • Budget and logging boundaries (about 12 minutes): read Virtual Keys — LiteLLM, especially “Upperbound /key/generate params”, and Logging — LiteLLM, especially “Redact Messages, Response Content”. Compare those controls with the gateway jobs in the notes (key held outside the work, listed routes, per-run caps, minimal logs), then say which checks would still need a record to show the setting enforced. (tools/litellm; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2)
  • A postmortem is reviewed before it counts (about 20 minutes): read the opening and the “Google’s Postmortem Philosophy” and “Collaborate and Share Knowledge” sections of Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure, Chapter 15 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book. It gives the parts a postmortem must cover, the triggers that call for one, a blameless way to describe contributing causes, and review questions such as whether the root cause is deep enough. Use those questions on the draft root-cause analysis in the notes. (studies/sre-postmortem-culture; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)
  • Alerts, rollback and changes (about 15 minutes): read the “Monitoring”, “Emergency Response” and “Change Management” sections of Introduction, Chapter 1 of the same book. It sorts monitoring output into alerts, tickets and logs, and treats changes to a live system as a common cause of outages, to be rolled out gradually and rolled back safely. Use it to decide which signals of your own project should interrupt someone and which only belong in a log, and to check that a rollback ends with a runnable check of the user path. (studies/sre-introduction; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)
  • Telemetry is not a storage backend (about 12 minutes): read What is OpenTelemetry? and Collector — OpenTelemetry, focusing on the signals and the collector's role. Use them to choose the smallest trace, metric and log fields an incident like this week's would need, and to state what a collector failure would leave unknown. (tools/opentelemetry; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2)

For each source you read, write one sentence that connects its claim to a line of your studio note and one sentence naming what the source does not show about your own project. Do not report a source's example as your own result.

docs.title: Week 11 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Use these explanations after your first attempt. Keep every conclusion tied to a line, a field or a run that another reader could check.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: No. The report can be true and the session can still have gone beyond the task, because a call is checked only against its grant. The missing comparison is what each grant can reach against what the task needs. A grant that names every repository lets every read pass; narrow it to the task's repository and keep one denied call as its test.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: The third request is refused. After two replies 1200 tokens are used; the third reservation would make 1200 + 900 = 2100, which is more than 2000. At that moment 800 tokens are unspent. It is refused because the gateway reserves the worst case before sending: the actual use is unknown until the reply arrives, and a cap checked only afterwards would already be passed.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: Four requests are sent and the fifth is refused. Each reply settles at 2 units, so four replies leave 8 units spent; the fifth reservation would make 8 + 5 = 13, more than 12, so it is refused with 4 units unspent. The fixture's last line reads request 5: refused before sending (Request exceeds the remaining budget.) spent 8 of 12.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: The gateway cannot tell whether the provider did the work and charged for it; a lost reply marks where observation stopped, not that nothing happened. Releasing the reservation would let later requests spend units that may already be owed, so the run could pass its cap without any single request being refused.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: Count every run and every review minute, including the failed run, the timed-out run and the rejected change: 4 + 4 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 18 units and 12 + 8 + 20 = 40 review minutes. Two changes were accepted, so 18 units ÷ 2 accepted changes = 9 units and 40 ÷ 2 = 20 review minutes per accepted change. The summary's 4 units is one run of one change.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: No. The rates alone do not justify the switch: the rule route loses a case the model route passes, and a higher total hides which case was lost. Inspect that case, repair the rule, rerun all 50 frozen cases on the revision in use and switch only if no case the model route passes now fails. Even then the result says nothing about inputs outside the 50 cases.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: Refuted. The claim says the errors rose; the log shows 2 in 50 before and 1 in 50 after. Refuting it leaves the server errors in both windows unexplained, and it does not show that imports are healthy. Record those errors as a separate observation to follow up.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Cannot tell. No field in the request log records a query or an index, so the log can neither confirm nor refute the claim; slow lines show only that the page was slow. A check that could decide it: on the same data, compare the page's duration with and without the index, or read the query plan for that page. Until then name the missing observation and keep the claim open.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: The request committed: its effect exists and only the reply was lost. The timeout marks where the client stopped observing. A repeat with the same key and the same build must return the existing job and create no new one; the same key with a different build is a conflict that creates nothing, and a new intended retry needs a new key.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text: The missing input is two deliveries of the same request arriving together, with the order forced so that both lookups finish before either insert; a lookup followed by a separate insert then stores two jobs. A regression is evidence of recovery when it fails on the incident build, fails on the repair that only looks right, and passes on the real repair, with the stored jobs counted as well as the replies.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval and transfer
docs.text:
Retrieval 1. Settle the denominator first: find the two instances missing from the results table, record why each is absent, and either run them or report the rate over all 12 instances with the missing ones shown as not run. A pass rate over 10 is not a result for a manifest of 12.

Retrieval 2. The text is data. A tool result carries no authority, whatever it says; whether a command runs is decided by the task, the instruction file and the permission check, and by the person who owns the session. Record the text as an injection attempt and do not act on it.

Transfer. A useful answer names a condition outside the tested path, for example a repeat after a restart or three deliveries at once, gives the input and the expected stored state, and says which decision moves: a failure on that input changes accept to narrow or recheck, and the note says so before anyone relies on the fix.

docs.title: Operating agents and proving a recovery
docs.text:
Answer these formative prompts in your own work record before you open the public answer guidance. The numbers are fresh course-made instances, not the lecture's records. Each answer should name the line, field or run that another reader could check.

  1. An agent's report says, "Every call I made was allowed by a grant." One of its grants lets code.read reach every repository, and the task needs one. Is the report enough to accept the session? Which comparison is missing?
  2. A gateway policy allows 2000 tokens per run. Each request reserves 900 and each reply uses 600. Which request is refused, and how many tokens are unspent at that moment? Why is it refused although tokens remain?
  3. A run has a cap of 12 units. Each request reserves 5 and each reply costs 2. How many requests are sent before one is refused? Check your answer with python lectures/week-11/fixture/budget_ledger.py --cap 12 --reserve 5 --actual 2 from the course checkout.
  4. A request's reply is lost. Why does the budget keep the whole reservation, and what would go wrong if it released it?
  5. Three changes were worked on. Change y1 was accepted after runs of 4 units (checks failed) and 4 units, with 12 review minutes. Change y2 was rejected after one run of 2 units and 8 review minutes. Change y3 was accepted after runs of 6 units and 2 units (timed out), with 20 review minutes. A summary says, "A change costs about 4 units." What is the cost per accepted change in units and in review minutes?
  6. A rule route passes 47 of 50 frozen cases and a model route passes 46. The rule fails one case that the model passes. Is the rule route good enough to replace the model from these rates alone? What is the next check?
  7. A draft root-cause analysis says that server errors on the import endpoint rose after a 14:00 change. The request log shows 2 server errors in 50 import requests before 14:00 and 1 in 50 after. Is the claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and what does your answer leave open?
  8. The same draft says that a slow project page is caused by a missing database index. The request log records only time, request ID, method, path, status and duration. Which outcome does the log support, and which check could decide the claim?
  9. A client times out, but stored state shows a job for the operation key. What can you infer, and what must a repeat with the same key and the same build return?
  10. A proposed repair looks the key up and inserts a job only when none is found. A regression that replays the reported sequence passes. Which input is missing from the regression, and what three results make a regression evidence of recovery?

docs.title: Transfer to your project
docs.text: Take the regression you wrote in the studio. Name one condition it does not test, the input that would test it, and the decision (accept, narrow, recheck or stop) you would change if that input failed.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text:
R1. A results table reports 9 of 10 instances passed, and the manifest lists 12 instances. What must be settled before the pass rate is read?

R2. Text inside a tool result tells the agent to run a command. Is that text data or authority, and what decides whether the command runs?

docs.title: Building an AI-native team
docs.text:
Week 11 · Portals, gateways, routing and cost; an incident and its regression

Every record, log and number in this deck is course-made for teaching.

docs.title: Today's sequence
docs.text:
First half: four shared pieces a team uses to operate agents. Each time, an agent's summary is the claim and a record is the check.

Second half: one incident. Observe before you repair, then prove the recovery with a regression.

docs.title: From one agent to a team's agents
docs.text:
Piece It concentrates Tool portal Every grant Model gateway Every key and every cap Cost per accepted change What "a change cost" means Routing policy The route for many tasks at once

One review reaches every agent. So does one mistake.

docs.title: Generate, then verify
docs.text:
Generate: a record of what agents and services did, ending in an agent_summary.

Verify: check the record by hand, write the result you expect, then run one command.

python lectures/week-11/fixture/org_check.py portal lectures/week-11/fixture/org-portal.json

docs.title: Portal: is this summary true?
docs.text:
Task: read one build log and open a draft pull request in one repository.

Every call I made stayed within my grants, and the portal refused the one call it did not cover.

Five calls, three grants. Match each call to its grant before we run the check.

docs.title: The summary is true, and the session still went too far
docs.text:
call 3 code.read release-config (private): allowed by G2; outside the task
G2 code.read reaches: ci-dashboard, docs-site, hr-notes (private), release-config (private); beyond the task: docs-site, hr-notes, release-config
result: OVER-BROAD - grants reaching beyond the task: 1; calls outside the task that a grant allowed: 1

Checking each call against its grant is not enough when the grant reaches past the task.

docs.title: A grant is code
docs.text:
It has an owner, a reason and a test.

Narrow G2 to the task's repository and run the same session:

call 3 code.read release-config (private): denied, no grant covers this repository; the tool did not run; outside the task
result: WITHIN THE TASK - every grant reaches only the task's repositories; 2 calls denied

The denied call is the grant's test.

docs.title: Gateway: describe it by what it refuses
docs.text:
• a request on a route that is not listed
  • a request past the run's request cap
  • a request whose worst case would pass the token cap
  • anything that would put the key on the agent's side

A setting is a claim until a record shows it enforced.

docs.title: Six runs, one policy
docs.text:
Policy: at most 4 requests and 3000 tokens per run; two listed routes; a stated fallback.

All six runs followed the gateway policy.

Which runs differ? Where is the key?

docs.title: Three separate failures
docs.text:
R2 route-small: request 5 was sent; the policy refuses it before sending (request cap 4); DIFFERS
R4 route-preview: request 1 was sent; the policy refuses every request on a route it does not list; DIFFERS
sandbox-side log: the key appears in R6 line 2

R6 matches the policy on every request and still leaks the key: a policy replay and a key search are two checks.

docs.title: A refusal can be the gateway working
docs.text:
R3 route-large: request 3 refused before sending (2000 used + 1200 reserved > 3000); matches the policy

1000 tokens remained. The request could have used 1200.

docs.title: Predict the ledger
docs.text:
Cap 10 units. Each request reserves 4. Each reply costs 1.

How many requests are sent?

Now request 2 loses its reply. How many are sent?

Units are course-made numbers, not prices.

docs.title: Reserve before sending, settle after the reply
docs.text:
request 7: sent, reply cost 1; spent 7 of 10
request 8: refused before sending (Request exceeds the remaining budget.) spent 7 of 10

With the lost reply:

request 2: sent, reply lost, reservation of 4 kept; spent 5 of 10
request 5: refused before sending (Request exceeds the remaining budget.) spent 7 of 10

A timeout marks where observation stopped. It does not show that nothing happened.

docs.title: Cost per accepted change
docs.text:
Change Runs (units) Decision Review minutes fix-118 a1 6 (checks failed), a2 6 accepted 20 fix-119 a3 3 accepted 10 fix-120 a4 3, a5 2 rejected 15 fix-121 a6 2 (timed out, retried), a7 2 accepted 15

A change costs about 3 units.

docs.title: Count everything the team paid for
docs.text:
all runs: 7 runs, 24 units; review: 60 minutes; accepted changes: 3
result: cost per accepted change is 8 units of model use and 20 review minutes

Failed, retried and rejected work counts. Review minutes stay minutes.

docs.title: Routing: "at least 90% of the frozen cases"
docs.text:
Task Current route Cheaper route status-is-failed 12 of 12 11 of 12 summarize-log 8 of 8 8 of 8 label-flaky-test 9 of 10 9 of 10

All three pass the rule. How many choices does the evaluator support?

docs.title: One of three
docs.text:
no-model: NOT SUPPORTED - fails case 7, which route-large passes
  route-small: NOT SUPPORTED - the results for route-small are for r1 and the route is now r2; rerun the frozen cases
result: 1 of 3 route choices supported by the evaluator

A rate hides which case was lost. A route's name does not guarantee unchanged behaviour.

docs.title: What each piece can hide
docs.text: Risk Check Keys copied into repositories Secret scanning; the gateway is the only holder Work that bypasses the gateway Compare visible model use with delivered work Logs that store prompts Read one record Adoption judged by usage Evaluator results and incident records

docs.title: An incident on the same example
docs.text:
Revision R2 went live at 10:05:00. A user reports that the project page is slow.

An agent drafts a root-cause analysis and proposes:

Roll back R2, and add automatic retries to imports.

docs.title: Observe before you repair
docs.text:
ID The draft claims H1 R2 broke imports: server errors since the deploy H2 From 10:05 the project page's p95 rose; other pages held H3 The cause is one database query per build

For each: confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and the line or field that decides it.

docs.title: What a request log can show
docs.text:
window       requests  5xx  error rate  p95 ms
10:00-10:05  20        2    10.0%       58.9
10:05-10:10  20        0    0.0%        884.1
  • Open every cited line: time, path and status.
  • Over six requests, p95 is the slowest one.
  • Timing that starts with a deploy confirms the timing, not the cause.

docs.title: Act only on what you confirmed
docs.text:
A mitigation that rests on timing must be reversible, state its rollback condition and end with a check of the user path.

A code repair waits for a check that can see its cause.

Drop what rests on a refuted claim.

docs.title: A user retries after a timeout
docs.text:
A developer requests a retry of build 42. The reply is lost and the client times out, so the developer retries. Two jobs now exist.

Did the request fail, or did its reply disappear? Which observation separates the two?

docs.title: The stored effect survives a lost reply
docs.text:
Event Request Stored state Request received req-a No job yet Transaction commits req-a J81 queued Reply lost; client times out req-a J81 still queued Repeat commits req-b J82 also queued

The job and its operation key supply evidence the client lacked.

docs.title: Write the requirement before the repair
docs.text: Row Input Required 1 Reply lost, then a repeat Same job, one stored 2 Two deliveries arrive together Same job, one stored 3 Same key, different build Conflict, nothing new 4 New key New job

docs.title: The agent's repair: look up, then insert
docs.text:
Its summary says the duplicate is fixed.

mode: check-then-insert
row  replies       jobs (build/attempt)  build 42 shows
1    J81 J81       J81 42/7              J81
2    J81 J82       J81 42/7, J82 42/7    J82
rows meeting the repaired requirement: 3 of 4

The reported sequence passes. The forced race still stores two jobs.

docs.title: Uniqueness belongs to the database
docs.text:
One statement stores a unique (pipeline, operation_key) with the job.

mode: repaired
2    J81 J81       J81 42/7              J81
rows meeting the repaired requirement: 4 of 4

Check the stored jobs, then the replies, then what the user sees.

docs.title: A regression that proves the recovery
docs.text:
1. It fails on the incident build: 1 of 4, exit 1.
  2. It fails on the repair that only looks right: 3 of 4, exit 1.
  3. It passes on the repair: 4 of 4, exit 0.

A test that has only ever passed cannot show it would catch the defect.

docs.title: A race test must force the order
docs.text:
Without the forced order, the same broken repair passed most runs on one machine:

4 of 4 in 17 of 20 runs, 3 of 4 in 3.

Seventeen green runs would have accepted it.

docs.title: Agents that keep running after deployment
docs.text:
Scoped credentials, a budget, a switch that stops it without a deploy.

A log of what it read, proposed and changed.

Irreversible operations behind a person's approval.

Put the agent in the runbook.

docs.title: Second session
docs.text:
CP2 takes the first 30 minutes of the second session, on paper, without AI.

Then a guest or the studio: in your own project, compare reach with need, count what one accepted change cost, and write one regression that fails before a fix and passes after.

docs.title: Exit: one decision line
docs.text:
Accept, narrow, recheck or stop, with the evidence behind it.

Name one condition your regression does not test.

docs.title: Team operation and incident practice fixtures
docs.text: Small course-authored files for the shared pieces a team operates, the log check and the incident replay. Every record, unit, log line and agent summary is synthetic. None of the scripts calls a model, opens a network connection or writes a file, and each uses only the Python standard library. Read each one as text before running it. Run the commands from the course checkout; if your system has no python command, type python3.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
• org_check.py checks one JSON record with one of four commands and ends with a result: line.
  • portal replays each call through the grants: a call is allowed when a grant for its tool names its repository, or every repository with *. It then lists what each grant can reach and marks the repositories the task does not need. It exits 1 when any grant reaches beyond the task.
  • gateway replays each run through the policy: a request is refused before it is sent when it would exceed the request cap, when the tokens already used plus its own reservation would exceed the token cap, or when its route is not listed; when the provider is unavailable, the policy's fallback must answer. It also searches every line logged on the agent's side (sandbox_log in the file) for the key. It exits 1 when a recorded decision differs from the policy or the key appears.
  • cost adds the units of every run, including failed, retried and rejected ones, and every review minute, then divides each total by the number of accepted changes. It prints one run's total beside the result. It exits 1 only when no change was accepted.
  • route supports a chosen route only when its evaluator results are for the route's current revision and it fails no case that the current route passes. It exits 1 when any choice is not supported.

A command exits 2 when its file is missing, is not JSON, lacks a field or holds a value of the wrong kind. - org-portal.json, org-gateway.json, org-changes.json and org-routes.json hold the records: a portal's grants and one agent session, a gateway policy and six runs, the runs and review minutes behind four changes, and a routing policy with its evaluator results. Each holds an agent_summary that stands in for an agent's report; no model wrote it. The route names are placeholders and the only key is the placeholder sk-EXAMPLE. - budget_ledger.py replays a per-run ledger through the small Budget class at the top of the file: reserve a worst case before sending, settle to the actual cost after the reply, and keep the whole reservation when a reply is lost. Its units are course-made numbers, not prices. Change the numbers with --cap, --reserve, --actual and --lost-reply N. - check_rca.py reads request_log.jsonl, forty request records, and agent_rca.json, a course-authored stand-in for an agent's draft root-cause analysis that no model wrote. For each five-minute window it prints the request count, the number and share of 5xx responses and the 95th-percentile duration by nearest rank; --path limits that summary to paths with one prefix. Then it prints every log line each claim cites. It never decides whether a claim is confirmed, refuted or cannot tell. - retry_replay.py plays the four replay rows from the notes against an in-memory SQLite database with one of three handlers: unprotected, check-then-insert (look the key up, then insert it if absent) and repaired. Row 2 forces the race: its two requests run in two threads, and each handler pauses just before its first write, so both finish any lookup before either one writes; put any lookup you add before that pause. The connection runs one statement at a time and no lock spans a lookup and an insert. In the repaired handler an operation key is unique within its pipeline, the whole batch is one statement so a conflicting row saves nothing, and the dashboard shows the job of a build's greatest attempt.

docs.title: Expected distinction
docs.text:
portal on the supplied file exits 1: every call but the deploy is allowed, and grant G2 reaches three repositories the task does not need, one of which the session read. With G2 narrowed to the task's repository it exits 0 and that read is denied. gateway exits 1: runs R2 and R4 differ from the policy and the key appears in a line of R6. cost exits 0 with 8 units and 20 review minutes per accepted change, beside a single run of 3 units. route exits 1 with one of three choices supported.

The default ledger (cap 10, reserve 4, actual 1) admits seven requests and refuses the eighth with three units unspent. A lost reply keeps its full reservation, so with request 2's reply lost the fifth request is refused.

The log check summarises 40 records, 20 in each window: 2 server errors before 10:05 and none after, and a p95 of 58.9 ms before and 884.1 ms after. It exits 0 and leaves every outcome to you.

The unprotected replay stores two jobs for a repeated or concurrent retry and a job for build 43 under a reused key; one row of four meets the repaired requirement and it exits 1. Check-then-insert handles the sequential repeat and the reused key but stores two jobs in row 2, because both lookups ran before either insert; three rows of four meet the requirement and it exits 1. The repaired replay returns J81 to both matching requests, even in row 2, answers the reused key with a conflict that writes nothing, creates J82 for the new key and exits 0. In row 4 the dashboard shows J82, the job of attempt 8.

A result is evidence about the rule a script applied to synthetic records. It is not evidence about a real portal, gateway, route or model, and the replay is not evidence that any service of yours recovered. The request log's durations say nothing about how fast any real build is.

docs.title: Optional variation
docs.text:
Test what the forced order adds to the evidence. Copy the replay into a new directory:

mkdir week11-replay
cp lectures/week-11/fixture/retry_replay.py week11-replay/

In week11-replay/retry_replay.py, delete the self.between() line in the check-then-insert branch of Store.handle, so the two requests in row 2 are no longer held until both lookups finish. Predict whether row 2 still fails on every run. Then run your copy about 20 times and read the last line of each run:

python week11-replay/retry_replay.py check-then-insert

Record how many runs printed 3 of 4. How often the race appears depends on the machine and on thread timing; any single run may print 4 of 4 and exit 0, so one pass proves nothing. Explain which line of the handler lets the duplicate through when it does appear, then delete week11-replay.

docs.title: Week 12: The software factory and what comes next
docs.text:
The lecture treats "the pipeline runs itself" as a claim with a test. You run a small course-written pipeline until it stops, read the evidence each stage leaves, see a change that passes every automatic stage and still breaks the contract, and verify a recorded review claim by claim. The lecture ends with a course review that walks the decision line (accept, narrow, recheck, stop) back through the term.

The second session explains the defense format of week 13 and is a studio on your own final project. Contribution 4 and the final project are due this week.

Start with the notes, then use the second session guide, the self-check and the reading path. The slide source follows the same sequence. The folder factory/ holds the pipeline example; fixtures/ holds the recorded review and its guide.

docs.title: Week 12 second session: defense walkthrough and studio
docs.text:
The second session has two parts: a walkthrough of the defense format you meet in week 13, then a studio on your own final project. Bring your project repository at the revision you intend to hand in. Keep the work in a dedicated directory, as Tools and model access describes.

Contribution 4 is due this week. The final project is due this week.

docs.title: Session sequence
docs.text:
Minutes Activity What you keep 0–15 Defense walkthrough: the format, from the syllabus your own questions about the format, asked now 15–35 Rehearse the three verbs on the practice repository a prediction, the output that checked it, a decision line 35–65 The same rehearsal on your own project, with a partner the frozen tag, your three statements, what the check showed 65–80 Final project: run your README from the tagged files only the output of the fresh-copy run 80–90 Decision line for the final project; confirm what is due one line with its evidence

A written exchange can replace the spoken parts, and every step works from a keyboard with plain text. Planned minutes organise the room; going over them costs nothing.

docs.title: Defense walkthrough
docs.text:
This is what the syllabus and the project page publish about the defense:

  • It takes place in week 13, after the expo.
  • Each student has fifteen minutes, without devices.
  • The examiner changes one thing or plants one fault in your own code. You locate it, explain it and decide what to do.
  • It is individual. In a two-person project each member has a separate defense and is marked separately; shared milestone marks do not replace your own explanation.
  • Defenses use a shared rubric and comparable answering time, and you may ask for equivalent time or an equivalent way of taking part (privacy, fairness and accessibility). The resit rule is in the assessment section.

Nobody in this room knows which change the examiner will choose, and nothing below predicts it. The rehearsal practises the three verbs on changes you and a partner make up:

  • Locate: point to the line or the decision that differs from the revision you froze.
  • Explain: name an input that separates the old behaviour from the new, and say what each version does with it.
  • Decide: choose accept, narrow, recheck or stop, and say what evidence you would need to see first.

Without devices you cannot run anything, so every statement in the defense is a prediction from reading. The rehearsal lets you make those predictions with the screen closed and then check them with it open.

docs.title: Rehearse on the practice repository
docs.text:
Use this small repository to learn the moves before you touch your project. From the course checkout, build it from the factory example of the notes:

mkdir week12-defense-practice
cp lectures/week-12/factory/evaluator.py lectures/week-12/factory/verify.py week12-defense-practice/
cd week12-defense-practice
git init -q
git config user.name "Week 12 practice"
git config user.email "week12@example.edu"
git add evaluator.py verify.py
git commit -q -m "Practice revision"

1. Freeze. Confirm the tree is clean, tag the revision and list what the tag holds:

git status --porcelain
git tag -a defense-practice -m "Revision I will defend"
git ls-tree -r --name-only defense-practice

evaluator.py
verify.py

git status --porcelain prints nothing on a clean tree. Run the gate once on the frozen revision, so you know what it says before anything changes. The -B keeps Python from leaving a bytecode cache in the repository, so the tree stays clean and every run reads the file as it is now:

python -B verify.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"cases": 9, "failed": []}
exit: 0

2. Plant. A partner changes one thing and does not say what. Working alone, plant this change yourself and practise on the prediction in step 3:

python - <<'__PLANT__'
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("evaluator.py")
old = 'expected = "yes" if status == "failed" else "no"'
new = 'expected = "no" if status == "passed" else "yes"'
source = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
assert source.count(old) == 1
path.write_text(source.replace(old, new), encoding="utf-8")
__PLANT__

3. Predict, screen closed. Read evaluator.py on paper or on your partner's screen and write three statements: where the change is; one input on which the frozen and the changed function differ, and what each returns; which of the nine cases in verify.py will fail. Do not run anything yet.

4. Check, screen open. Compare your three statements with the repository:

git diff defense-practice -- evaluator.py
python -B verify.py; echo "exit: $?"

diff --git a/evaluator.py b/evaluator.py
index f59231c..5b851d5 100644
--- a/evaluator.py
+++ b/evaluator.py
@@ -11,5 +11,5 @@ def score(status: str, output: object) -> str:
     """Classify one answer as pass, fail or unknown."""
     if not isinstance(output, str):
         return "unknown"
-    expected = "yes" if status == "failed" else "no"
+    expected = "no" if status == "passed" else "yes"
     return "pass" if output == expected else "fail"
{"cases": 9, "failed": [{"case": "correct_no_running", "observed": "fail", "required": "pass"}]}
exit: 1

The diff is the answer to "locate". The failed case is one answer to "explain": for the status running, the contract's answer is no, and the changed function now expects yes. If your prediction named a different case, find out why before you move on.

5. Decide and restore. Write the decision line, then put the frozen file back and confirm the tree is clean:

git checkout defense-practice -- evaluator.py
git status --porcelain
python -B verify.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"cases": 9, "failed": []}
exit: 0

Decision: stop — the change breaks the contract for every status other than failed and passed; evidence: the diff and the failed case correct_no_running

A planted change will not always trip a check. If your gate stays green after the plant, as it did for the second proposal in the lecture, the diff and a separating input you choose yourself are the only evidence, and the honest decision is usually narrow or recheck.

Delete week12-defense-practice when you finish.

docs.title: Rehearse on your own project
docs.text:
Work in pairs; swap roles after one round. In your project repository:

  1. Freeze the revision you intend to hand in, with the commands of Freeze the revision you hand in. Run your own gate once, the command your README names, and keep its output.
  2. Your partner changes one thing in your working tree: one line of code, one configuration value or one test expectation. They do not say what, and they do not commit it.
  3. Screen closed, read the code your partner points you to. Say or write the three statements: where, which input separates the two behaviours, and your decision with the evidence you would want.
  4. Screen open, check each statement. Replace final-week-12 with your tag if you named it differently:

sh git diff --stat final-week-12 git diff final-week-12

Then run your gate again. If it stays green, write the separating input as a new test or case before you decide anything. 5. Restore the frozen files and confirm that nothing else changed:

sh git checkout final-week-12 -- . git status --porcelain

If your partner added a new file, git status --porcelain lists it with ??; delete that file by name.

Your partner's change is practice between two students. It is not an examiner's question and does not show what the defense will ask.

docs.title: Final project: run it from the tagged files only
docs.text:
A project that runs on your machine may depend on a file you never committed. Check the tag in a fresh copy beside your repository, then remove the copy:

git worktree add -q --detach ../final-week-12-check final-week-12

Change into ../final-week-12-check and run the setup, run and verification commands exactly as your README gives them. Keep the output. Then, back in your project repository:

git worktree remove ../final-week-12-check

If Git refuses because the copy "contains modified or untracked files", your README's commands left files behind. Look at what they are, delete them and run the command again, or add --force once you are sure nothing in the copy is worth keeping.

If a command fails in the fresh copy and works in your working tree, something the project needs is missing from the tag. Commit it, tag the new commit under a new name such as final-week-12b, run the check again on that tag and hand in the new name. Do this before you push a tag, so that a pushed tag never has to move. The project page lists what the final revision must contain.

docs.title: Decision line
docs.text:
End the session with one line in your project notes:

Decision: accept | narrow | recheck | stop — evidence: the tag, the fresh-copy run and the gate output

Choose the word your evidence supports. A fresh-copy run that passes supports accepting "the tagged revision runs as the README says"; it does not support claims the README's commands never exercise.

docs.title: Week 12: The software factory and what comes next
Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this week you can:

  • restate "the pipeline runs itself" as a claim about every change, name the one observation that refutes it and the smaller claim a single run supports (LO9);
  • say, for each stage of a pipeline, what evidence it must leave and where a named person still accepts or rejects (LO9);
  • exercise a stop path and read from the record which stage stopped and which never ran;
  • treat an automated review as a list of claims, each confirmed, refuted or undetermined by a check you chose yourself; and
  • walk the decision line (accept, narrow, recheck or stop) back through the term and decide again where an input has changed (LO9).

Everything on this page is course-written practice material: the pipeline, the proposed changes, the recorded review and every count. No model wrote any of it, and none of it measures a model or a tool.

docs.title: "It runs itself" is a claim
docs.text:
A software factory is a pipeline in which each stage triggers the next: a request becomes a specification, a change, a set of checks, a review and a release. The strong version of the idea is that the pipeline runs itself: no person reads anything between the request and the release. That sentence is a claim about every change that will ever enter the pipeline, and a claim has a test. This week asks three questions of it:

  1. What would have to be observed for the claim to be true?
  2. What evidence must each stage leave so that someone else can check its verdict?
  3. Where does a named person still accept or reject, and what are they accepting?

docs.title: What one run can decide
docs.text:
A claim's wording sets what one observation can show. Read the wording before you run anything.

The claim is about One run can One run cannot one input ("this change went through unattended") confirm or refute it some input ("a bad change can get through") confirm it, if the run shows the problem refute it: an input that behaves shows only where the problem is not every input ("the pipeline runs itself") refute it, with one counterexample confirm it: an input that behaves is one case of many each member of a set you can list ("every stage leaves a record") decide that member decide the others; check each member something outside the snapshot ("it also holds in production") show that the snapshot cannot read it decide it

A demonstration in which one request becomes one merged change is the first row. It says nothing about the third row, however impressive it looks. The claim you can support is always smaller: this stage, on this kind of change, behind this check, with this stop path.
