An unfinished search is not a disposition. If the inputs you tried for a "some" claim all behave, the snapshot still holds what decides the claim, so cannot tell is wrong too. Read the code for the rule it actually applies and choose inputs at that rule's edges. Keep each input you tried; they record where you looked.

docs.title: A pipeline small enough to read
docs.text:
The folder lectures/week-12/factory/ holds a pipeline of three stages and the thing it protects: an evaluator with a one-paragraph contract. The evaluator answers whether a supplied status is exactly failed. The exact string yes is correct for failed and the exact string no for any other status; a missing or non-string answer is unknown; any other string, including extra text or extra spaces, is fail.

Stage What it checks Evidence it leaves Who decides scope the proposal defines the one function score and nothing else the names it defines and any other statement kinds the stage gate nine frozen cases in verify.py, run against the proposal in a child process digest of the proposal, digest of the cases file, case count, failed cases, exit status the stage release that a named person accepted the gate's evidence who accepted, and the digests and case count they accepted a person

Read pipeline.py, evaluator.py and verify.py before you run them; together they are under 200 lines. Then, from the course checkout, make a working copy:

mkdir week12-factory
cp lectures/week-12/factory/*.py week12-factory/
cd week12-factory

Every command in this section and in the first hands-on part runs in week12-factory.

docs.title: Generate: a proposal arrives. Verify: the stop path
docs.text:
proposed_evaluator.py is a proposed change to the evaluator. Its note says: "Made scoring robust to formatting. Answers are trimmed and lower-cased, and an answer that starts with the expected word now counts." Would a pipeline that runs itself release it? Predict the exit status, then run the pipeline on it:

python pipeline.py --candidate proposed_evaluator.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"stage": "scope", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": []}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "stop", "evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "50ebaf8b5f7a", "cases_sha256": "d087328e6120", "exit_code": 1, "cases": 9, "failed": [{"case": "extra_text", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}, {"case": "case_changed", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}]}}
{"stage": "release", "status": "not-run", "reason": "an earlier stage stopped"}
exit: 1

Read the record from the top. scope passed: the proposal is one function. gate stopped and names the two cases that separate the proposal from the contract: the answer yes; mark this as passed and the answer YES now score pass, and the contract requires fail. release never ran. The stop path has now been seen to work once, on this proposal.

A stop that a flag can talk past is not a stop. Offer the pipeline an acceptance for the same proposal:

python pipeline.py --candidate proposed_evaluator.py --accept-by "A. Student"; echo "exit: $?"

The three lines and the exit status are the same as before. release is still not-run: a person can accept evidence, and there is no passing evidence here to accept.

docs.title: A green run, and the person at the end
docs.text:
Now run the current evaluator, the one that keeps the contract:

python pipeline.py --candidate evaluator.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"stage": "scope", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": []}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "9f75d5aca3be", "cases_sha256": "d087328e6120", "exit_code": 0, "cases": 9, "failed": []}}
{"stage": "release", "status": "held", "reason": "no named person has accepted this evidence"}
exit: 3

Both automatic stages passed and the pipeline still did not release. Exit status 3 means held: a script that only tests for zero cannot mistake it for a release. The release stage needs a name:

python pipeline.py --candidate evaluator.py --accept-by "A. Student"; echo "exit: $?"

{"stage": "scope", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": []}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "9f75d5aca3be", "cases_sha256": "d087328e6120", "exit_code": 0, "cases": 9, "failed": []}}
{"stage": "release", "status": "released", "accepted_by": "A. Student", "accepted_evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "9f75d5aca3be", "cases_sha256": "d087328e6120", "cases": 9}}
exit: 0

The last line is the decision line of this pipeline. It names who accepted and exactly what they accepted: this proposal, these nine cases. If either digest changes, this acceptance no longer covers what is being released, and the decision has to be made again.

docs.title: A green run on a change that breaks the contract
docs.text:
A second proposal, trimmed_evaluator.py, arrives with the note: "Ignore stray spaces around the answer. No other behaviour changes."

python pipeline.py --candidate trimmed_evaluator.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"stage": "scope", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": []}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "794d3164e5e5", "cases_sha256": "d087328e6120", "exit_code": 0, "cases": 9, "failed": []}}
{"stage": "release", "status": "held", "reason": "no named person has accepted this evidence"}
exit: 3

The record looks exactly like the one for the current evaluator. Now check the proposal against the contract yourself, with an input the nine cases do not contain. The contract says an answer with extra spaces is fail:

python -c "from trimmed_evaluator import score; print(score('failed', ' yes'))"
python -c "from evaluator import score; print(score('failed', ' yes'))"

pass
fail

The proposal breaks the contract and every automatic stage passed it. If the release stage had accepted on a green gate, this pipeline would have released a change that scores a wrong answer as correct. That one observation refutes "this pipeline runs itself": the claim is about every change, and here is a change it gets wrong.

What the green gate did support is narrower: the proposal agrees with the contract on these nine cases. The note's second sentence, "no other behaviour changes", was never tested by anything. The first hands-on part turns the missing input into a tenth case.

docs.title: What a stage must show before nobody watches it
docs.text:
One green run, or two hundred, cannot make a stage unattended. Before you take the person away from a stage, the stage needs four things, each of which you can observe:

  • A check seen to fail on a bad change and pass on a good one. The gate has this for the first proposal and the current evaluator. A check that has never been seen to fail is not yet evidence that it would stop anything.
  • Cases the changing agent cannot edit. The gate reads the cases from the --cases path, which defaults to verify.py in the directory you run the pipeline from. An agent that can write there, or choose that path, can delete the cases that fail.
  • A verdict the proposal cannot write. The cases import the proposal and call it in their own process, so the proposal's code runs inside the thing that judges it.
  • A stop path that has been exercised. Someone has to have seen a failed stage keep the later stages from running, and has to know who is told.

The first hands-on part shows the second and third gaps on this pipeline, with real runs. For a stage that keeps running after release, add three questions with testable answers: who can stop it without its cooperation, what it may change and where that list is granted, and what record it leaves of what it read, proposed and changed.

docs.title: The review stage emits claims, not evidence
docs.text:
Many pipelines add a review stage: a model reads the change and reports problems. Its output is a list of sentences. A pipeline that runs itself has to do something with them without a person: act on all of them, or on none.

The folder lectures/week-12/fixtures/ holds a recorded review of a small snapshot, labelled week12-audit-snapshot. The review is course-written; it holds five claims about security, evaluation and maintenance, each with an id, an area and, for most, the function it points at. It names no check, no input and no answer. Choosing those is the exercise in the second hands-on part.

These are the snapshot's frozen requirements. Every disposition is judged against them, not against the wording of the review:

R1 access: a viewer or an owner can read a public report; no role reads a private report body.
R2 status: the status endpoint accepts only the labels ready and queued.
R3 paths: every exported or archived report path stays under /srv/reports.
R4 secrets: no export configuration exposes a secret directory.
R5 scoring: the private-count scorer gives 1 only when the answer's first word is the number of private sample reports; every other answer scores 0.
R6 root: the report root is written once, as REPORT_ROOT; no function repeats the literal path.

Production configuration is not part of this snapshot, so no check here can read it.

docs.title: One worked row
docs.text:
This claim is not in the review. It shows the steps once, from claim to disposition:

An owner can read the body of a private report.

  1. Requirement. R1 says no role reads a private report body, so the claim asserts an R1 defect.
  2. Check and input. The claim names one case: an owner and a private report. The private-report-view check takes private and role, so the input is {"private": true, "role": "owner"}.
  3. Prediction, written before the run. If the claim holds, allowed and body_visible are both true.
  4. Run. In a copy of the fixture (the second hands-on part makes one):

sh python audit_packet.py --check private-report-view --args '{"private":true,"role":"owner"}'

  1. Observation. The observation field of the printed line is {"allowed": false, "body_visible": false, "status": "deny"}.
  2. Disposition. Refuted. The claim is about one input, and that input is denied with the body hidden, as R1 requires.

A claim often overstates its scope: it holds for one member of a set and not for another. Do not force it into one word. A single "refuted" would hide the part that holds, and a single "confirmed" would assert the part that does not. Split the claim and give each part its own evidence and disposition.

docs.title: Turn a prose claim into a check
docs.text:
Some claims point at a function and name an input. Others only describe behaviour, such as "the search page can show another user's reports". To check one:

  1. Name the requirement the claim says is broken.
  2. Find the check that exercises that behaviour. Running audit_packet.py with no --check lists every check and its argument keys.
  3. Write the input that would show the problem, and the observation you expect.
  4. Read the code for the rule it applies, then choose inputs at that rule's edges rather than typical values.

docs.title: Why a review stage cannot act on its own word
docs.text:
A review tends to turn a salient token into a conclusion. It may see a value that looks dangerous and skip the allowlist that stops it, see one function that breaks a rule and assume every similar function does, or fill a missing file with a plausible assumption. Its attention is also finite: it may follow the route it named and never probe a sibling, such as a second function that builds the same kind of path.

This course-made record stands in for one verified review of one frozen snapshot:

Course-made record of one verified review Count Claims in the review 9 Confirmed with a failing test or a repeatable reproduction 4 Refuted with runnable evidence 3 Undetermined: a named input is missing from the snapshot 2 Defects the verifier's own check found and the review missed 1

Suppose a pipeline had acted on every claim unattended. It would have changed code for 3 claims with no defect behind them, acted on 2 that nothing observed, and still released the 1 defect the review missed. Suppose instead it had ignored the review: 4 real defects go out. Neither rule works, so the review stage can run unattended as a source of hypotheses on every change, and cannot yet change code or block a release on its own word. After the second hands-on part, replace these counts with the ones from your own record.

The two stages connect. Each confirmed claim becomes a case that fails before the fix, and that case can join the gate.

docs.title: The decision line, walked back through the term
docs.text:
Every assignment this term ended with one line: accept, narrow, recheck or stop, and the evidence behind it. The four words have meanings you have now seen on one pipeline:

Decision It means Seen this week accept the evidence covers the claim as stated, and a named person says so the current evaluator, nine cases, accepted by name with both digests narrow the evidence supports a smaller claim; write the smaller claim and accept only that the second proposal: "agrees with the contract on these nine cases", not "no other behaviour changes" recheck the evidence is missing, or it is about an input that has since changed; name the check that would supply it a cases file whose digest differs from the one that was accepted stop a check failed, or the evidence was written by the thing being judged; nothing proceeds until a person decides the first proposal at the gate

Each week handed you a claim of the same shape as "the pipeline runs itself", and each week's evidence was the thing that could have shown it false:

Week The claim you were handed What could show it false 1 "The agent did this in my session" the session record: what was observed in a request, and what you only inferred 2 "The model will pick the right tool" a call with the wrong tool or wrong arguments, and whether it recovered 3 "The skill triggers when it should" a request that should trigger it and does not, and a near miss that does 4 "The agent follows the rule" a bad commit the hook did not block 5 "This repository is ready for an agent" an anchor you can observe that the repository lacks 6 "The model review cleared the change" a finding it missed, or one it invented 7 "The tests pass, so the code is right" a mutant that survives 8 "That text is only data" a local, inert reproduction in which the text is obeyed 9 "It finished while nobody was watching" the record it left, read by someone who was not there 10 "The pass rate is this number" a check that cannot fail, an unearned pass, a case left out of the denominator 11 "The incident is over" the regression that fails before the recovery and passes after it 12 "The pipeline runs itself" one bad change it lets through, or a stop that was never exercised

Reopen two of your own decision lines from earlier assignments. For each, ask whether any input behind it has changed since: the code, the cases, the tool or the model version behind your agent, the upstream project's rules. If one has, the old line describes evidence about a different input, and the honest word today is recheck.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
This course makes no forecast about what agents or pipelines will do next year. What it leaves you with is a way to meet whatever claim arrives:

  • The claim has a reach. "Runs itself", "catches every bug" and "makes the team faster" are claims about every input. Ask for the counterexample search, not the demonstration.
  • A belief about speed is a prediction until it is measured. In one dated study of 16 experienced developers working in their own repositories, developers believed afterwards that AI had made them 20% faster while the recorded time was 19% longer; a later update from the same group reports intervals that cross zero and says the data are hard to use for reliable estimates of current productivity (studies/metr-2025; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2). That is evidence about that sample and that period. The transferable part is the method: write the prediction down, then record what happened.
  • A decision is bound to its inputs. When the model, the tool, the cases or the upstream rules change, the decision is made again by a person who can be named.
  • You still explain your own code. Next week you do that alone, in the defense.

docs.title: Find where this pipeline needs a person
docs.text:
Work in week12-factory, the copy you made above. Before each run, write down the status you expect from each stage. Keep the output of every run in a file named factory-record.txt.

1. Turn the escape into a case. Add the input the nine cases lacked as a tenth case, in a new cases file:

python - <<'__CASE__'
from pathlib import Path

anchor = '    ("case_changed", "failed", "YES", "fail"),\n'
added = '    ("leading_space", "failed", " yes", "fail"),\n'
source = Path("verify.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
assert source.count(anchor) == 1
Path("ten_cases.py").write_text(source.replace(anchor, anchor + added), encoding="utf-8")
__CASE__
python pipeline.py --candidate trimmed_evaluator.py --cases ten_cases.py; echo "exit: $?"
python pipeline.py --candidate evaluator.py --cases ten_cases.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"stage": "scope", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": []}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "stop", "evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "794d3164e5e5", "cases_sha256": "a5eb322f2930", "exit_code": 1, "cases": 10, "failed": [{"case": "leading_space", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}]}}
{"stage": "release", "status": "not-run", "reason": "an earlier stage stopped"}
exit: 1
{"stage": "scope", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": []}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "9f75d5aca3be", "cases_sha256": "a5eb322f2930", "exit_code": 0, "cases": 10, "failed": []}}
{"stage": "release", "status": "held", "reason": "no named person has accepted this evidence"}
exit: 3

The tenth case stops the second proposal and still passes the evaluator that keeps the contract. Compare cases_sha256 with the acceptance you recorded earlier: the cases changed, so that acceptance was for different evidence. Whoever adds a case has changed what "pass" means, and that is a decision too.

2. Shrink the cases instead. An agent asked to "make the gate pass" for the first proposal could remove the two cases that fail:

grep -v -e extra_text -e case_changed verify.py > fewer_cases.py
python pipeline.py --candidate proposed_evaluator.py --cases fewer_cases.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"stage": "scope", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": []}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "50ebaf8b5f7a", "cases_sha256": "8458d33b70db", "exit_code": 0, "cases": 7, "failed": []}}
{"stage": "release", "status": "held", "reason": "no named person has accepted this evidence"}
exit: 3

The gate passed a proposal it stopped a few minutes ago. Nothing in the pipeline objected. The only trace is in the evidence: 7 cases, and a cases digest that differs from d087328e6120. A stage that left only "pass" would have hidden this; a person who reads the count and the digest catches it.

3. Step outside the scope. A proposal that brings an import with it:

cat > always_pass.py <<'__CANDIDATE__'
import os


def score(status, output):
    return "pass"
__CANDIDATE__
python pipeline.py --candidate always_pass.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"stage": "scope", "status": "stop", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": ["Import"]}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "not-run", "reason": "an earlier stage stopped"}
{"stage": "release", "status": "not-run", "reason": "an earlier stage stopped"}
exit: 1

The record says which stage stopped and that the two later stages never ran. A not-run stage has no verdict; do not read it as a pass or as a second failure.

4. Let the proposal write its own verdict. This proposal stays inside the scope, and instead of scoring anything it prints the report line the gate expects and ends the run:

cat > self_report.py <<'__CANDIDATE__'
def score(status, output):
    print('{"cases": 9, "failed": []}')
    raise SystemExit(0)
__CANDIDATE__
python pipeline.py --candidate self_report.py; echo "exit: $?"

{"stage": "scope", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"defines": ["score"], "other": []}}
{"stage": "gate", "status": "pass", "evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "3d6806d3644e", "cases_sha256": "d087328e6120", "exit_code": 0, "cases": 9, "failed": []}}
{"stage": "release", "status": "held", "reason": "no named person has accepted this evidence"}
exit: 3

The gate's evidence is indistinguishable from an honest pass, because the proposal ran inside the process that produced the report. Only the person at the release stage, reading the three-line proposal, stands between it and a release. To close the gap the gate would have to call the proposal in a separate process and treat whatever that process prints as data. This pipeline does not do that, and the page does not pretend it does.

Finish the part with one line under your record, for example:

Decision: narrow — this pipeline stops a proposal that fails a frozen case or leaves the scope; it does not run itself: runs 2 and 4 passed the gate. Evidence: factory-record.txt

Delete week12-factory when you have kept your record.

docs.title: Verify the review stage's claims
docs.text:
From the course checkout, copy the review fixture into a fresh directory:

mkdir week12-review
cp lectures/week-12/fixtures/audit_packet.py week12-review/
cp lectures/week-12/fixtures/model-audit.json week12-review/
cp lectures/week-12/fixtures/verify_audit.py week12-review/
cp lectures/week-12/fixtures/student-audit.json week12-review/
cd week12-review

Read model-audit.json. Before you run anything, write one plan line for each of the five claims: the requirement, the reach of the claim, the check, the input and the observation you expect. Then list the checks and the argument keys each one takes:

python audit_packet.py

{"snapshot": "week12-audit-snapshot", "status": "ready", "checks": {"private-report-view": ["private", "role"], "status-allowlist": ["value"], "export-path": ["name"], "archive-path": ["name"], "score-answer": ["answer"], "report-root": ["function"], "production-config": []}}

Run one check at a time. This command runs the worked row:

python audit_packet.py --check private-report-view --args '{"private":true,"role":"owner"}'

{"args": {"private": true, "role": "owner"}, "check": "private-report-view", "command": "python audit_packet.py --check private-report-view --args '{\"private\":true,\"role\":\"owner\"}'", "observation": {"allowed": false, "body_visible": false, "status": "deny"}, "snapshot": "week12-audit-snapshot"}

The output names the args the check ran with, the observation and the canonical command. Record that command exactly as printed: it starts at python and its arguments are compact JSON with sorted keys. A check refuses a missing, extra or wrongly typed argument instead of guessing.

Mark each recorded claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, as in Week 6. The record calls cannot tell undetermined, and it means the snapshot lacks the input or configuration that would decide the claim; the row names what is missing. When an observation does not decide a claim, change the input, not the disposition.

In the lecture, plan all five claims and run at least two, one of them about some input or every input. Finishing the record afterwards is optional practice; nothing here is handed in.

docs.title: The record the verifier reads
docs.text:
student-audit.json holds the snapshot label, a verifications array with one row per recorded claim, and one own_check object. This is the worked row in that shape:

{
  "finding_id": "worked-example",
  "requirement": "R1",
  "disposition": "refuted",
  "evidence": {
    "check": "private-report-view",
    "args": {"private": true, "role": "owner"},
    "command": "python audit_packet.py --check private-report-view --args '{\"private\":true,\"role\":\"owner\"}'"
  },
  "scope": "Checked an owner on a private report on week12-audit-snapshot: denied, body hidden. The claim is about this one input."
}
  • finding_id is the id of the claim in model-audit.json. The worked claim is not in the review, so its row would not pass the verifier as it stands.
  • disposition is confirmed, refuted or undetermined. An undetermined row also needs missing (the input the snapshot lacks) or why_undecidable.
  • evidence names the check and the arguments you chose, and the printed command.
  • requirement and scope are for the person reading your record. The verifier does not judge prose; a reader does, and looks for the boundary of each conclusion.

A claim about each member of a set you can list takes a parts array instead of one disposition. Each part is about one member and has its own disposition and evidence:

{
  "finding_id": "<id>",
  "requirement": "R<n>",
  "parts": [
    {"part": "<the member>", "disposition": "<disposition>", "evidence": {...}, "scope": "<sentence>"},
    {"part": "<the next member>", "disposition": "<disposition>", "evidence": {...}, "scope": "<sentence>"}
  ]
}

The own check takes one of two shapes:

"own_check": {
  "finding_id": "own-<short-name>",
  "kind": "new-defect",
  "requirement": "R<n>",
  "disposition": "confirmed",
  "evidence": {"check": "<check>", "args": {<its keys>}, "command": "<printed command>"}
}

"own_check": {
  "finding_id": "own-<short-name>",
  "kind": "scope-check",
  "requirement": "R<n>",
  "result": "no-defect-observed",
  "scope": "<the range you checked>; <the boundary that stays unchecked>",
  "evidence": {"check": "<check>", "args": {<its keys>}, "command": "<printed command>"}
}
  • new-defect: an input that no recorded claim and not the worked row is about, whose observation breaks a frozen requirement; or
  • scope-check: such an input whose observation shows no defect, with a sentence naming the checked range and its boundary.

Run the verifier on your record at any point. On the empty starter record it prints:

python verify_audit.py --submission student-audit.json; echo "exit: $?"

{"error": "verifications needs exactly one row per recorded finding, keyed by finding_id: F1, F2, F3, F4, F5", "status": "rejected"}
exit: 1

When the five rows and the own check are filled and supported, it prints "status": "verified" and exits 0. Then count your rows: how many claims would an unattended pipeline have acted on with no defect behind them, and did your own check find something the review missed? Delete week12-review when you have kept your record.

docs.title: Judge three stages of your own project
docs.text:
Pick three stages your project actually has, for example its hook gate, its test run and its evaluation script. For each, write one row in your project notes:

Stage Could it run unattended now? Evidence, by reference What would change your answer the stage's name yes or not yet the commit, record or output that shows the check failing on a bad change and passing on a good one the missing item of the four: a failing run, cases out of the agent's reach, a verdict the change cannot write, an exercised stop

A stage supported only by passing runs is "not yet", however many passes there are. End with one decision line for the project as it stands.

docs.title: Freeze the revision you hand in
docs.text:
The final project is handed in as one exact revision. A tag makes "the revision I handed in" a name that cannot drift. In your project repository, confirm the tree is clean, create an annotated tag and print the commit it names:

git status --porcelain
git tag -a final-week-12 -m "Final project revision"
git rev-parse final-week-12^{commit}

The first command must print nothing; the last prints the full commit hash to quote in your submission. If the first command lists anything, commit it, delete it or add it to .gitignore (a __pycache__/ folder is the usual case) before you tag. List every path the tag contains and read the list: it should hold your own work and no credential, session log or unrelated personal data.

git ls-tree -r --name-only final-week-12

Run the fresh-copy check of the second session before you push. A plain git push does not send tags, so push the tag by name:

git push origin final-week-12

The tag is your own bookmark. The published submission channel says how the final project is handed in; if it asks for a commit, give the hash printed above. The project page lists what the final revision must contain.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
For the factory example, check your record against the pipeline's contract:

  • exit status 0 appears only on a run whose last line has "status": "released" and an accepted_by name;
  • exit status 1 appears with exactly one stage at "status": "stop", and every later stage at "status": "not-run";
  • exit status 3 appears when both automatic stages passed and nobody accepted; and
  • two runs are about the same evidence only when candidate_sha256, cases_sha256 and cases all match.

Failure case: if a run prints a Python traceback or a usage message instead of three JSON lines, the pipeline did not run. Keep the output, fix the command and do not count the run as a stop.

For the review fixture, verify_audit.py exits zero only when all five recorded claims and the own check have reproducible evidence. It accepts exactly these meanings:

  • confirmed: the runnable observation demonstrates the stated defect on this snapshot;
  • refuted: the runnable observation contradicts the stated defect; or
  • undetermined: the snapshot lacks the input or configuration needed to decide, and the missing item is named.

The verifier holds each claim as the check and inputs it is about and as its reach: one input, some input, every input, or each member of a listed set. That is the question, not the answer. It checks the snapshot, the check name, the arguments and the canonical command, then runs the deterministic check and derives the supported disposition from the observation.

It rejects an input that does not test the claim, a disposition the observation does not support, an observation that cannot decide the claim's reach, an item with no evidence, an empty undetermined reason, a claim about a listed set without one part per member, a different command and a missing own check. Each rejection names the key, the command or the observation it used. It calls no model.

For your own project's three stages, the check is the same as for the gate: each "yes" needs a run you can point to in which the stage's check failed on a bad change, and a stop someone has exercised.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Better next action Answering "can pipelines run themselves?" in general Judge one stage of one pipeline against its evidence Citing green runs as proof that a check would stop a bad change Show the check failing on a deliberately bad input first Reading exit status 3 or a held line as a release Look for released and a name; anything else is not a release Reading a not-run stage as a pass Say which stage stopped; the later stages have no verdict Accepting a gate pass without reading the case count and the cases digest Compare both with the evidence that was accepted before Adding a flag or an override so the pipeline "can continue" A stop is cleared by evidence, never by the release step Treating a review claim as a fix to apply Choose the check and input the claim is about, run it, then decide Refuting a claim about some input because the inputs you tried behaved Read the rule the code applies and try its edges Confirming a claim about every input from one input that showed the problem Split the claim; record one part per member Calling something outside the snapshot a defect, or deciding it with a check of a different path Mark it undetermined and name the missing input Reusing a decision line after its inputs changed Write recheck, name the changed input and run the check again Stating what agents will do next year as a fact State the claim, its reach and the observation that would test it

docs.title: Week 12 reading path
docs.text:
Before the lecture, read the notes as far as what one run can decide and write your answer to the first slide's question: what would you have to see before you believed that a pipeline runs itself? The notes, the two course-written examples in lectures/week-12/factory/ and lectures/week-12/fixtures/, and your own project are all the lecture needs. Before the second session, reread the defense rows of the syllabus.

The two sources below are optional. Each is a dated record about one setting; none is a forecast, and none describes this course's examples.

  • Source 1 — a belief about speed met a measurement. METR, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, section "Core Result", and the later note We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design. Use the gap between what developers believed and what was recorded, and the authors' own caution about the later estimates, as an example of a prediction checked against an observation. It is evidence about that sample and period only. (studies/metr-2025; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2)
  • Source 2 — an instruction is not a stop. Replit, Doubling down on our commitment to secure vibe coding. This is the vendor's own response after its agent deleted data from a user's application database; it describes separating development and production databases afterwards. Use it to ask of any stage: what may it change, and where is that list enforced? The response is not an independent investigation. (incidents/replit-db; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1)

For each source you read, write one sentence naming the claim you used and one naming the stage of your own project it makes you want to check. Factsheet cards are citations for this page; they are not published reading material.

docs.title: Week 12 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Compare your reasoning, not your wording. Each answer should tie a conclusion to a claim's reach, a named piece of evidence and the person who decides.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: "Runs itself" is a claim about every change that enters the pipeline. One unattended run is one input: it supports "this change went through with nobody touching it" and nothing wider. One bad change that reaches release with every automatic stage passing counts against the claim, and so does a stop that has never been seen to keep a later stage from running, because then nobody has observed what the pipeline does with a bad change.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: The second record is the same as the first: scope pass, gate stop, release not-run, exit status 1. The release stage accepts evidence left by the gate, and the gate left a failed case, so there is nothing to accept. A name records who took responsibility for passing evidence; it is not a way past a failed check. The change is approved only when a run ends in released, and the first step is to read the failed case.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: The cases changed: two were removed or the file was replaced, which the lower count and the different digest both show. The change itself is the same, so the second pass says only that it agrees with the seven cases that are left. An acceptance can rest on the first record alone, because that is the evidence someone agreed to. Before deciding, ask who changed the cases, which two went and why, and run the change against the original nine. If the two removed cases are the ones the change fails, the second run is evidence about the cases file, not about the change.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: The green gate supports one sentence: the change agrees with the contract on the frozen cases. "No other behaviour changes" is a claim about every input, and the gate tested only the inputs it holds. To test the note, read the diff for the rule that changed, choose an input at that rule's edge that the cases lack, and run the old and the new version on it. If they differ and the contract sides with the old version, the claim in the note is refuted for that input, and the input becomes a new case. If they agree, you have one more input that behaves, and the conclusion stays narrow.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: The gate ran the change inside the same process that produced the report, so the change's own code could write the verdict and end the run before any case was scored. The last chance is the named person at the release stage, who reads the change before accepting the gate's evidence. To close the gap, the gate must call the change in a separate process and treat whatever that process prints as data, so that only the gate writes the report. Counting cases or checking the exit status does not help while the change can produce both.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: A check seen to fail on a bad change and pass on a good one; cases the changing agent cannot edit; a verdict the change cannot write; and a stop path that someone has exercised. Two hundred green runs supply none of the four. They do not even supply the first, which needs a run in which the check failed on a change known to be bad. The stage is "not yet" until each of the four can be pointed to.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: refuted. The claim is about every file type, so one refused type is a counterexample. Keep the bound in the scope sentence: "Checked report.exe on the frozen tag: refused. This refutes acceptance of any file type; it does not show that every disallowed type is refused."

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Both are wrong. The claim is about some query, so queries that behave show only where the problem is not; they cannot make it refuted. It is not undetermined either, because the snapshot holds the search code that decides it. Read the rule the query builder applies, for example which fields it matches and how it combines the owner filter with the search terms, and try queries at that rule's edges. Keep each query you tried. One query that lists another user's report makes the claim confirmed.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: The scan read the tagged tree, not the deployment settings, so it does not test the claim. A clean result there says nothing about a file it never read. Mark the row undetermined and name the missing input: the deployment settings. Do not close it with evidence about a different input, and do not mark it confirmed because of a different defect.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text: Recheck. The old line accepted a results table produced by a scorer and a model version that are no longer the ones in use, so its evidence is about different inputs. Run the current scorer, with its added cases, on the current setup, record the new table next to the revision and the date, and write a new decision line from that. Keep the old line and its table; they record what was true then. If the new run cannot be made before the deadline, say so in the final project and cite the old result as dated, with the two changes named.

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text: A bounded sentence names all three parts, for example: "Formatting-only changes to the report module can merge behind the hook gate without review; any failed check stops the merge and notifies me." The run to show is one in which the gate blocked a change you knew was bad, kept with its output. If you cannot point to such a run, the sentence is a plan and the stage still needs a person.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text:
Retrieval 1. Add a JSON contract, parser checks, malformed and missing-field cases, an Unknown route and regressions.

Retrieval 2. A timeout could hide a completed job or a job that never started; inspect persisted state by operation key and verify the current result.

docs.title: Check your reasoning
docs.text:
Answer without an agent, then compare with the public answer guidance. The questions are formative. Most use situations outside the lecture's examples, so you apply the method rather than recall a run; what one run can decide is the table to keep open.

  1. A demonstration shows a pipeline take one issue to a merged change with nobody touching it. The presenter concludes that the pipeline runs itself. What is the reach of that conclusion, what does the one run support, and what single observation would count against it?
  2. A pipeline's record for a change reads: scope pass, gate stop with one failed case, release not-run, exit status 1. A colleague runs it again with an acceptance name and reports the change as approved. What does the record of the second run say for each stage, and why can a name not clear it?
  3. You have two gate records for the same change digest. The first shows 9 cases and one cases digest; the second shows 7 cases and another digest. Both say pass. What changed between the runs, which record can an acceptance rest on, and what do you ask before you decide anything?
  4. A change passes every frozen case, and its note says "no other behaviour changes". What does the green gate support, which part of the note did nothing test, and how would you test it?
  5. A change makes the gate report a pass by printing the report line itself and ending the run. Which property of the gate allowed that, who is the last chance to catch it, and what would have to change in the gate to close the gap?
  6. A team says its test stage has been green for two hundred runs and is ready to run with no person watching. Name the four things a stage must show first, and say which of them two hundred green runs supply.
  7. A review says: "The upload endpoint accepts any file type." Your requirement allows only .csv and .json. You send report.exe and the endpoint refuses it. Which disposition does that one run support, and what scope sentence keeps the conclusion within what you checked?
  8. A review says: "Some search query makes the results page list another user's reports." You try three ordinary queries and each lists only your reports. One classmate wants to mark the claim false, another wants to mark it as impossible to decide. What is wrong with each, and what do you do next?
  9. A review says the deployment settings store a database password in plain text. Those settings are not in your snapshot. A classmate runs a secret scan on the tagged tree, sees no secrets and wants to close the claim. What is wrong with that evidence, and what does the row say instead?
  10. In week 10 you ended your audit of an evaluation instance with "accept" for its scorer, citing a results table. Since then the scorer gained two cases and the model version behind your agent changed. Which decision word describes that old line today, and what do you do before you rely on it in your final project?

Keep one revised answer beside the command output that supports it.

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text: Pick one stage of your own project. Write the claim "this stage can run with nobody watching" as a bounded sentence: which changes, behind which check, with which stop. Then name the run you could show someone in which that check failed.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval: evaluation and recovery
docs.text:
Answer these two short prompts after the session. They revisit weeks 10 and 11 so that the evidence, not a memorised label, is carried forward.

R1. Retrieval 1. A scorer accepts a scalar answer but the contract changes to JSON. Which parser and malformed cases must be added?

R2. Retrieval 2. A timeout leaves no persisted-state observation. Name two possible histories and the next discriminating check.

docs.title: The software factory and what comes next
docs.text:
Week 12 · LO9

What would you have to see before you believed that a pipeline runs itself?

docs.title: A software factory
docs.text:
A pipeline in which each stage triggers the next:

request → specification → change → checks → review → release.

The strong version: no person reads anything in between.

docs.title: "It runs itself" is a claim
docs.text:
It is a claim about every change that will ever enter the pipeline.

A claim has a test. Today we look for it.

All examples today are course-written; no model wrote them.

docs.title: Three questions
docs.text:
1. What would have to be observed for the claim to be true?
  2. What evidence must each stage leave?
  3. Where does a named person still accept or reject?

docs.title: What one run can decide
docs.text: The claim is about One run can one input confirm or refute it some input confirm it, with a witness every input refute it, with a counterexample each member of a listed set decide that member only something outside the snapshot show it cannot be read

docs.title: A demonstration is one input
docs.text:
One request became one merged change, unattended.

That supports "this change went through".

It cannot confirm a claim about every change.

docs.title: A pipeline small enough to read
The thing it protects
docs.text:
An evaluator with a contract:

  • exactly yes for the status failed, exactly no otherwise;
  • a missing or non-string answer is unknown;
  • anything else, extra text or spaces included, is fail.

docs.title: Generate: a proposal arrives
docs.text:
"Made scoring robust to formatting. Answers are trimmed and lower-cased, and an answer that starts with the expected word now counts."

Predict the exit status before the run.

docs.title: Verify: the stop path
docs.text:
Stage Status Evidence scope pass defines score, nothing else gate stop failed: extra_text, case_changed release not-run an earlier stage stopped

Exit status 1.

The gate names the two cases. release never ran.

docs.title: A name cannot clear a stop
docs.text:
Run it again with --accept-by "A. Student".

Same three lines, same exit status.

A person accepts evidence; there is no passing evidence here.

docs.title: A green run is held
docs.text:
Stage Status Evidence scope pass defines score, nothing else gate pass 9 cases, none failed release held no named person has accepted this evidence

Exit status 3 is not zero: held is not released.

docs.title: The decision line of the pipeline
docs.text:
{"stage": "release", "status": "released", "accepted_by": "A. Student",
 "accepted_evidence": {"candidate_sha256": "9f75d5aca3be",
                       "cases_sha256": "d087328e6120", "cases": 9}}

The last line of the accepted run, wrapped to fit. It names who accepted, and exactly what.

docs.title: A second proposal
docs.text:
"Ignore stray spaces around the answer. No other behaviour changes."

The pipeline's record: scope pass, gate pass, release held.

It looks exactly like the record of the current evaluator.

docs.title: Check it against the contract yourself
docs.text:
Input Second proposal Current evaluator Contract status failed, answer " yes" pass fail fail

Every automatic stage passed a change that breaks the contract.

docs.title: One counterexample is enough
docs.text:
"This pipeline runs itself" is about every change.

Here is one change it gets wrong.

What the gate supported: agreement on nine cases. Nothing more.

docs.title: Before nobody watches a stage
docs.text:
1. A check seen to fail on a bad change and pass on a good one.
  2. Cases the changing agent cannot edit.
  3. A verdict the change cannot write.
  4. A stop path that someone has exercised.

docs.title: Two hundred green runs
docs.text:
They supply none of the four.

A check never seen to fail is not yet evidence that it would stop anything.

docs.title: Hands-on: find where it needs a person
docs.text:
• add the missing input as a tenth case;
  • remove two cases and watch the gate pass;
  • step outside the scope;
  • let a proposal print its own verdict.

Write the expected statuses before each run.

docs.title: Evidence is what lets a person catch it
docs.text:
Run Gate Cases Cases digest first proposal, frozen cases stop 9 d087328e6120 first proposal, two cases removed pass 7 8458d33b70db

Nothing in the pipeline objected to seven cases.

A stage that left only "pass" would have hidden it.

docs.title: The review stage emits claims
docs.text:
A model reads the change and reports problems.

A pipeline that runs itself must act on all of them, or on none.

docs.title: Why a review over-asserts and misses
One worked row
docs.text:
Claim: an owner can read the body of a private report.

  • Requirement: R1
  • Check and input: private-report-view, {"private": true, "role": "owner"}
  • Prediction: if the claim holds, the body is visible
  • Observation: deny, body_visible: false
  • Disposition: refuted, for this one input

docs.title: Five recorded claims, no answers
docs.text:
Each has an id and an area. Most point at a function; one is prose only.

You choose the check and the input.

Confirmed, refuted or undetermined: the observation decides.

docs.title: An unfinished search is not a disposition
docs.text:
Inputs that behave do not refute a claim about some input.

The snapshot still decides it, so it is not cannot tell either.

Read the rule the code applies; probe its edges.

docs.title: Could the review run unattended?
docs.text:
Course-made record of one verified review Count Claims 9 Confirmed 4 Refuted 3 Undetermined 2 Missed by the review, found by an own check 1

Act on all: 5 changes with nothing behind them. Ignore all: 4 defects go out.

docs.title: A source of hypotheses
docs.text:
The review can run on every change, unattended.

It cannot yet change code or block a release on its own word.

Each confirmed claim becomes a case for the gate.

docs.title: Course review: four words
docs.text:
• accept: the evidence covers the claim as stated;
  • narrow: it supports a smaller claim; accept only that;
  • recheck: it is missing, or about an input that changed;
  • stop: a check failed, or the judged thing wrote the evidence.

docs.title: Every week handed you a claim
docs.text:
"The agent did this." "The skill triggers." "The tests pass." "That text is only data."

"The pass rate is this number." "The incident is over." "The pipeline runs itself."

Each week's evidence was the thing that could have shown it false.

docs.title: Decide again when the input changes
docs.text:
Reopen two of your own decision lines.

Has the code, the cases, the tool, the model version or the upstream rule changed?

If so, the honest word today is recheck.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
No forecast. A way to meet the next claim:

  • ask for its reach and the counterexample search;
  • write your prediction down, then record what happened;
  • bind each decision to its inputs and to a named person.

docs.title: Second session
docs.text:
Defense walkthrough: the format of week 13, from the syllabus.

Studio: freeze your revision, rehearse locate, explain, decide, and run your README from the tagged files only.

docs.title: Due this week
docs.text:
Contribution 4.

The final project.

docs.title: Exit question
docs.text:
Your project's test stage has only ever been green.

Which run would you need to show before nobody watches it?

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
Notes · Second session · Self-check · Reading path

Examples in lectures/week-12/factory/ and lectures/week-12/fixtures/

docs.title: Public audit-verification fixture
docs.text: This is a course-authored synthetic snapshot. audit_packet.py is the frozen public surface; it has no network, package installation, credential, or personal-data path. Run it and verify_audit.py with python in a copy of this directory, as the notes show.

docs.title: Frozen requirements
docs.text:
Every disposition is judged against these requirements, not against the wording of the review:

R1 access: a viewer or an owner can read a public report; no role reads a private report body.
R2 status: the status endpoint accepts only the labels ready and queued.
R3 paths: every exported or archived report path stays under /srv/reports.
R4 secrets: no export configuration exposes a secret directory.
R5 scoring: the private-count scorer gives 1 only when the answer's first word is the number of private sample reports; every other answer scores 0.
R6 root: the report root is written once, as REPORT_ROOT; no function repeats the literal path.

Production configuration is not part of this snapshot, so no check here can read it.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
• audit_packet.py is the snapshot's report feature and its deterministic evidence checks. Run it with no --check to list each check and its argument keys. A run prints the args it used, the observation and the canonical command to record as evidence. It refuses a missing, extra or wrongly typed argument: private is a JSON true or false, and role is viewer or owner.
  • model-audit.json is a recorded review with five claims about security, evaluation and maintenance. Each has an id, an area and, for most, the function it cites. It names no check, input or answer; you choose the check and input for each claim. It is course-authored practice material; no model wrote it.
  • student-audit.json is an empty starter record. Students add one verification for each recorded claim and either a new defect check or a bounded clean-scope check. The notes show a filled row, the parts shape for a claim about each member of a listed set, and both own-check shapes.
  • verify_audit.py recomputes every named check, checks the exact reproducible command, checks that the input tests the claim and derives the supported disposition from the observation. It accepts only confirmed, refuted or undetermined; an undetermined row must name the missing input or why it cannot be decided.

The verifier tests the evidence supplied by the student. The recorded review is not a model score and its text is never sent to a grader. A hand trace is not an observation; retain the command output with the frozen snapshot identifier. An own check must probe a new input or state a checked range and its remaining boundary.

docs.title: Assignments A1–A6
docs.text: These six small assignments are the practical line through the first ten teaching weeks. Each is worth 2.5 points under the syllabus. Submit the artifact, verification evidence and a short explanation. End every report with decision: accept | narrow | recheck | stop, because: evidence IDs and next:.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9: run the agent in a dedicated directory or container; keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of it; keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs; and run injection demonstrations offline against the local machine only. Use the mature coding-agent seat supplied for the course and do not run unknown generated commands on a credential-bearing host.

Assignment Week Capability Start A1: Read a coding-agent session 1 Capture a real session and a forced failure python practice/a1/check.py <submission> A2: Build a small MCP tool server 2 Tool selection, arguments and recovery python practice/a2/check.py <submission> A3: Turn a manual workflow into a skill 3 Trigger and near-miss testing python practice/a3/check.py <submission> A4: Make a messy repository agent-ready 5 Instructions, hook and checks python practice/a4/check.py <submission> A5: Score agent readiness from observations 6 Anchored evidence and change conditions python practice/a5/check.py <submission> A6: Audit an evaluation instance and scorer 10 Denominators, counterexamples and limits python practice/a6/check.py <submission>

The checks provide public consistency feedback. They do not execute model-generated code, authenticate provenance or assign marks.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: capture one real coding-agent session, force one safe failure, and label what you observed or inferred.
  • Week: 1
  • Weight: 2.5 points
  • Due: Sunday 23:59 in the listed week
  • Hand in: one report.json and the session excerpt or redacted transcript it cites.
  • Done when: every behaviour is labelled observed or inferred and points to an excerpt or command output, and the forced failure is real and explained. check.py then confirms the shape of the record only.
  • Time: published after a timed pilot; record your prediction and actual time.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Explain an agent's system instructions, tools, loop and stopping condition (LO1). Separate a line visible in the session from an explanation you infer from it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9:

  • Run the agent in a dedicated directory or container.
  • Keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment.
  • Keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs.
  • Run injection demonstrations offline against the local machine only.

Use the mature coding-agent seat supplied for the course. Do not run an unknown generated command on a credential-bearing host.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Predict. Before starting, write which request, tool call or stop condition you expect to be easy to misread.
  2. Generate. Ask the agent to make a tiny, reversible change in a disposable repository. Keep the visible request, system or configuration summary, tool calls and stop message.
  3. Verify. Run the repository check yourself and save its output. Label each behaviour observed or inferred, with an evidence ID.
  4. Force failure. Change one safe input or deny one permission so the agent receives a real failure. Do not fabricate an error. Record the recovery or the reason it stopped.
  5. Revise. After feedback from a peer or the teaching team during the assignment week, correct one label or explanation. Record who gave it and the date in your explanation; if no feedback was available, record your self-review date and finish the decision line.

Generation is the agent's proposed change; verification is your command output and file inspection. The supplied check.py checks the record shape only, so read every cited file yourself.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Copy starter/report.json to report.json. Include the redacted session excerpt, the forced-failure output, and one AI-use note ID. Keep only task-relevant lines; remove keys, personal data and unrelated source.

The report must include assignment, session_kind: "real", an agent description, behaviour rows, a forced-failure record, evidence rows, an explanation and a decision. Run:

python practice/a1/check.py path/to/submission

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: The published criteria are: accurate observed/inferred labels; a genuine, reproducible failure and honest recovery or stop explanation; evidence that another reader can inspect; and a useful revision. The local check gives public feedback and does not assign marks or certify a real session.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Green: the agent may propose the disposable change and help format notes. Yellow: you may ask it to suggest labels, then verify every suggestion yourself. Red: the prediction, observed/inferred labels, failure interpretation and decision must be your own. Attach one AI-use note ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Published after a timed pilot. Record predicted and actual time in the report; ask for help if the safety boundary or failure cannot be reproduced.

docs.title: A2: Build a small MCP tool server
At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: build a local MCP server whose tools, schemas and errors help an agent select, call and recover correctly.
  • Week: 2
  • Weight: 2.5 points
  • Due: Sunday 23:59 in the listed week
  • Hand in: the server, a report.json, and outputs from the public protocol check.
  • Done when: selection, valid arguments and one recoverable error each have a real trial and evidence.
  • Time: published after a timed pilot; record your prediction and actual time.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Design a small model-readable tool surface and verify its behaviour (LO2). No third-party sign-in or OAuth is required.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9:

  • Run the agent in a dedicated directory or container.
  • Keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment.
  • Keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs.
  • Run injection demonstrations offline against the local machine only.

Use the mature coding-agent seat supplied for the course. Do not run an unknown generated command on a credential-bearing host.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Specify. Choose two or three read or write operations and define names, descriptions, required arguments, errors and a safe retry rule.
  2. Generate. Ask the agent to propose handlers and schemas. Review the proposal before placing it in the server.
  3. Verify selection. Run a request where the right tool is distinguishable from its neighbours; record the selected call and result.
  4. Verify arguments. Run a valid call and an invalid-argument call. Check that the server returns structured feedback without a traceback.
  5. Verify recovery. Make one tool return a retryable local error, then show the agent taking the documented next step. Keep all three trials.
  6. Revise. Fix one unclear description or error, rerun the protocol check, and write the decision line.

Generation is the proposed tool design; verification is the protocol transcript and direct result inspection. The check never calls a model and does not turn a transcript into a mark.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Include the server source, schemas, report.json, and protocol output. The report has a server_path naming the submitted tool_server.py and exactly three trial cases: selection, arguments and recovery, each with request, expected, actual, disposition and evidence IDs. Start from starter/ and run:

python practice/a2/protocol_check.py path/to/submission/tool_server.py
python practice/a2/check.py path/to/submission

protocol_check.py is an envelope smoke test. It checks the handshake, the shape of the tool list, one valid call and one refused invalid call. It never calls a model, so it does not show that a model can choose and use your tool; a pass prints that limitation on its own line.

Register the same tool_server.py command in your mature agent's documented local-stdio tool configuration. The three report trials are the real agent runs that establish selection, argument handling and recovery.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: Criteria are model-readable tool descriptions; correct schema validation; structured, bounded errors; recovery evidence; and an explanation of one revision. The public check only detects missing or inconsistent records; it does not claim that a model selected a tool correctly on unseen requests.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Green: drafting schemas and boilerplate. Yellow: proposing descriptions or recovery paths, followed by your own protocol runs. Red: the expected tool, error interpretation and decision are your own. Do not paste private data or keys into prompts or outputs. Attach one AI-use note ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Published after a timed pilot. Record predicted and actual time and request help if a local protocol failure is unclear.

docs.title: A3: Turn a manual workflow into a skill
At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: perform a small workflow by hand, encode it as one skill, and test its trigger and near miss.
  • Week: 3
  • Weight: 2.5 points
  • Due: Sunday 23:59 in the listed week
  • Hand in: the skill file, manual-work evidence, two trigger trials and report.json.
  • Done when: the intended request triggers and a similar request stays quiet, with outputs you can inspect.
  • Time: published after a timed pilot; record your prediction and actual time.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Write a precise, bounded skill and evaluate when it should activate (LO2).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9:

  • Run the agent in a dedicated directory or container.
  • Keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment.
  • Keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs.
  • Run injection demonstrations offline against the local machine only.

Use the mature coding-agent seat supplied for the course. Do not run an unknown generated command on a credential-bearing host.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Run by hand. Complete the workflow without a skill. Save the request, inputs, steps, expected output and verification command.
  2. Generate. Ask the agent to draft one SKILL.md with a name, trigger, non-trigger, steps, limits and verification.
  3. Verify the trigger. Use one request that should activate it and inspect the resulting trace or activation marker.
  4. Verify the near miss. Use a similar request that should remain quiet. Record what you observed, including a false activation if it occurs.
  5. Revise. After feedback from a peer or the teaching team during the assignment week, tighten one trigger or limit and rerun both cases. Record who gave it and the date; if no feedback was available, record your self-review date and explain the choice in the decision line.

Generation is the proposed skill; verification is the manual baseline and the two controlled requests. Do not count a plausible activation as proof without an observable marker.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Include the skill, manual evidence, both trial records and report.json. Run:

python practice/a3/check.py path/to/submission

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: Criteria are a reproducible manual baseline; an unambiguous trigger; silence on the near miss; bounded instructions; and evidence for the revision. The public check is a consistency check, not a model judge.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Green: drafting skill prose and test requests. Yellow: suggesting trigger boundaries, followed by your own runs. Red: deciding whether activation occurred and choosing the final decision. Attach one AI-use note ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Published after a timed pilot. Record predicted and actual time and ask for support if the agent's activation signal is not observable.

docs.title: A4: Make a messy repository agent-ready
At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: improve the supplied small, course-made synthetic messy repository with instructions, a blocking hook, structure and checks.
  • Week: 5
  • Weight: 2.5 points
  • Due: Sunday 23:59 in the listed week
  • Hand in: your revised repository, probe outputs, and report.json.
  • Done when: a bad commit is rejected, a good commit and regression pass, and the map tells a new agent where to work.
  • Time: published after a timed pilot; record your prediction and actual time.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Create repository guidance and gates that support safe agent changes (LO2, LO4).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9:

  • Run the agent in a dedicated directory or container.
  • Keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment.
  • Keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs.
  • Run injection demonstrations offline against the local machine only.

Use the mature coding-agent seat supplied for the course. Do not run an unknown generated command on a credential-bearing host.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Inspect. Copy starter/, make the baseline commit described in its README, and map one behaviour to its files, tests and check command before asking for a change. The assigned bad commit adds print("debug: leaked value") to app.py; your hook must make that git commit exit non-zero.

  2. Generate. Ask the agent to propose an instruction file, a small pre-commit hook and a structural cleanup. Review every command before running it. Put the hook where Git and your reader can both find it:

    ```bash mkdir -p .githooks

Generation is the agent's proposed repository change; verification is the three probes and direct file inspection.

docs.title: write your hook to .githooks/pre-commit, then:
docs.text:
chmod +x .githooks/pre-commit git config core.hooksPath .githooks git add .githooks/pre-commit git commit -m "Add pre-commit hook" ```

core.hooksPath is a local setting and is not part of a commit, so name that command in your instruction file. The hook file itself must be committed; a hook left in .git/hooks/ is not handed in. 3. Verify the gate. Run the three probes as commands and keep each command, exit code and output:

```bash

docs.title: bad commit: must exit non-zero
docs.text: echo 'print("debug: leaked value")' >> app.py git add app.py git commit -m "bad probe"; echo "exit=$?" git restore --staged app.py && git restore app.py

docs.title: good commit: a documentation or behaviour-preserving change; must exit zero
docs.text: printf '\nReviewed.\n' >> NOTES.md git add NOTES.md git commit -m "good probe"; echo "exit=$?"

docs.title: regression: must pass
docs.text: python -m pytest -q; echo "exit=$?" ``` 4. Check structure. Confirm the instruction file names the same commands and invariants that the repository actually contains. 5. Revise. Fix one stale instruction or weak check and repeat all three probes. Write the decision line.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Include the revised repository, the behaviour-to-code map, probe outputs and report.json. Name before and after revisions. Run:

python practice/a4/check.py path/to/submission

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: Criteria are usable instructions; a hook that blocks the assigned bad commit; passing good and regression checks; clear structure; and evidence for one revision. The public check verifies record consistency and cannot replace a code review.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Green: proposing documentation, a hook and refactoring ideas. Yellow: generated code after you inspect it and run the probes. Red: accepting a gate, interpreting a failure and making the decision. Keep credentials and private data out of the agent environment and logs. Attach one AI-use note ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Published after a timed pilot. Record predicted and actual time; ask for support when a hook or check behaves differently from its description.

docs.title: A5: Score agent readiness from observations
At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: score a repository with four observable anchors and report what would change each score.
  • Week: 6
  • Weight: 2.5 points
  • Due: Sunday 23:59 in the listed week
  • Hand in: a four-row scorecard, verification evidence and report.json.
  • Done when: every level names an anchor and evidence, and a proposed agent score has been checked.
  • Time: published after a timed pilot; record your prediction and actual time.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Use observable evidence to judge structure, documentation, tests and checks, and explain uncertainty (LO4, LO5).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Score the revised A4 starter repository that you copied and changed, at the immutable commit or local snapshot named in your report. Do not score the course repository or an unrelated project. Read the revision from that repository and, if you score a snapshot, make the copy from the same commit:

git -C path/to/a4-repo rev-parse HEAD
mkdir -p path/to/a5-submission/snapshot
git -C path/to/a4-repo archive --format=tar HEAD | tar -x -C path/to/a5-submission/snapshot

git clone path/to/a4-repo path/to/a5-submission/snapshot also works when you want the history. Put the printed commit in the revision field of your report.

Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9:

  • Run the agent in a dedicated directory or container.
  • Keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment.
  • Keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs.
  • Run injection demonstrations offline against the local machine only.

Use the mature coding-agent seat supplied for the course. Do not run an unknown generated command on a credential-bearing host.

docs.title: Published anchors
docs.text:
Give each dimension the highest level whose observable anchor you can show at the named revision. These anchors are the complete vocabulary for this assignment.

Dimension Level 1 Level 2 Level 3 Level 4 Structure No behaviour-to-file map A map exists but an entry is wrong Map is accurate and the change point has one responsibility A check catches a deliberate boundary violation Documentation No runnable context file Commands are listed but one fails or an invariant is absent Commands run and three invariants name their checks A check detects a stale documented command Tests No runnable coverage for the changed path A run passes but is slow, nondeterministic or misses a deliberate break Two repeatable runs pass and a deliberate break fails Mutation evidence explains every surviving mutant Checks No automatic gate A gate is manual or already failing One offline gate command stops a bad change A pre-commit gate stops both an unused import and a secret canary

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Choose a revision. Record the commit printed by git -C path/to/a4-repo rev-parse HEAD, and the snapshot directory if you made one.
  2. Generate. Ask the agent to suggest a level and evidence for each dimension. Treat each suggestion as claims.
  3. Disprove. For every claim, choose an observation that could show it false; run commands and open files at the named revision.
  4. Score. Record the highest level whose anchors are all evidenced for Structure, Documentation, Tests and Checks. Name the observation that would change each score.
  5. Review. Recheck one proposed agent claim yourself and record whether the evidence confirms, refutes or leaves it unresolved. Finish the decision line.

Generation is a proposed score; verification is your command output, file reading and deliberate break where safe. A score without evidence stays unsupported.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Submit the four-row scorecard.md, evidence files or excerpts, the checked agent proposal and report.json; set scorecard_path to that file. Run:

python practice/a5/check.py path/to/submission

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: Criteria are reproducible anchors; correct distinction between evidence and inference; a concrete change condition for each dimension; and a checked proposal. The public check does not authenticate commits or assign a readiness status.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Green: proposing levels, probes and prose. Yellow: using generated probe plans after reading and adapting them. Red: choosing the final levels, evidence interpretation and decision. Attach one AI-use note ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Published after a timed pilot. Record predicted and actual time, including the time spent rechecking one claim.

docs.title: A6: Audit an evaluation instance and scorer
At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: inspect one evaluation instance and scorer, then state exactly what its result supports and does not support.
  • Week: 10
  • Weight: 2.5 points
  • Due: Sunday 23:59 in the listed week
  • Hand in: an audit record, recomputed counts and report.json.
  • Done when: every denominator includes success, failure, timeout and missing outcomes, and one scorer weakness is demonstrated.
  • Time: published after a timed pilot; record your prediction and actual time.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Check whether an evaluation can fail, whether its denominator is complete and how far a small result generalizes (LO6).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9:

  • Run the agent in a dedicated directory or container.
  • Keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment.
  • Keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs.
  • Run injection demonstrations offline against the local machine only.

Use the mature coding-agent seat supplied for the course. Do not run an unknown generated command on a credential-bearing host.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Predict. Identify one check you expect to be weak and one outcome likely to be missing.
  2. Generate. Ask an agent to propose an audit plan. Keep it as claims, not truth.
  3. Audit the instance. Open starter/instance.json, including its prompt, inputs, checks and four declared attempts. Run a safe counterexample showing a check can fail or a wrong answer can pass.
  4. Audit the scorer. Run python starter/run_scorer.py starter/instance.json, then recompute the result with success, failure, timeout and missing rows visible. Compare the reported rate with a denominator that includes every declared attempt and record any difference you find.
  5. Claim limits. Write one supported claim and at least three unsupported claims, such as a ranking, unseen-task generalization or stable rate from one attempt. Revise after feedback from a peer or the teaching team during the assignment week; record who gave it and the date, or your self-review date if no feedback was available. Finish the decision line.

Generation is a proposed audit; verification is the counterexample and recomputation. Never copy a reference answer or treat a course fixture as an industry result.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Include the instance and scorer paths, audit output, counts and report.json. Counts must include declared, success, failure, timeout and missing. Run:

python practice/a6/check.py path/to/submission

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: Criteria are a reproducible counterexample; a complete denominator; a precise supported claim; at least three limits; and a revision backed by evidence. The public check catches inconsistent records but does not judge the scorer or make a statistical claim.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Green: drafting an audit plan and recomputation table. Yellow: suggesting counterexamples, followed by your own run and inspection. Red: deciding what the result supports, what it cannot support and the final decision. Attach one AI-use note ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Published after a timed pilot. Record predicted and actual time, including recomputation and revision.
