docs.title: Scoring rubrics
docs.text: This directory holds the machine-readable canonical source for the course's eight-dimension rubric. Students use the rubric pages linked from the course site; rendering commands and scoring-tool maintenance remain instructor material. Rubric wording and scoring thresholds are checked by a second reader; actual human grading remains a separate requirement.

docs.title: How this course works
docs.text: A coding agent proposes a change; you decide whether the evidence supports it and whether you can explain it. Every example shows generation and verification. A test you can rerun is evidence; an agent saying “done” is a claim to check.

docs.title: Twelve teaching weeks, then assessment
docs.text: The course follows the public Fall 2026 calendar of Stanford CS146S, with two verification weeks added. Each teaching week has two 90-minute sessions: a lecture with live generation and verification, then a practitioner guest or a studio. When no guest is available, you work on your project or contribution in a studio with teaching support. Week 13 has the project expo followed by individual defenses. The schedule gives topics and deadlines.

docs.title: Three lines of work
docs.text:
• Six assignments: A1–A6, due in weeks 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 10. Each earns up to 2.5 points (15 total). Keep the artifact, verification results and a short explanation, ending with one decision: accept, narrow, recheck or stop, and the evidence supporting it.
  • Four open-source contributions: 30 points across two repositories. A small fix and a substantial change in the first repository earn up to 5 and 10 points in weeks 4 and 8; repeat in the second repository for 5 and 10 points in weeks 9 and 12. A TA performs acceptance review when the repository has no partner contact or the maintainer has not replied within seven days. Your mark does not depend on a maintainer replying.
  • A term project: choose a topic and build runnable software with an agent, alone or with one other student. Proposal, technical specification, alpha and final milestones earn 2, 4, 6 and 8 points in weeks 2, 4, 7 and 12 (20 total). In a two-person project, milestone marks are shared; each student defends their own understanding separately.

Your term project has its own topic and repository. Attach an AI-use note once to each work item and reuse its evidence ID rather than copying logs into multiple submissions.

docs.title: Explain your work without AI
docs.text:
CP1 in week 6 and CP2 in week 11 are thirty-minute, in-class paper checkpoints, each worth 7.5 points. The week 13 defense is worth 15 points: without a device, respond to a change or fault introduced in your own code during a fifteen-minute sitting. These three items provide 30 points of individual evidence without AI. Participation earns the remaining 5 points through guest questions, studio work and the expo.

Passing requires at least 60/100 overall and at least 15/30 across CP1, CP2 and the project defense. Each of those three items permits one resit after feedback when the first mark is below half; the replacement mark is capped at half the item's maximum. Invalid technical or approved accommodation sittings are replaced by an equivalent sitting without consuming that resit. Incomplete assessments stay missing. Read the syllabus for the full rules.

docs.title: Practise making a decision
docs.text:
Save a prediction before discussion, inspect a candidate or trace, run a discriminating check, revise after feedback and try a changed input. After checking, choose whether to accept, narrow, recheck or stop. Another generation call helps only when it answers a question you can name.

Follow the safety practices in Week 0 setup before using your supplied coding agent. Ask for help when access or a concept prevents progress.

docs.title: Open-source contributions rubric
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

This rubric is the marking contract for the open-source contributions. They are worth 30 points in two samples: C1, the warm-up contribution, is worth 8 and C2, the substantial contribution, is worth 22. The project kit's open-source contributions guide, capstone/kit/open-source-contributions.en.md, explains how to choose a project, do the work and submit it.

Both samples are marked on the same evidence as your other open work, the explanation check, verification evidence and one AI-use note, and on your upstream collaboration. Three rules apply to every row:

  • Merge and replies do not count. Marks never depend on whether the pull request is merged, or, for a pull request opened on time (see Late opening), on whether a maintainer replies or reviews it.
  • The course-hosted route is marked the same way. On that route, "upstream" means the course practice repository and the TA who reviews it as a maintainer would. The rubric, the dates and the maximum mark are the same.
  • Model use is optional. Work done without a model, or on the replay route, uses the same rows and reaches the same maximum mark.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines the evidence and point boundaries the teaching team uses for C1 and C2.

docs.title: Records
docs.text: Each sample has one work record. It links the issue and pull request (or the course-hosted equivalent), the head commit at opening, one line for each later push, the launcher outputs before and after your change, your summary of the review comments and what you changed in response, your explain-gate answers and your AI-use note. Link each claim to one evidence ID. One evidence ID supports one criterion; repeating a citation never earns extra points. The TA records the evidence IDs, the head commit marked and each criterion score on the score sheet.

docs.title: Review
docs.text: A second calibrated reviewer checks the evidence mapping, arithmetic and boundary rules before the contributions score is released. The TA who reviews your pull request as a maintainer, on the course-hosted route or by the review date below, never marks that sample. Appeals follow the assessment and appeals process.

docs.title: How to use the tables
docs.text: Award the points in a row only when the listed evidence is present, attributable to you and verified. Each sample is marked on the last head you pushed before its deadline. Only your own commits count; commits that maintainers or others push to your branch do not. Scores are whole or half points, and each row lists every score it allows: full credit, the partial-credit values in its partial column (from lowest to highest), or zero. A score is not a prediction of effort and never depends on code volume, commit count, the project's popularity or whether an assistant produced text.

docs.title: Dates for opening and review
docs.text:
"End of week N" means Friday 23:59 course time. Every day count is in calendar days. The dates apply to every pull request in the sample: C1, and each C2 pull request.

Sample Open ready for review by Review date Deadline C1 End of week 5 Monday of week 6 End of week 6 C2 End of week 11 Monday of week 12 End of week 13 (Friday 23:59 course time)
  • Opening. Open each pull request ready for review by its opening date. Ready for review means it contains the change being marked. Note the head commit at opening in your work record. A pull request whose opening head does not contain the change counts as opened late.
  • Review date. The review date is 3 days after the opening date. A pull request with no human maintainer review by then gets a TA review, posted by the review date in your course submission and never in the public project; the TA never contacts the project's maintainers. Only a human maintainer's or the TA's review counts. Comments from bots, CI or other contributors may be answered, but they never stop the TA review or lower a mark.
  • Cutoff. Revision after review is judged on the comments received by the review date. Comments that arrive later may be answered and never lower this kind. For a pull request opened on time, a later human maintainer or TA review that is fully answered raises weak to sound. If the TA review is late, your review date and deadline move by the same number of days, but never past the C2 deadline.
  • Later pushes. You may push anything after opening: review responses, rebases, CI and format fixes, a sign-off, or fixes for problems you find yourself. The sample is marked on the final head. Give one line per later push in your work record, saying what it changed and why. A follow-up pull request that a maintainer asks for counts as a review response.
  • Late opening. A pull request opened late is marked the same way but gets no TA review. If no human maintainer review arrives by the review date, revision after review is missing. Comments that arrive after the review date do not raise it.
  • Course-hosted route. The same dates apply, and the TA is the maintainer.

docs.title: If your issue disappears
docs.text: If your issue is fixed by someone else first, or stops being feasible (for example, the project changes its licence or AI rules, or its tests no longer fit the launcher's limits), tell the instructor. You choose, without penalty: the instructor approves a substitute issue with dates that restore the working time you lost, or you keep the work and it is marked against the part of the agreed scope that was still achievable. A pull request rejected on direction, timing or project policy has no effect on the mark.

docs.title: Explanation check answers
docs.text: The explanation check has four questions: what changed, why, which inputs are most likely to fail and what you verified yourself. An answer is sound when it is concrete, matches the marked diff and claims as verified only what the evidence shows. For C2 in two pull requests, a question counts as sound only when its answer is sound in both pull requests' records. If any answer claims a verification that the evidence contradicts, the whole row scores 0, whatever the other answers show.

docs.title: Upstream collaboration evidence
docs.text:
The collaboration row looks at three kinds of evidence. Each kind is sound, weak or missing:

Kind Sound Weak Missing Issue discussion Before you started, you said on the issue, or where the project's guide asks, what you planned, and you updated the discussion when the plan changed. The discussion exists but came only after the work was done, or does not say what you planned. No discussion. Revision after review Every review comment received by the review date is answered, either with a change verified by a new launcher run or with a reasoned reply that gives evidence for why your change stands. A review with nothing to answer counts as sound. For a pull request opened on time, a later human maintainer or TA review that is fully answered raises weak to sound; for a pull request opened late, comments after the review date do not raise this kind. Some comments received by the review date are answered, or answers lack the new launcher run or the evidence. No comment received by the review date is answered, or no review arrived by the review date. Contribution rules The pull request meets every requirement of the project's contribution guide that applies, such as its template, commit message format and rules for disclosing AI use. One requirement other than AI disclosure is not met. Two or more requirements are not met, or AI use is not disclosed where the project requires disclosure.

This kind leaves out requirements already scored in another row, such as the tests the project asks for, which the C1 complete-fix row and the C2 verification row score. A contributor licence agreement (CLA) or a sign-off is never scored. If a project requires one you will not sign, choose another project or take the course-hosted route.

Score each kind sound 2, weak 1 and missing 0, and add the three to a collaboration total from 0 to 6. C2 scores that total. C1 converts it:

Collaboration total 0–1 2 3–4 5 6 C1 points 0 0.5 1 1.5 2

docs.title: C1 — warm-up contribution (8 points)
docs.text:
C1 is one small, complete fix to a defect, a test or documentation, due at the end of week 6.

Criterion Points Full credit Partial credit Zero Complete fix within the C1 scope 2 The pull request resolves the issue it names with one small fix, carries the tests or checks the project asks for, and contains no unrelated changes. 1: the fix resolves the issue, but a test or check the project asks for is missing, or the change includes unrelated edits. 0: no pull request at the marked head, or the change does not address the issue it names. Verification evidence 2 The launcher output of the project's relevant tests or checks before and after the change is linked at the marked head, with failing-first evidence: when the change touches code, a test fails for the reported reason before the change and passes after it; when the contribution adds a test for code that already works, the test fails on a deliberately broken version of that code, which you then revert; when the contribution is documentation only, the project's documentation build or link check runs before and after the change, or you link the rendered diff of the corrected page. 1: before-and-after runs exist, but the failing-first evidence is missing, or one run cannot be tied to the marked head. 0: no runnable verification evidence, or the evidence is falsified. Explanation check 1.5 All four answers are sound. 0.5: two sound answers. 1: three sound answers. 0: one sound answer or none, or a contradicted verification claim. Upstream collaboration 2 Total 6: all three kinds are sound. 0.5: total 2. 1: total 3–4. 1.5: total 5. 0: collaboration total 0–1. AI-use note 0.5 One AI-use note for the work, reused by its ID, names the tool and purpose, or states that no AI was used. No partial credit: a note that omits the tool or the purpose scores 0. 0: no AI-use note.

docs.title: C2 — substantial contribution (22 points)
docs.text:
C2 is one approved feature or non-trivial fix, in one or two pull requests, due at the end of week 13 (Friday 23:59 course time). Both pull requests are marked together as one sample. The C2 proposal is not scored separately: the scope and acceptance cases the instructor approves before week 7 are what the rows below are marked against, including any later change the instructor approves.

Criterion Points Full credit Partial credit Zero Complete change within the approved scope 5 The approved feature or fix reaches its acceptance cases across normal, boundary and failure inputs, within the approved scope, with callers and data handling preserved. 1: a failing acceptance test or reproduction for the change exists at the marked head. 2: the main path is partly demonstrable. 3: the main path and one verification class work. 4: all but one required path or explanation is verified. 0: no failing acceptance test, reproduction or demonstrable change at the marked head, whether or not the proposal was approved. An approval or proposal without this evidence earns 0. Verification evidence 6 Launcher outputs of the project's relevant tests before and after the change are linked at the marked head. Tests fail for the reported reason before the change and pass after it, each approved acceptance case is checked, and every change pushed after review is verified with a new launcher run. 2: before-and-after runs exist, but the tests that fail first or the acceptance-case checks are missing. 4: all evidence classes are present, but one acceptance case or one pushed change lacks a launcher run. 0: no runnable verification evidence, or the evidence is falsified. Explanation check 4 All four answers are sound. 1: one sound answer. 2: two sound answers. 3: three sound answers. 0: no sound answer, or a contradicted verification claim. Upstream collaboration 6 Total 6: all three kinds are sound. The collaboration total from 1 to 5. 0: collaboration total 0. AI-use note 1 One AI-use note for the work, reused by its ID, names the tool and purpose, or states that no AI was used. 0.5: the note is present but omits the tool or the purpose. 0: no AI-use note.

docs.title: Evidence and boundaries
docs.text:
Contributions go only to public repositories or the course-hosted practice repository. Code from a residency, an employer or a partner company's internal systems never supplies evidence. Participant material, keys and credentials never appear in the evidence. Oral-defense marks, code lines, commit counts, rankings, awards, the project's popularity and a maintainer's reply or opinion never supply contribution points.

The teaching team records the contributions mark after reviewing the submitted evidence. Keep an unresolved or contradictory item pending; do not turn missing future work into zero by assumption.

docs.title: Course glossary
docs.text:
These definitions describe classroom usage. They do not claim product capabilities, industry metrics or universal standards. The terms match the preferred English column of the course bilingual glossary.

Term Definition agent A program that observes its environment, chooses actions and uses feedback to continue working toward a given goal within defined boundaries. coding agent An agent whose main task is to modify and verify code. agent loop A control flow that repeatedly observes, decides, acts and processes feedback. tool call The process by which a model requests a program operation through an explicit interface. tool interface A calling contract that defines a tool's inputs, outputs, errors and permissions. stopping condition A rule that ends an agent loop and returns a result or evidence of failure. context The input information available to the current reasoning or generation step. context window The amount of context a model can process at one time. context engineering The engineering practice of selecting, organizing and maintaining information needed for a task. context compression Shortening context while preserving information relevant to the task. context file A file that provides constraints, operating instructions and verification entry points for repository tasks. system prompt A prompt that sets high-level behavior and constraints in a model interaction. prompt The text or structured input submitted to a model to guide the current operation. token A discrete text or data unit used to measure model input and output. pretraining The stage in which a model learns basic representations and predictive ability before adaptation to downstream tasks. supervised fine-tuning Adjusting model behavior using examples with target outputs. reinforcement learning Optimizing a policy using feedback on actions. inference Computing outputs using a trained model. sampling Selecting candidate model outputs according to a specified distribution or rule. temperature A parameter that adjusts how concentrated the output sampling distribution is. subagent An agent that takes on a bounded subtask for a main task. plan mode A working mode that develops and checks an action plan before making changes. skill A mechanism that packages instructions, resources and steps for a class of tasks into a reusable unit. skills A collection of skills that a task can select and combine. hooks Extension points that trigger checks or operations at specified events. MCP The name of an interface protocol for connecting model applications to external tools or resources. worktree A working directory associated with a version-control repository for independent checkout and modification of files. permission An authorization constraint on whether an actor may access a resource or perform an operation. least privilege The security principle of granting only the capabilities required for the current task. sandbox An execution environment that limits the resources a program can access and the effects it can produce. safety launcher An entry program that configures sandbox boundaries and resource limits before execution; retained course tools use it for teacher and CI checks. gateway A single entry point that model or tool calls pass through, where access, budgets and records are enforced. trust boundary A boundary at which inputs and outputs must be validated between domains with different trust levels or permissions. deny by default A policy that refuses any operation that has not been explicitly permitted. fail closed Blocking a protected operation when a check fails or evidence is insufficient. timeout A termination or error condition triggered when an operation exceeds its allowed duration. resource budget A predefined allowance for a task's time, number of calls or computing resources. deterministic replay Reproducing outputs for the same inputs using fixed records. replay route Running a task with a recorded model reply instead of a live API call, with evidence labelled as replay; used by course CI, graders and offline checks. mock service A service that responds according to predefined behavior and substitutes for another service to isolate a test. user discovery Using verifiable activities to understand users' problems, tasks and constraints. jobs to be done An analytical perspective that understands requirements through the tasks users want to accomplish. product requirements document A document that records target users, the problem, scope and acceptance requirements. executable specification A specification whose required behavior can be checked by a program. acceptance criteria A set of verifiable conditions for deciding whether a deliverable meets agreed requirements. acceptance test A test that executes and verifies agreed requirements and acceptance criteria. specification-driven development A development method that organizes implementation and verification around an explicit specification. brownfield engineering Engineering work that extends or transforms a system within existing code, data and constraints. legacy code Code that must be understood and maintained within existing behavior and historical constraints. characterization test A test that records a system's observable behavior to protect it during subsequent changes. refactoring A change that improves the internal structure of code while preserving its agreed external behavior. dependency upgrade Moving an external component to a new version and verifying compatibility. lockfile A file that fixes dependency-resolution results to support reproducible installation. continuous integration A process that automatically verifies whether integrated changes meet project quality requirements. pull request A collaboration record that submits a set of changes for review and merging. code review Examining code changes against requirements, correctness and risk. model audit A review of a frozen snapshot that the teaching team runs with a model; each finding is a claim the student confirms, refutes or marks cannot tell. explain gate A review checkpoint requiring the author to explain why a change works, identify risky inputs and provide evidence of verification they performed themselves. commit trailer Text in agreed fields at the end of a commit message that records provenance or assistance. code ownership The allocation of responsibility for maintaining and reviewing specific code. unit test A test that verifies a relatively small program unit in isolation. integration test A test that verifies how multiple components work together. regression test A test that checks whether an existing feature or a previously fixed problem has regressed. property-based testing A testing method that verifies general properties across sets of generated inputs. mutation testing A method that introduces controlled program changes to check whether tests detect faults. mutant A program version produced by a mutation operation for tests to detect. mutation score The proportion of mutants killed by tests, calculated using denominator rules declared in advance. equivalent mutant A mutant whose behavior is equivalent to that of the original program within the semantic scope under discussion. fuzzing A testing method that explores program failures using many or varied inputs. test-driven development A development method in which tests express behavioral requirements and guide implementation and refactoring. test harness A test program that organizes inputs, executes the subject under test and collects results. test oracle The basis or mechanism for deciding whether an execution result meets expectations. static analysis Examining a target program's structure or semantics without running it. false positive A check reports a problem when the reported case is not actually an instance of the target problem. false negative A check fails to report an instance of the target problem that is actually present. prompt injection An attack in which untrusted content attempts to change a model's intended task or constraints. lethal trifecta In this course's risk analysis, the combination of access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and external communication. supply chain security Practices for managing risks introduced through dependencies, builds and delivery chains. sandbox escape A program breaks through its intended execution boundary and gains the ability to produce additional effects. attack surface The set of entry points that an attacker can reach and attempt to exploit. threat model An analysis describing assets, adversaries, boundaries and potential failure paths. inert payload A payload that only records behavior in the course-designated local mock environment and produces no real external effects. red team A testing role that finds and verifies system weaknesses within an authorized scope. hardening Changes that reduce risk by restricting permissions, reducing entry points and adding verification. evaluation Collecting and interpreting system performance under explicit tasks, environments and decision rules. evaluation quadruple In this course, the decomposition of an evaluation into a request, environment, stopping condition and scorer. benchmark A set of tasks and evaluation rules used to compare or track performance. data split An arrangement that partitions data by purpose into sets such as training, calibration and testing. data contamination Evaluation information enters the tested system's training or development process and compromises independence. cheating agent An agent that gains scores by exploiting flaws in an evaluation instead of completing the intended task. trajectory Evidence recording an agent's inputs, actions, tool results and final state in chronological order. scorer A component that converts execution evidence into scores or decisions using fixed rules. LLM-as-judge An evaluation approach that uses a language model to assess outputs against given criteria. judge calibration Comparing judge outputs with trusted annotations and adjusting or assessing decision rules. pass@k A metric for at least one success among several candidates, with the sampling and estimation rules declared. latency The time from initiation of a request until completion of the specified response. observability The ability to understand a system's internal behavior through logs, metrics and trajectories. regression gate A checkpoint requiring specified evaluations to continue meeting their conditions after a change. software factory An engineering concept that organizes requirements, generation, verification and delivery into a repeatable production process. runbook A document listing diagnosis, operation and verification steps for known operational situations. incident response The process of identifying, mitigating and recovering from service problems and recording evidence. postmortem A retrospective analysis of an incident's sequence, causes, impact and verification of improvements. idempotency The property that repeating an operation, such as a retried request, produces its effect only once. automated program repair A process in which a program generates candidate repairs and verifies them against explicit conditions. disclosure statement A statement recording sources, AI assistance or the absence of AI use. work record The single record for an assignment: the artifact, verification results, a short explanation and one AI-use note. AI-use note One short note per work record saying what AI assistance was used, for what, and how its output was checked; later items refer to it by ID. calibration Comparing predictions made in advance with measured results to adjust judgment. reflection A record explaining changes in learning, mistakes and subsequent improvements based on one's own evidence. reproducibility The property that others can obtain comparable results again using fixed inputs and procedures. confirmed The verdict that a review point holds, shown by evidence someone else can recheck: an input with its actual result, a diff line or an evidence line. falsifiable Stated specifically enough that runnable evidence could overturn it, as with a diagnosis that names a checkable condition. refuted The verdict that a review point does not hold, shown by runnable counter-evidence or by a contract or issue showing that the requirement it asserts does not exist. cannot tell The verdict when the available inputs cannot decide a review point; it must state what is missing and why. Record files write it as undetermined. independent review An actual examination of evidence by a session or person who did not implement the content under review. secure track The course assessment track that verifies the student's own learning outcomes through controlled individual assessment. open track The course assessment track that evaluates outcomes through artifacts and process evidence while allowing AI collaboration. equivalent alternative An arrangement that changes the activity or interaction format while preserving learning outcomes and assessment requirements. factsheet A record of external facts with a date, sources and evidence for individual claims.

docs.title: Agentic Software Engineering: Build, Verify, Evaluate
docs.text:
Agents generate. You verify, decide and explain.

Over twelve teaching weeks and an assessment week you learn to deliver changes in a real codebase with a coding agent, confirm that the agent got them right, and explain and modify your own work without an agent. The course is taught in English.

docs.title: How this course works
docs.text:
• Generate, then verify

    Every example shows both steps. A check you can rerun is evidence; an agent saying "done" is a claim.

  • Predict before you look

    Each class opens with a decision you can get wrong. Save your prediction, run a check that tells the answers apart, then revise.

  • Decide, don't regenerate

    When a candidate passes, accept it, narrow the task, recheck something specific or stop.

  • Explain it without the agent

    Two checkpoints and a project defense, 30 of 100 marks, are done without AI.

docs.title: Three lines of work
docs.text:
Six assignments, mostly in the first six weeks; four contributions to two real open-source repositories; and one term project, alone or in a pair, on a topic you choose.

Weeks Topics 1-4 Agent internals, context engineering, skills, and customizing your agent and repository 5-8 Agent-ready codebases, agentic code review, tests that notice a fault, security 9-12 Background agents, evaluating agents, AI-native teams, the software factory 13 Project expo and individual defenses

docs.title: Assessment at a glance
docs.text:
Component Marks When Term project: proposal, technical specification, alpha, final 20 Weeks 2, 4, 7, 12 Project defense, AI-off 15 Week 13 Four open-source contributions 30 Weeks 4, 8, 9, 12 Six assignments 15 Weeks 1-3, 5, 6, 10 CP1: AI-off diagnosis, test and repair 7.5 Week 6 CP2: AI-off code review and recovery reasoning 7.5 Week 11 Participation 5 All term

You pass with at least 60 overall and at least 15 of the 30 AI-off marks. The syllabus and the schedule say what is due each week.

docs.title: Capstone milestone rubric
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

This rubric is the marking contract for the individual project. The five milestones total 20 points: M0 2, M1 6, M2 6, M3 3 and M4 3. Each student submits one ci-dashboard work record and links each claim to an evidence ID. One evidence ID supports one criterion; repeating a citation never earns extra points. Optional features and extra integrations are not conditions for full marks.

The complete feature is not part of the project: you build it in your C2 open-source contribution, marked by the open-source contributions rubric.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines the evidence and point boundaries used by the teaching team for the five project milestones.

docs.title: Records
docs.text: The TA records the evidence IDs, revision and criterion score on the score sheet. The student keeps the work record with the submitted project.

docs.title: Review
docs.text: A second calibrated reviewer checks the evidence mapping, arithmetic and boundary rules before the project score is released. Appeals follow the assessment and appeals process.

docs.title: How to use the tables
docs.text: Award the points in a row only when the listed evidence is present, attributable to the submitted revision and verified. Scores are whole or half points, and each row lists every score it allows: full credit, the partial-credit values in its partial column, or zero. A row whose partial column names no value has no partial credit; score it at full credit or zero. Award zero when the required behaviour or evidence is missing. A score is not a prediction of effort and never depends on code volume, commit count or whether an assistant produced text. The teaching team records the rubric version and the evidence IDs on its score sheet.

docs.title: M0 — discovery and specification (2 points)
docs.text: Criterion Points Full credit Partial credit Zero Context and discovery 1 Two discovery activities identify a bounded need and constraints, separate observations from assumptions and freeze the discovery record; the context workshop traces a call path, compares two fixed-budget context packets, checks one permission boundary, and records the standard skill trigger test and tested MCP tool server. 0.5: the discovery record is usable but one context-workshop evidence class is missing, or the context evidence is complete but one discovery activity, observation/assumption separation or freeze decision is missing. No usable discovery or context evidence. Executable specification 0.5 The agreed small change has executable acceptance criteria, including normal, boundary and failure behaviour. No partial credit: criteria in which one important case cannot be executed or checked score 0. 0: no executable criteria. Traceability and scope 0.5 The work record connects discovery, criteria and the agreed change; the scope is small enough to finish. No partial credit: one unclear connection or scope decision scores 0. 0: the change and evidence cannot be identified.

docs.title: M1 — reliable change (6 points)
docs.text: Criterion Points Full credit Partial credit Zero Behaviour-preserving change 1 The reviewed change implements the M0 criteria, preserves existing callers and explains a bounded diff. 0.5: the change is bounded and partly verified, but one caller, criterion or explanation is incomplete. The change is not reviewable or breaks a required existing behaviour. Agent workflow design 0.5 The M1 agent-readiness scorecard records start and end observations and one measured blocker removed. Deleting or skipping tests, or turning off a gate, is not a removed blocker. This row takes only the scorecard evidence: both scorecards and the before-and-after observation of the removed blocker. It is not the eight-dimension assessment rubric's dimension of the same name. No partial credit: a scorecard missing attribution or a measured blocker scores 0. 0: no scorecard evidence, or the only "removed blocker" deletes or skips tests or turns off a gate. AGENTS.md and hook gate 0.5 At the submitted revision, the repository's AGENTS.md lists run and test commands that run as written through the launcher and at least three invariants that must not change, each with the test or check that protects it; one hook gate stops a deliberately bad change before a commit, with its failing and passing output linked. This row takes the AGENTS.md file, its command outputs and the hook's failing and passing output. When the removed blocker on the scorecard is the AGENTS.md or the hook, both rows can be earned: the scorecard row cites the scorecard's observation and this row cites the file and hook outputs. No partial credit: a context file whose commands fail as written, or a hook with no failing case shown, scores 0. 0: no AGENTS.md or no hook gate at the submitted revision, or the hook is turned off or bypassed. Tests and evaluation of the change 1.5 Regression checks, a surviving-mutant challenge with one property, and a reproducible fuzz input cover the acceptance criteria; failures identify the fault and the green run is reproducible. 0.5: feature checks run but mutant or fuzz evidence is missing. 1: all check classes run but one failure explanation or reproducibility link is missing. 0: checks are absent, falsified or unrelated to observable behaviour. Security repair 1.5 The supplied local attack is reproduced, the repair closes it, positive and negative regressions preserve allowed behaviour, and the instructor-side seed check reports CLOSED for every seed in the student's assigned variant. Any OPEN seed in that variant leaves this row below full credit. 0.5: the repair or one regression is present but the seed result is missing or OPEN. 1: the repair, regressions and CLOSED seed result are present but one boundary or explanation is incomplete. 0: the issue is ignored, the payload is used outside the local mock, or evidence is unsafe. Review and verification record 1 An independent review identifies a real risk or confirms the bounded change; the work record states what was checked, why it could fail and the observed result. 0.5: a review or verification record exists but omits the risk or expected result, or the record is causal but not reproducible. 0: no credible review or verification evidence.

docs.title: M2 — evaluation and operation (6 points)
docs.text: Criterion Points Full credit Partial credit Zero Evaluator 2 The evaluator declares request, environment, stop and score, has a fixed oracle and reproducible output, calibrates a judge on 30 human-labelled cases, runs a local regression gate, and includes error analysis of its limits. 0.5: a draft contract exists; 1: the evaluator runs but oracle or calibration is incomplete; 1.5: it is reproducible and calibrated but one required limit or local regression boundary is missing. The evaluator is absent, non-reproducible or uses an undisclosed moving target. Preview and incident recovery 2 A local preview uses synthetic data, and the incident drill records detection, bounded recovery and a post-recovery check. 0.5: only preview or recovery evidence is present. 1.5: both are present but one step or post-recovery check is missing. 0: no usable preview or recovery evidence. Freeze, evidence and explanation 2 The week-10 freeze and week-11 incident change are identified; the work record links revision, checks, observations and a short explanation. 0.5: the revision is identified but checks or observations are missing. 1.5: revision and checks are linked but one observation or explanation is missing. 0: the evidence cannot be tied to a revision.

docs.title: M3 — model audit verification (3 points)
docs.text:
The teaching team runs the model audit on the student's frozen revision. The number or severity of model findings does not determine the score; the rubric measures the quality of the student's verification evidence.

Criterion Points Full credit Partial credit Zero Runnable verification evidence 1 For the teaching team's model audit of the student's frozen revision, each finding is addressed with a runnable reproduction, counterexample or bounded unresolved result. 0.5: the evidence is useful but one step, input or revision is missing. 0: the verification cannot be rerun. Evidence supports the conclusion 1 The verification evidence supports the stated conclusion across the review's evaluation, security and maintenance checks; the student distinguishes a demonstrated result from an untested suspicion. 0.5: one conclusion or boundary is unsupported. 0: the student's conclusions are unsupported by the evidence or merely restate the model output. Self-check and uncertainty 1 The student adds one meaningful check of their own and records a no-finding or bounded limitation without presenting an unverified claim as confirmed. No partial credit: an unclear check or boundary scores 0. 0: no self-check or uncertainty boundary is recorded.

docs.title: M4 — repair and delivery (3 points)
docs.text: Criterion Points Full credit Partial credit Zero Review response 1.5 The student responds to each confirmed model-audit finding, links repair commits and reruns the relevant checks; disagreements are reasoned. 0.5: one confirmed finding has a response but its repair or rerun is missing. 1: most responses and reruns are complete but one is incomplete. 0: the review is ignored or the response cannot be verified. User-informed iteration 0.5 Three usability sessions scheduled across weeks 11–13 (or an approved equivalent) produce de-identified observations and a justified product change. No partial credit: incomplete sessions or an incomplete resulting change, even with the gap recorded, score 0. 0: no admissible user evidence or the evidence contains restricted material. Final product and demo 0.5 The final product, deployment evidence and demo show the agreed change on the submitted revision with synthetic data. No partial credit: a demo with one product or deployment check incomplete scores 0. 0: the final product or demo is not usable or is from another revision. Delivery record 0.5 The final work record lists the revision, checks, unresolved limitations and one AI-use note when applicable. No partial credit: a record with one required entry unclear scores 0. 0: no auditable delivery record.

docs.title: Evidence and boundaries
docs.text:
M0 and M4 live evidence must reference the teacher-checked consent and purpose record; students submit only de-identified material and the confirmation reference. A withdrawal removes the evidence and uses the approved equivalent route without lowering the score ceiling. A classroom rehearsal is not a participant session. Oral-defense marks, code lines, commit counts, rankings, awards and external-judge opinions never supply milestone points.

The teaching team records the project mark after reviewing the submitted evidence. Keep an unresolved or contradictory item pending; do not turn missing future work into zero by assumption.

docs.title: Term project
docs.text:
Build working software from scratch on a topic of your choice, using a coding agent in development and checking the work it produces. Choose a core scenario whose expected behaviour you can explain and test. The project develops your specification, workflow, verification, evaluation and security skills (LO2, LO3, LO5–LO8).

Work alone or with one other student. A two-person project has a correspondingly larger scope. Both members receive the same marks for the four milestones; each student takes and is marked on a separate defense. The milestones total 20 marks, and the individual defense is a separate 15 marks.

docs.title: Four milestones
docs.text:
Deadlines are Sunday at 23:59 in the due week. Use the linked templates as the body of your submission; link existing evidence rather than copying it into a second report.

Milestone Due Marks What to submit Proposal Week 2 2 What you will build, who it is for, the core scenario, and the agent's role in development. Technical specification Week 4 4 Requirements, key decisions with rejected alternatives, interfaces and data models, test strategy, and what is out of scope. Alpha and task backlog Week 7 6 A minimal path that runs end to end, the repository instruction file, one hook gate, and the remaining task backlog. Final Week 12 8 Working software, tests and their mutation result, one evaluation script, security-scan dispositions, and a README.

For each milestone, identify the submitted revision, link its artifacts and verification results, and explain any missing result or known limitation. Include one AI-use note for the work and reuse its ID as you carry the project forward. Submit through the published course submission channel and milestone assignment links.

docs.title: What engineering evidence means
docs.text:
An interface and a collection of features alone earn no milestone marks. The evidence must show what the software should do, how you constrained the agent, and how you checked whether the result was earned. Build this evidence as the project develops:

  • Specification: turn each requirement into an observable acceptance case, with normal, boundary and failure inputs. Explain why you chose a design and rejected an alternative; update the specification when new evidence changes the decision.
  • Instruction file and hook gate: give the agent the repository's conventions and verification commands. Demonstrate a bad change the gate blocks and a valid change it permits; disabling the gate does not establish correctness.
  • Tests and mutation result: preserve a regression that fails before a repair and passes after it. Record the mutation configuration, what was tested, and surviving faults; inspect a survivor and strengthen the test or explain the result's limit.
  • Evaluation script: fix its inputs, expected outcomes and denominator. Show a correct candidate and a deliberately wrong candidate so you can demonstrate that the check detects failure, rather than merely producing a favourable result.
  • Security-scan disposition: identify the scanned revision and scope. For each finding, record your reproduction or other evidence, the repair or reason it does not apply, and the rerun result. An unexplained clean summary is insufficient evidence.
  • README: provide reproducible setup, run and verification commands and the known limitations. Check those instructions against the final revision.

Keep generated changes small enough to inspect. Before accepting one, compare it against the specification, run the relevant checks, and explain what could still go wrong. Results must identify the revision and command that produced them; a predicted result or an unexecuted command is not a passing check.

docs.title: Expo and individual defense
docs.text:
The expo takes place in week 13 before the defenses and counts towards participation. Demonstrate the submitted software and the evidence supporting your main claims.

Each student then has a fifteen-minute defense without devices. The examiner changes one thing or plants one fault in your own code; you locate it, explain it, and decide what to do. Shared milestone marks do not replace your individual explanation. The syllabus defines the project and defense rules.

The four open-source contributions are a separate work stream.

docs.title: Assessment rubric
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Rubric version 0.9.3. This is an explicit English migration of the canonical eight-dimensional rubric. Each dimension has four bands: 1 Missing or untrustworthy, 2 Basic, 3 Professional, and 4 Exemplary. Scores depend on observable work and evidence, never a guess about whether writing or code was generated by AI.

Only the dimensions selected by an assignment count. They have equal weight unless the assignment explicitly provides reviewed positive weights for every selected dimension. Unselected dimensions do not enter the denominator. A grader records the rubric version, selected dimensions and either default equal weighting or the normalized assignment override with its source. Human items remain pending until actually assessed. The selected dimensions guide evidence review; the teaching team records the course mark in the teaching team's score sheet.

docs.title: Specification and acceptance criteria
docs.text:
1. No specification, or acceptance criteria cannot be executed or are unrelated to the need.
  2. Specification and acceptance criteria exist, but boundary cases or traceability to user needs are missing.
  3. Each feature has executable acceptance criteria traceable to real user research or approved equivalent discovery evidence, with boundary cases stated.
  4. Acceptance criteria cover exceptional paths and security constraints and are reused directly by the evaluator.

docs.title: Testing strategy
docs.text:
1. No tests, or assertions cover no observable behavior and cannot detect known defects.
  2. Unit tests exist, but the mutation score is below the threshold and there is no property-based testing.
  3. Tests precede agent implementation; the mutation threshold is met and key logic has property-based testing.
  4. The mutation score is substantially above the threshold; fuzzing or contracts are present, and test failure messages directly help locate the problem.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Scans were not run, or unresolved high-severity alerts or leaked secrets remain.
  2. Scans ran, but some alerts have no disposition record and lockfiles are incomplete.
  3. SAST, secret scanning and dependency audits have no remaining findings or each alert has a disposition record; lockfiles are complete.
  4. LLM features have injection probes and mitigations; permissions are minimized and explained.

docs.title: Review quality
docs.text:
1. No review of agent PRs, or the review merely repeats the diff.
  2. Review comments are general and identify no real defect.
  3. Review comments identify real defects and suggest corrections.
  4. Review systematically covers correctness, security and maintainability and records problems the compared review, such as an AI review, missed.

docs.title: Human verification evidence
docs.text:
1. A merged PR lacks a causal explanation, or its explanation contradicts the diff.
  2. The explanation says what changed but does not explain why or where it might fail.
  3. Every merged PR explains why the change was made, what might fail and what was personally verified.
  4. A new reader can reproduce the verification; the decision log records rejected alternatives and the reasons for rejecting them.

docs.title: Agent workflow design
docs.text:
1. No context files or configuration; the student cannot explain how the agent was used.
  2. Context files and configuration exist, but evaluation gates or cost records are missing.
  3. Context files, skills, hooks, permission policies and evaluation gates are evidenced; costs are recorded.
  4. A/B or cost comparisons informed workflow changes, and reusable team conventions exist.

docs.title: Process integrity
docs.text:
1. After the evidence-completion deadline, verification, explanation or the single AI-use note explicitly required by this assignment is still missing; the process cannot be checked.
  2. One AI-use note and some verification and explanation exist, but required evidence or applicable individual work records are incomplete.
  3. One record connects the work product, verification result, personal explanation and one AI-use note. Applicable work records match version history. Required trajectory fragments or approved alternative evidence are supplied only when the assignment explicitly requires them; a commit trailer on every commit and separate disclosure files are not required.
  4. A third party can audit process evidence and reproduce key decisions.

docs.title: Reflection and calibration
docs.text:
1. Reflection or calibration records are absent, or statements contradict observable submission evidence without explanation.
  2. Reflection is general; calibration records are incomplete.
  3. The gap between predictions and measurements narrows over the semester; reflection identifies specific personal mistakes.
  4. Reflection proposes verifiable improvements and carries them out in later milestones.

docs.title: Use the rubric to verify a change
docs.text: For a course-authored example, generate a small function from an acceptance criterion, then run its assertions through the course launcher (Week 0 setup). Keep the original failing case, the corrected result and your own explanation. Identify which published assignment dimensions this evidence supports and what is still missing. A passing example does not establish every rubric dimension. Use the assignment's allowed scaffold and published scope; optional extensions do not become conditions for full marks. The rubric does not change the course's assessment weights or pass gates.

docs.title: Project scoring and appeals
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

The project is individual: there is no contribution adjustment, and your project score is your own 0–20.

Your ci-dashboard project is scored individually across five milestones: M0 2, M1 6, M2 6, M3 3 and M4 3, for 20 points. The public project rubric defines the evidence, whole- or half-point partial credit and zero-credit boundaries. Your open-source contributions, C1 and C2, are scored with the contributions rubric and use the same review and appeals process.

The teaching team records the score from your submitted revision and evidence IDs. A second calibrated reviewer checks the evidence mapping, arithmetic and boundary decisions. Keep an unresolved or contradictory item pending while it is reviewed; missing future work is not silently turned into zero.

Appeals follow the assessment and appeals process. Submit the revision, evidence IDs, a short explanation of the disputed criterion and the specific check that supports your request. Do not include keys, raw participant material or private code.

The project score is not inferred from code volume, commit count, model-finding count, rankings, awards or oral-defense evidence. M3 measures runnable verification evidence, support for each conclusion, clear uncertainty boundaries and one self-check; the number or severity of model findings does not determine that score.

docs.title: Help with setup and learning
docs.text: Use Week 0 setup before your first agent session and the fallback checklist if you cannot start. Ask for help with account activation, devices, accessibility, a failed check or an unclear requirement. Students do not pay for agent seats or credit. The teaching team publishes current contact, office-hour, device-support and accessibility details before the first class.

docs.title: Prepare a useful help request
docs.text: Record the course version, exercise, operating system, command, expected result, observed result and smallest check you tried. Share a minimal synthetic example where possible. Inspect excerpts before sharing; include only information needed to reproduce the problem. Keep waiting, help and rework time in your existing work record. Seek support when blocked; there is no penalty for needing help or exceeding an estimate.

docs.title: Teaching contact and access
docs.text: The teaching team will publish its support channel, office hours and private routes for accessibility, assessment questions and appeals before class. Use the private route for individual circumstances and the public route for a question useful to other students.

docs.title: While waiting for help
docs.text: Read the conceptual material, predict outputs or trace a small example on paper. Label reasoning as reasoning and unexecuted work as unexecuted. When access is restored, run the required check and keep its result. Public formative feedback is separate from a formal assessment mark; an incomplete assessment remains missing until resolved.

docs.title: Course syllabus
docs.text: Read the course syllabus.

docs.title: Assessment and appeals
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Read the current syllabus for weights, passing conditions and equivalent resits. Each work record contains the artifact, verification, your own explanation and one AI-use note. Reuse evidence between a practice unit and its project milestone.

The two AI-off checks and individual defense establish independent ability. Project quality cannot substitute for the independent passing requirement. A future or missing assessment is not a zero and cannot establish a completed course result.

Receive feedback before the next related acceptance. If you disagree with a judgment, identify the criterion and evidence you want reconsidered and use the teaching team's published appeal route. Suspected inconsistency requires human examination and an opportunity to respond. No writing-style detector decides authorship or guilt.

The adopting teaching team supplies actual submission dates, reassessment appointments, approved accommodations and appeal contacts before teaching. Ask the team for these arrangements if they are not yet provided.

docs.title: CP1: individual diagnosis, test and repair
docs.text:
CP1 is a 30-minute, 10-point, individual, closed-book, AI-off paper in Week 5. It asks you to locate a reported defect in an unfamiliar ci-dashboard path, write a contract-based regression test, describe a minimal repair and protect other callers. The marking categories may be public so that the task is accessible and predictable.

The actual code excerpt, planted change, distinguishing input, line numbers, trigger observations and answer remain private teacher material. Public practice teaches the defect category and the verification method; it does not reuse a CP1 instance. The question shape may be public; the instance is not.

If the initial CP1 result is below 50%, one equivalent resit is available after feedback. It keeps the same learning outcomes, time and difficulty. The replacement is capped at 5/10, and the effective mark is the higher of the original and capped replacement. An approved invalid sitting is replaced without using the resit opportunity; a valid pass cannot be retaken for a higher mark. Both records remain. CP1 results do not change model access.

docs.title: CP2: individual unfamiliar-code review
docs.text:
CP2 is the Week 11 individual checkpoint. It lasts 30 minutes and is completed on paper, without AI, agents, devices or reference material. You review an unfamiliar code listing, identify evidence-backed defects, and give a bounded recovery and verification argument. The paper and answer sheet are collected at the end; project work cannot substitute for this individual evidence.

After feedback, an initial CP2 mark below 5/10 permits one equivalent resit with the same construct, timing and difficulty. The replacement mark is capped at 5/10 and the original attempt remains recorded; the effective mark is the higher of the original mark and the capped replacement mark. A technical failure or an approved accommodation failure is replaced by an equivalent sitting and does not consume the resit. Ask the teaching team for the published appointment and accessibility arrangements.

Request a review by naming the rubric point and the evidence on your script. A person reviews the evidence and gives you an opportunity to respond; no writing-style or authorship detector decides the mark. The teaching team publishes the review contact and response timetable before teaching.

docs.title: Oral defense
docs.text:
The individual oral defense is worth 20 points. Book a 15-minute slot in Week 13 or Week 14: 12 minutes are for your answers and 3 minutes are for the examiner to record the result. Bring your own work and work records. Complete the defense without AI.

The defense connects four domains: requirements and code paths; verification and evaluation; security and incident recovery; and a changed-input responsibility decision. LO3, LO6, LO7 and LO8 are required. It transfers your evidence across these domains rather than re-testing all nine learning outcomes one by one, and the project demonstration cannot replace it.

The explanation check asks what you changed, why you changed it, which inputs are most likely to fail, and what you verified yourself. Keep claims tied to the evidence in your work. If your first mark is below 50% of the defense (below 10/20), feedback is followed by one equivalent resit with the same outcomes, time and difficulty. The resit mark is capped at 50% of the defense (10/20), the effective mark is the higher of the original and capped resit marks, and both records remain.

A second calibrated examiner reviews a case near the threshold or a case with a scoring disagreement, or when you ask for a review. Recording audio or video is not a default requirement; any recording follows the published notice, permission and retention rules.

docs.title: Fallback checklist
docs.text:
Use this checklist if you cannot activate the supplied agent access, obtain the course materials or run an exercise. Follow the safety practices in Week 0 setup.

  1. Agent access is missing. Contact the teaching team through the course's published support channel. Do not buy a subscription or API credit to make up for missing course access. While waiting, predict the outputs of the primer's supplied candidate, repair it manually and label your work as manual. This keeps learning moving; it does not count as a real coding-agent session when an assignment explicitly requires one.
  2. A command or dependency fails. Keep the command, expected result and a short, inspected error excerpt. Check the exercise's prerequisites and ask for help. Record the operation as not executed until you can run it; do not invent output.
  3. You cannot establish the required workspace or network boundary. Stop execution. Trace the primer's checks on paper and mark them as reasoning, then request a supported environment. Do not grant wider permissions to get past the problem.
  4. An account, device or accessibility barrier prevents participation. Ask the teaching team for supported access or an approved equivalent arrangement. Keep the affected work pending; an access failure is not evidence of an incorrect algorithm.

Return to generation and verification when access is restored. Keep waiting, help and rework time in your existing work record so the course can plan support from actual use.

docs.title: From a plausible answer to checked work
docs.text: This course-authored example uses a deliberately faulty candidate. Follow Week 0 setup before running it.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
Explain the difference between a language model and an agent (LO1). Identify evidence that supports a generated answer (LO5). Describe why tools need a workspace boundary and a stop condition (LO2, LO7).

A language model produces a response from the context it receives. Fluent text can still be wrong. An agent adds a program around the model: observe, request, validate, call an allowed tool, inspect its result and decide whether to continue. The program owns permissions and stop conditions; a model request is never permission to read every file on your computer.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
Consider: “Given two integers, return the larger value; equal values are returned unchanged.” Before asking for a candidate, predict the outputs yourself. Use this request with your agent:

Write only a Python function larger_of_two(a, b). Inputs are integers (not booleans).
Return the greater input, or that same value when equal. Negative integers are valid.
No input(), printing, imports, Markdown or explanation.

For the first check, use the course's deliberately faulty candidate.py:

def larger_of_two(a, b):
    return a

Choose an input where the candidate and requirement disagree. Save these checks as check_generated.py; the expected values come from the requirement, not generated text.

from candidate import larger_of_two

assert larger_of_two(3, 7) == 7, "second input is larger"
assert larger_of_two(9, 4) == 9, "first input is larger"
assert larger_of_two(5, 5) == 5, "equal inputs"
assert larger_of_two(-8, -2) == -2, "negative inputs"
print("PASS: four specified cases")

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
1. Create week0-guided in your dedicated course directory. Put candidate.py and check_generated.py there. Predict which check fails first.
  2. Inspect both files, then run python3 check_generated.py from that directory. Expected: AssertionError: second input is larger. Keep the failed baseline.
  3. Add an assertion with an input you chose and a value derived from the requirement. Run it again; adding a check does not repair the candidate.
  4. Ask your supplied coding agent for a replacement using the request above. Inspect the proposed function before copying it to candidate.py. If access is unavailable, repair it yourself and label that work as manual; see fallbacks.
  5. Run the same checks again. A correct candidate prints PASS: four specified cases and exits successfully. If a check fails, decide whether the candidate or expected value is wrong. Keep that result as evidence and try a different input independently.

docs.title: Verify and explain
docs.text: Keep the candidate, failed baseline, check results and a brief explanation under one evidence ID. State which input exposed the defect and what check you added. Attach one AI-use note identifying actual agent use or manual repair. Four passing examples do not prove correctness for every integer. A model statement that its code works is not a test.

docs.title: Set up for the course
docs.text: Before week 1, prepare an agent, a code-hosting account and the course materials. Read the primer to practise generating a candidate and checking it. If access fails, use the fallback checklist and ask for help.

docs.title: Before the first class
docs.text:
1. Activate your coding-agent seat or credit. The teaching team will notify you before the course begins how the supplied access is provided and activated. Students do not pay for it. Check that you can sign in and ask the agent to explain a small function in your course directory. The tool should support instruction files, hooks, permission modes, MCP, subagents and readable session records.
  2. Prepare a code-hosting account. Check that you can sign in and create a course repository using the teaching team's submission instructions. For contributions, use the account and contribution rules of the assigned public repository; a permitted pseudonym or the course-hosted equivalent path is available.
  3. Get the course materials. Use the course checkout or student package supplied by the teaching team. Locate the schedule and the instructions for your current assignment. Check that Git and the language tools it requires work before asking the agent to change code. For Python exercises, check python3 --version and git --version; use Python 3.12. Read a repository's instructions before running its commands.

docs.title: Four required safety practices
docs.text:
Practice What it means 1. Run the agent in a dedicated directory or container. Start in a new directory or container that holds only this course's public materials and your current work. File access must stay inside that boundary. A directory alone is not isolation. 2. Keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment. Use a fresh environment with no credential mounts and no inherited credential variables. Do not delete credentials from your host; start a fresh environment that does not inherit them. 3. Keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs. Inspect what you are about to send, share or commit. If a key appears, stop sharing it, revoke it immediately with the provider and notify the teaching team. Example keys are always sk-EXAMPLE. 4. Disconnect injection demonstrations from external networks and connect only to local mock services. The demonstration runs offline and reaches only services on your own computer. If it needs an external destination or a real credential, stop and ask for help.

Check each practice yourself before you start. Run the commands in the environment where the agent will run. On Windows, run them in WSL or Git Bash.

Practice 1. From the directory where you will start the agent:

pwd
find . -type l -exec ls -l {} +

Expected: pwd prints your dedicated course directory, and no listed link points outside it. In a container, ls ~ also shows no files from your own home.

Practice 2. List the names of credential-like variables, never their values:

awk 'BEGIN{for(n in ENVIRON)if(tolower(n)~/token|key|secret|credential|password/)print n}'

Expected: no output, or only the variable your agent's own sign-in uses.

Practice 3. Before committing, search what is staged:

git diff --cached | grep -n -i -E 'sk-|token|secret'

Expected: no output, or only the placeholder sk-EXAMPLE. For any other line, read it and decide whether it is a real secret before committing. Read a prompt or a screenshot the same way before you send it.

Practice 4. Before running an injection demonstration, replace DEMO_DIR with the demonstration's directory named in that week's activity:

grep -rnE 'https?://|[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' DEMO_DIR

Expected: every reported destination is 127.0.0.1 or localhost. A bare hostname without a scheme is not caught by this check, so also read the demonstration's target list.

These checks apply to agent-generated code and commands as well as work you write yourself. Check a proposed command's scope before granting permission, then verify its result against an acceptance criterion. Keep the work product, verification results and a brief explanation with one AI-use note; share only the excerpts the assignment requires.

docs.title: Try a small request
docs.text: In your dedicated directory, write the requirement for a function that returns the larger of two integers. Predict a result for negative and equal inputs. Ask your agent for a candidate, inspect the code, then use the primer checks. A fluent response is a proposal; a check you can explain is evidence.

docs.title: course_llm: generate once, then verify
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

course_llm is the shared offline interface used by the course launcher. It returns text and tool-call requests; it never executes generated code or tools. Student programs send only a prompt through the launcher’s prompt-only IPC. The host-side broker applies the approved course configuration and keeps any credential on the host; the sandbox receives neither credentials nor provider connection details. Generated code and shell commands must be checked and run through the launcher.

Follow Week 0 setup for admission, launcher use and the approved access or replay route. This page deliberately documents the package contract, not host configuration.

docs.title: Start offline
docs.text:
The default scripted provider needs no network or credential:

uv run course-llm ping --provider fake --trace /tmp/course-ping.jsonl
uv run course-llm cost /tmp/course-ping.jsonl
uv run pytest src/course_llm -q

A successful ping prints OK without printing a response, configuration or request body. cost validates each trajectory line and prints USD <amount>. These commands create only synthetic evidence; remove temporary traces after checking them.

from course_llm import Client, FakeProvider, TracePolicy, Tracer
from course_llm.trajectory import validate_record
import json
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("/tmp/course-example.jsonl")
with Client(
    FakeProvider([{"content": "synthetic answer"}]), tracer=Tracer(path, TracePolicy())
) as client:
    response = client.chat([{"role": "user", "content": "synthetic question"}])
    assert response.content == "synthetic answer"  # Verify the generated result.
for line in path.read_text().splitlines():
    validate_record(json.loads(line))  # Verify the recorded evidence separately.

docs.title: Replay and the launcher boundary
docs.text:
Replay is an equal learning route when a hosted run is unavailable. Use the reviewed record and the launcher command supplied by Week 0; choose replay without explaining why. Write a prediction first, inspect the returned text, run the local checks, and record that the result came from replay. A replay is not a new model call.

A typical replay invocation has this shape; copy the concrete version, digest and reviewed record path from the setup page or the teaching team:

sh scripts/course-sandbox \
  --profile approved-hosted \
  --version VERSION \
  --digest DIGEST \
  --model replay \
  --replay-file REPLAY_FILE \
  --replay-digest REPLAY_DIGEST \
  --workspace example-work \
  -- python generate.py

The broker accepts a bounded prompt and returns text only. It rejects extra fields, direct URLs, credentials, tools, shell commands and requests that exceed the per-run limits. The sandbox cannot read the host broker’s configuration. Inspect the proposed result and run the verifier as a separate step; a generated answer never counts as its own verification.

docs.title: Public interface and tool calls
docs.text:
Client.chat(messages, tools=None, **opts) -> Response is synchronous and non-streaming. Response contains content, usage.input_tokens, usage.output_tokens, tool_calls and decimal cost_usd. Response.message() returns the assistant message needed for the next request. Close the client with with Client(...) or close().

Messages use {"role": "user", "content": "..."}. Supported roles are system, user, assistant and tool; every message must have string content. An assistant message containing only tool calls still has an explicit empty string. A tool definition is {"name": "read", "description": "...", "parameters": {"type": "object", ...}}. A tool request is {"id": "call-1", "name": "read", "arguments": {"path": "fixture.txt"}}. After a request, the caller validates the name, arguments and workspace permission before the launcher executes anything. Package tests use fixed tool results and perform no shell or file operations.

The scripted fake provider accepts a JSON/YAML script, a Python list or a callable. Script items can assert exact messages and tools before returning a fixed response. An exhausted script or failed assertion raises an error without echoing the hidden content. Fixed scripts make local checks reproducible and require no network.

docs.title: Budget and evidence
docs.text:
The launcher bounds prompt size, request count, output size and wall-clock time for each run. Budget also prevents a client from reserving more output than the run allows. A rejected reservation sends no request. A completed call records usage and status; an uncertain call is recorded as uncertain and is not silently retried. These are conservative local checks, not a promise about a remote bill.

Use the supplied FakeProvider or a reviewed replay in tests and ordinary offline work. Do not add another model route, call a provider directly, or put connection details in a student script. Any real route is selected by the host-side broker and documented in the central setup page.

docs.title: Minimal traces and filtering
docs.text:
TracePolicy() defaults to minimal. Each message, argument and tool result keeps only its state, encoded length and digest. An explicit redacted policy may retain fixed synthetic content; every string outside its allowlist is replaced in full, as are sensitive scalar values. Never build an allowlist dynamically from a user message or a model response.

The tracer always filters credential patterns, personal identifiers, long identifiers, course canaries and other registered sensitive values. Raw requests, responses and tool results are application data, not safe logs. Minimal trajectories cannot reconstruct a conversation, and a digest cannot recover the original value.

docs.title: JSONL contract
docs.text:
The canonical schema is evals/trajectory.schema.json. The package includes a byte-identical copy for offline validation. Each line represents one call, not a cumulative snapshot:

  • schema_version is "1"; run records a random id, sequence, model label, status, timestamp, trace policy and cost status.
  • steps records the input snapshot and returned assistant message. Only the returned step has this call’s usage and latency; other steps use null, which is not zero usage.
  • A missing value is distinct from a redacted value. Consumers must preserve that distinction.
  • Unknown cost is recorded as unknown and cannot be reported as a completed total.

validate_record checks the schema and state rules. It does not prove that a log is authentic or that a human has reviewed it. Keep only the minimum synthetic evidence needed to explain the work and run the local verifier again after any change.

docs.title: Safe log handling
docs.text: Keep traces in a controlled course workspace, restrict access, and delete temporary files and known copies after verification. Do not submit environment files, credentials, raw interviews, or full tool output. If private content appears, stop, remove the copy and use the course reporting route. Passing schema validation does not replace a privacy check or an explanation of what was verified.
